sections.heading: How 4GE1 is assessed, and what each paper rewards
paragraphs: Pearson's International GCSE Geography splits into a physical paper and a human paper, each with an options section where the centre chooses the topics, and a second section that tests something broader. The physical paper carries a fieldwork-style Geographical Investigation; the human paper carries a synoptic, resource-led question that pulls topics together. The two papers do not carry equal weight, and the human paper is both longer and worth more, which changes how revision time should be allocated in the final term.

The table below sets out the structure as the current specification describes it. Treat the durations and weightings as a planning guide and confirm them against the live 4GE1 specification on qualifications.pearson.com before you build a revision timetable on them, because Pearson revises specification documents between series and your child's centre will hold the version that applies. The structural point survives any revision: option breadth is chosen by the school, and the second section of each paper is where unprepared candidates lose the most.

What this means in practice is that two students at the same Abu Dhabi school can need completely different revision plans. A student entered for rivers and coasts has a different physical workload from one entered for coasts and hazards, and the synoptic question rewards a student who has read across the human options rather than one who has revised a single topic to perfection. The first job of a 4GE1 tutor is therefore administrative: establish which paper combination applies, then build backwards from the weightings rather than from the textbook order.

sections.heading: The evidence file: what the first six weeks should put in your hands
paragraphs: The reason to anchor geography tutoring on evidence is that geography improvement is slow to feel and fast to measure. A student can spend three weeks getting materially better at extended answers while still reporting that the subject feels hard, and a parent paying weekly has no way to tell the difference between progress and a pleasant hour. The answer is to make each week produce an artefact: something written, marked and dated that you can compare with the one from the week before.

The schedule below is the default for a student starting mid-course. It is not a promise about grades, and no tutor can promise one. It is a promise about documentation: if you reach week six and cannot see a coded paper, a case-study file and a tracker showing which command terms are still misread, then the sessions have not been run the way this page describes and you should say so. Families who ask for the file at week two get better sessions than families who ask at week ten, which is why we hand it over unasked.

The tracker is the part parents find most useful and tutors find most uncomfortable, because it makes stalling visible. If assess questions are still scoring half marks in week five, that is on the teaching plan, not on the student, and the plan changes. Abu Dhabi families are often paying for two or three subjects at once, and an evidence file is how you decide which one to keep funding and which one has done its job and can stop.

sections.heading: Where 4GE1 marks disappear, question type by question type
paragraphs: Low-tariff questions go wrong for mechanical reasons. A one or two-mark question asking the student to describe a pattern from a figure is marked on the figure, and a candidate who writes a correct general fact about rivers without touching the graph scores nothing. The fix is a habit rather than knowledge: quote a value, name a direction, give a unit. Students trained on this stop losing a handful of marks per paper within two or three sessions, which is often worth more than a month of content revision.

Mid-tariff explanation questions go wrong on sequencing. Explaining the formation of a spit, the downstream change in a river's gradient, or why a storm causes more deaths in one place than another all require a chain: this happens, which causes this, which produces that. Students who have learned the vocabulary but not the chain produce a paragraph of correct terms in the wrong order, and the mark scheme cannot credit it. Drawing the chain as four boxes before writing is the single most reliable repair we use, and it survives exam-hall pressure better than any mnemonic.

High-tariff assessment questions go wrong on judgement. Assess and evaluate require the student to weigh, not to list, and to reach a stated position supported by the evidence they have just given. The commonest Abu Dhabi script we see writes two strong paragraphs of description and then stops. Adding a short, explicit conclusion that answers the question in one sentence is worth more than another paragraph of detail, and it is the easiest change to make in the final month before a series.

The fourth failure is timing, and it is specific to the human paper. The longest extended answer sits at the end, which means a student who over-writes the option questions arrives at the highest-tariff question with eight minutes left. Timed practice is therefore not optional revision; it is the only way to find out whether the problem is knowledge or pacing. Many students described as weak at the synoptic question are simply arriving at it exhausted.

sections.heading: Case studies an Abu Dhabi 4GE1 student can genuinely use
paragraphs: Examiners do not award marks for geography that happens in Britain. They award marks for named, located, dated and accurately described places, and a student who has walked the Eastern Mangroves boardwalk or driven past the Sweihan solar field can describe those places with a level of detail that a borrowed Lake District example will never reach. This is the clearest advantage a UAE candidate has over the textbook, and almost nobody tells them to use it.

The mapping below pairs specification topics with UAE examples that are checkable, current and close enough to home that a student can add their own observation. Every one of them needs to be researched properly before it goes in an exam answer: a case study without a date, a figure or a named place is a general statement with ambition. The tutor's job is to insist on that discipline, supply the official sources worth citing, and then make the student write the card rather than receive it.

A practical warning about this approach. Local examples work in Section A option questions and in the synoptic question, but they do not excuse ignorance of the specification's required content. If the syllabus expects knowledge of a tropical storm and the UAE does not experience them, the student needs a tropical storm case study from somewhere that does. The aim is to replace vague borrowed examples with vivid local ones where the geography genuinely matches, not to answer every question with Abu Dhabi.

sections.heading: Fieldwork and the Geographical Investigation from an Abu Dhabi classroom
paragraphs: Paper 1 Section B asks about an enquiry: how a hypothesis is framed, how data is collected, how it is presented and analysed, and what went wrong with the method. The questions are not about a specific site, which is fortunate, because fieldwork provision varies widely between Abu Dhabi schools and some students arrive at the exam having done very little primary data collection at all. What the section actually tests is whether the student can think like someone who has collected data, and that is teachable without a coach trip.

The vocabulary is finite and that makes it high-value revision. Systematic, stratified and random sampling. Quantitative against qualitative data. Primary against secondary. Bipolar and Likert scales for environmental quality surveys. Pilot studies. Anomalies. Interquartile range, median, mode and the reasons to prefer one measure over another. A student who can define each of these and say when to use it has secured most of the section before touching a question, and this is drilled explicitly in sessions rather than hoped for.

Local context makes the practice concrete. A beach profile at Saadiyat, a pedestrian count on the Corniche, an environmental quality survey comparing two streets in Khalifa City, a land-use transect along a mainland arterial: each one is a plausible enquiry that an Abu Dhabi student can design on paper, critique for sampling bias, and use to answer an evaluation question. Designing an enquiry is also the fastest way to learn why evaluation marks exist, because the flaws in your own method are much easier to see than the flaws in a textbook's.

sections.heading: The Pearson calendar counted backwards from the exam
paragraphs: Every tutoring page in this market talks about exam preparation and almost none of them names a session, a deadline or a results date. That is strange, because the calendar is the thing that decides whether starting now is sensible or late. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE subjects are available in a May/June series and a November series each year, and the entry deadlines sit months before the papers. A family deciding in March whether to start geography tutoring is making a different decision from a family deciding in September.

The milestones below are the ones that actually constrain a plan, with the sourced Pearson facts attached. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and revises them, so every plan should be built against the live timetable page rather than against a date restated on a tutoring site, including this one.

Counted backwards, the practical reading is this. Technique change needs roughly six to eight weeks of weekly marked work to show up in a timed paper. Case-study recall needs longer, because it depends on spaced repetition rather than explanation. If your child's series is in May and it is currently February, both are available. If it is April, prioritise the synoptic question and timing, because those move fastest. If the series is November and it is now October, the honest advice is that an intensive block on the human paper will do more than an attempt to re-teach the physical options.

sections.heading: ADEK, equivalency, and the line a tutor must not cross
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi private schools are supervised by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which u.ae describes as supervising the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. ADEK is named by none of the competitor pages researched for this market, which is a strange omission on a page written for Abu Dhabi parents. Knowing the regulator matters practically: ADEK publishes inspection outcomes, and an inspection report tells you about a school's overall performance, not about whether your child's geography set is being prepared for the right 4GE1 option combination. Those are different questions and only the second one a tutor can help with.

Equivalency is the other regulatory thread Abu Dhabi families ask about, usually in Year 11 rather than Year 13 when it would be more useful. On the British track, the sourced requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not counted among the five, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. A competitor page currently ranking in this market states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the sourced rule. Equivalency is a ministry process; IB Gram neither performs it nor guarantees an outcome, and the ministry's own channel is where to verify it.

The honesty line on the work itself is simple and worth stating plainly, because this market contains providers who cross it. A tutor teaches, explains, models and gives feedback on work the student has produced. A tutor does not produce assessed material for a student, and any provider offering finished coursework is handing a family a malpractice risk rather than a service. On 4GE1 that means marking past-paper answers, correcting a case-study card the student wrote, and showing how an assess question is structured, never supplying the answer that gets submitted. That distinction is also what makes the evidence file meaningful: it only documents progress if the work in it is the student's own.

faqs.question: How much does an Edexcel IGCSE Geography 4GE1 tutor cost in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Market rates for qualified online IGCSE subject tutors in the UAE run roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, with specialists in the AED 200 to AED 450 band and budget options from AED 45 upwards. Those figures come from published provider pages and the Bestimate 2026 rate survey, not from us. In-home rates sit higher because they include travel. For IB Gram the rate depends on level, session length and how many weeks you book, so the trial lesson and a short consultation are where you get a number rather than a range.

faqs.question: Is 4GE1 the same qualification as the Cambridge IGCSE geography syllabus?
faqs.answer: No. 4GE1 is Pearson Edexcel's International GCSE in Geography; Cambridge International runs a separate geography qualification with its own code, paper structure and fieldwork expectations. Past papers are not interchangeable, and a student revising the wrong board practises question stems that will not appear. Abu Dhabi schools use both, sometimes within a short drive of each other, so the first thing we check is which board your child's centre entered. Look at the front of a past paper in their folder, or ask the head of department; the code is printed on it.

faqs.question: Can my child use UAE examples in 4GE1 answers, or do examiners expect British case studies?
faqs.answer: Examiners mark the geography, not the location. A named, located, dated UAE example described in real detail scores better than a vague Lake District example copied from a textbook. The Corniche breakwaters, the Eastern Mangroves, Liwa's date farming, the Al Ain aflaj and the national energy mix all map onto specification content. The condition is rigour: each case study needs a place name, a date, a figure and a source. Where the specification requires a phenomenon the UAE does not experience, such as a tropical storm, your child still needs an example from somewhere that does.

faqs.question: How many case studies does a 4GE1 candidate actually need to learn?
faqs.answer: Fewer than most students try to learn, and in far more detail. A workable target is two solid examples per option topic entered, each with a place name, a date, two or three figures and a clear link to the process being examined. Six well-built cards beat twenty half-remembered ones, because extended answers are marked on detail and judgement rather than breadth. We build the file in the student's own handwriting across four to six weeks and then test recall without the file open, which is the only honest check that it has transferred.

faqs.question: Does Paper 1 Section B test fieldwork my child's school never did?
faqs.answer: It tests whether your child can reason like someone who has collected data, not whether they visited a particular site. Fieldwork provision varies widely between Abu Dhabi schools, and students do reach the exam with limited primary data collection behind them. The section is still winnable, because its vocabulary is finite: sampling methods, data types, presentation choices, statistical measures and method evaluation. We drill those explicitly and then have the student design a local enquiry on paper, such as a Corniche pedestrian count, so the evaluation questions stop being abstract.

faqs.question: My daughter writes long geography answers but keeps scoring five out of eight. What is going wrong?
faqs.answer: Almost always judgement rather than knowledge. Eight-mark questions using assess or evaluate require the student to weigh competing points and state a position; a long answer that describes two factors well, with no weighing and no conclusion, caps around the middle of the band. The repair is short and reliable: a four-box chain planned before writing, then one explicit closing sentence that answers the question asked. A marked paper will show this immediately, which is why the trial includes a diagnostic section coded by cause of lost mark.

faqs.question: Which 4GE1 topics do Abu Dhabi students tend to find hardest?
faqs.answer: Three recur. River and coastal landform sequencing, because students learn the vocabulary without the order of processes. Hazardous environments, because answers conflate the size of an event with its human impact instead of separating physical magnitude from vulnerability. And the extended synoptic question on the human paper, which is as much a timing problem as a content one: students over-write the option questions and reach the highest-tariff answer with minutes to spare. All three are visible on a timed past paper, which is where any plan should start.

faqs.question: Do you send a geography tutor to our villa in Khalifa City or Al Raha?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi, and home tutoring is a service we provide only in India. Every lesson described on this page is one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. For 4GE1 specifically the online format is an advantage rather than a compromise: your child is matched to a tutor who has actually taught this specification and marked its extended answers, instead of whoever happens to live within a short drive of Khalifa City, and the hour is spent teaching rather than travelling.

faqs.question: When should a Year 11 student in Abu Dhabi start 4GE1 revision properly?
faqs.answer: Technique change needs roughly six to eight weeks of weekly marked work before it shows up in a timed paper, and case-study recall needs longer because it depends on spaced repetition. Counting backwards from a May or June series, that puts a sensible start somewhere in the first term of Year 11 for recall and no later than February for technique. Starting in April is not pointless, but the plan narrows to timing and the synoptic question. Confirm your child's series and the live Pearson timetable before building any schedule on these intervals.

faqs.question: Does geography count towards UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: On the British track, the sourced requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at E or above or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. Geography can sit inside either count as an accredited subject. One page currently ranking for UAE tutoring queries states six IGCSE subjects are required, which does not match the sourced rule. Equivalency is a ministry process; verify the current requirements through the ministry's own channel before relying on them.

faqs.question: Can a tutor mark my child's 4GE1 past papers against the official mark scheme?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is most of what the service is. Pearson publishes mark schemes for past series, and a tutor marks against the published scheme rather than against an impression. What we will not do is reproduce or distribute Pearson's documents as downloads; they are referenced and linked to their official source instead. Marked answers come back with codes naming the cause of each lost mark, so a parent can compare week three against week one without needing to understand the geography themselves.

faqs.question: How do sessions work around ADEK school hours and Abu Dhabi bridge traffic?
faqs.answer: The reason online delivery works here is that it removes the commute from both ends of the lesson. School finish times differ across the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor and the newer mainland communities, and bridge traffic makes a 4pm start unreliable for anyone crossing. Most Al Reem and Saadiyat families settle on 5.30pm or later; Khalifa City families often take 6pm. Slots are agreed in Gulf Standard Time and can be moved by the week, which matters in a city where after-school sport and sibling schedules collide constantly.

faqs.question: Will the tutor help with a geography assignment my child's school has set?
faqs.answer: A tutor teaches the skill the assignment is testing, reviews what your child has written and explains where the marks sit. A tutor does not produce assessed material on a student's behalf, and any provider offering finished coursework is selling a malpractice risk rather than a service. In practice that means working through a planning structure, modelling an answer on a different question, correcting a case-study card the student wrote, and marking a draft with written feedback. What gets submitted stays your child's own work, which is also what makes the evidence file worth reading.

faqs.question: Can our 4GE1 sessions move to post-Iftar slots during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and we expect to be asked. School hours shorten during Ramadan, energy levels shift, and an afternoon slot that worked in January is often the wrong hour entirely. Families commonly move to a later evening session after Iftar, or to a shorter, more frequent pattern. Because delivery is online and tutors are scheduled rather than driven to a location, changing the slot is an administrative matter rather than a renegotiation. The UAE academic calendar and the exam series are both factored into the plan at the start for this reason.

faqs.question: Is there a free trial lesson before we commit to weekly 4GE1 sessions?
faqs.answer: Yes: one lesson per student, with no card details taken and nothing to cancel if you do not continue. The trial is a working session rather than a sales call. Your child answers one section of a past 4GE1 paper, the tutor marks it against the published scheme and codes each lost mark by cause, and you receive that coded page whether or not you book. If the tutor is not the right fit you can ask for a different one, and if the honest answer is that tutoring is not what your child needs, we will say so.

intro.heading: History is not a memory subject, and that is why strong students stall
paragraphs: The students who struggle most with Edexcel IGCSE History are rarely the ones who have not read the book. They are the ones who have, and who then write everything they know in answer to a question that asked for something narrower. 4HI1 rewards a small set of trained moves: reading a source for what its origin and purpose reveal rather than what it says, supporting an inference with a quotation, explaining consequences in a chain, and reaching a judgement in a breadth essay instead of parading two sides. None of those moves is intuitive and none is taught by reading more.

An Edexcel IGCSE History 4HI1 tutor in Abu Dhabi is therefore most valuable in the margin between content and performance. We begin by looking at a marked answer, because the diagnosis is almost always visible there. A script that scores well on short recall and badly on the twelve or sixteen-mark questions has a structure problem. A script that scores well on the depth study and loses the source section has a provenance problem. A script that fades in the final third has a pacing problem. These three need different lesson plans and are routinely treated as the same thing: more revision.

The specification detail matters in Abu Dhabi more than it would in a single-system city. Pearson's 4HI1 lets each centre choose its depth studies and its breadth study, so two students living in the same Khalifa City compound can be sitting entirely different papers. Germany, Russia, the USA, India under colonial rule, the development of medicine, South Africa, superpower relations and the Middle East all appear as options across the emirate's British-curriculum schools. We confirm which combination applies from your child's own exercise book before planning anything, and we confirm the board, because Cambridge runs a separate history qualification that is not interchangeable.

What a session actually fixes is worth describing concretely, because history tutoring is sold vaguely across this market. In a typical hour your child writes one timed answer, the tutor marks it against the published Pearson scheme, and the lesson is spent on the specific reason marks were withheld: an inference stated without support, a source answered on content alone, a consequence asserted rather than explained, a conclusion that repeats the introduction. The student then rewrites the same question type the following week. That loop, repeated six to eight times, is what moves a mid-band essay mark, and it is observable from the marked work rather than inferred from how the hour felt.

Delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video, and that is a deliberate choice rather than a limitation. The emirate has excellent history teaching in places and very little of it available privately for a specific option combination. A student entered for the Middle East breadth study needs a tutor who has taught that option, not the nearest available humanities graduate, and the pool of people who have taught it does not cluster conveniently around Al Reem or Al Shamkha. Working over video also removes the drive, which in a city split by bridges is often the difference between a session happening at 5pm and not happening at all.

programmes.description: The common next step in the emirate's British-curriculum schools. A-Level history raises the demand on historiography, source evaluation at length and independent coursework, and assumes a student can already build an argument. The 4HI1 source section is the direct ancestor of the A-Level document paper, which is why technique learned at IGCSE repays itself twice.
programmes.countryNote: On the British route to UAE equivalency the sourced requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. History counts as an accredited subject in either column. Check the current wording with the ministry before you plan around it.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme History
programmes.description: The alternative post-16 route for families who move between the British and IB sectors mid-phase, which happens often in Abu Dhabi because the two sit side by side. DP history keeps the source paper and adds an internal assessment requiring an independent historical investigation, so 4HI1 provenance training transfers directly rather than being set aside.
programmes.countryNote: We map a student's 4HI1 holdings against the DP history syllabus before Year 12 opens, so the summer is spent on genuine gaps such as historiography and the research question, not on re-covering twentieth-century content the student already holds securely from the depth studies.

abu-dhabi/edexcel-igcse-history-4hi1-tut.subjectsIntro: 4HI1 is built from named options, and your child's centre selects them. Match the list below against their option sheet before revising anything: the single most expensive mistake in this subject is three weeks spent on an option the school did not enter.

subjects.name: Germany: development of dictatorship, 1918-45
subjects.description: Weimar instability, the Nazi rise to power, consolidation, the police state, the economy and the war years. Marks go missing on the consolidation questions, where students narrate events in order instead of explaining why each step removed a specific constraint on Hitler's power.

subjects.name: Russia and the Soviet Union, 1905-24
subjects.description: Tsarist decline, 1905, the two 1917 revolutions, the civil war and early Bolshevik rule. Chronology is the trap: students conflate February and October, and answers about the Provisional Government lose marks for attributing to it decisions it never made.

subjects.name: The USA, 1918-41
subjects.description: The boom, prohibition, immigration and intolerance, the crash, the Depression and the New Deal. Strong answers separate the causes of the boom from the causes of the crash rather than treating one as the mirror of the other, and they quantify rather than describe the Depression.

subjects.name: Colonial rule and the nationalist challenge in India, 1919-47
subjects.description: Amritsar, non-cooperation, civil disobedience, the Second World War, partition and independence. Popular in Abu Dhabi schools with large South Asian cohorts, and the option where students most often substitute family-held narrative for the specification's named events and dates.

subjects.name: Changes in medicine, c1848-c1948
subjects.description: Anaesthetics, antiseptics, germ theory, public health, surgery and the founding of state healthcare. A development study rather than a political one, so the examined skill is change and continuity over a century, which demands a different essay shape from the dictatorship options.

subjects.name: South Africa: union to the end of apartheid, 1948-94
subjects.description: Apartheid legislation, resistance, Sharpeville, Soweto, international pressure and negotiated transition. Students handle the legislation well and the resistance movements poorly, usually because the organisations and their shifting strategies are learned as a list of names.

subjects.name: A world divided: superpower relations, 1943-72
subjects.description: Wartime conferences, the division of Europe, Berlin, the arms race, Cuba, Vietnam and detente. The crisis questions reward precise sequencing of days and decisions, which is exactly the detail that disappears when a student revises from a summary sheet.

subjects.name: The origins and course of the First World War, 1905-18
subjects.description: The source-led half of the second paper on many Abu Dhabi option lists. Here the examined skill is provenance: what an author's position, date and intended audience let you conclude, and how far two sources together support a stated claim.

subjects.name: The changing nature of warfare, 1919-1991
subjects.description: Technology, tactics, civilian impact and the experience of war across seven decades. Breadth essays are marked on argued change over time, so the failure mode is a well-written account of two wars with no thesis about what actually changed between them.

subjects.name: The Middle East: conflict, crisis and change, 1917-2012
subjects.description: Mandates, the creation of Israel, the Arab-Israeli wars, oil, the Gulf conflicts and attempted settlements. Chosen by several schools in the emirate. Students arrive with strong contextual awareness and must learn to write it as evidenced argument with dates rather than as inherited position.

subjects.name: China: conflict, crisis and change, 1900-89
subjects.description: The end of empire, warlords, the republic, civil war, Mao's China and reform. The long chronology is the difficulty: students who have not built a decade-by-decade spine cannot answer a change-over-time question without drifting into one or two familiar episodes.

subjects.name: Source and essay skills across both papers
subjects.description: Inference with support, utility judged on nature, origin and purpose, explanation written as consequence chains, and the judged breadth essay. These four moves carry most of the mark separation on 4HI1 and are the backbone of every weekly session.

regions.note: High-rise living with a growing school presence and genuinely unpredictable bridge traffic. Later slots work better; 5.45pm onwards is common. Several Al Reem enquiries involve a student who changed school mid-course and inherited an option list they had not started.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island

regions.name: Khalifa City

regions.note: Mainland and Dubai-side communities with long bus journeys in both directions. For these families the case for online lessons is arithmetic: the round trip to a tutor would cost more time than the lesson itself.

sections.heading: What 4HI1 asks a student to do that reading the textbook will not teach
paragraphs: Edexcel IGCSE History tests four trained behaviours, and a student can know the period thoroughly while performing none of them. The first is inference: stating something a source implies but does not say, then supporting it with a short quotation from that source. The second is utility, which is judged on the nature, origin and purpose of a document rather than on whether its content is accurate. The third is explanation written as a chain of consequences instead of a list of factors. The fourth is judgement in an extended essay, which requires a position stated early and sustained, not a balanced survey that declines to conclude.

None of those four is the same as knowing more. A student who has read widely and writes everything they know in answer to a narrow question is being penalised for relevance, not rewarded for effort, and the feedback loop in a busy classroom rarely makes that clear. This is the specific gap that private sessions close, because closing it needs one-to-one marking of the student's own writing, repeated, with the reason for each withheld mark named. It does not need a second course of content delivery, which is what most tutoring in this market quietly supplies.

The practical consequence is that the first session should not be a lesson. It should be a diagnostic: your child writes one source question and one extended answer under time, the tutor marks both against the published Pearson scheme, and the two scripts are read together to establish which of the four behaviours is missing. In a surprising number of cases three are present and one is absent, which means the plan is narrow and fast rather than broad and long. Establishing that before you commit to months of weekly sessions is simply better buying.
bullets: Inference: say what the source implies, then quote the words that imply it
Utility: argue from nature, origin and purpose, not from accuracy
Explanation: write consequence chains, not factor lists
Judgement: state a position early and hold it to the conclusion

sections.heading: The two papers, and why your neighbour's child is sitting a different exam
paragraphs: 4HI1 is an options qualification. Paper 1 carries depth studies chosen by the centre from a published list; Paper 2 pairs a source-based historical investigation with a breadth study in change, both also chosen. The result is that two Year 11 students in the same Al Raha compound can share a bus and sit almost nothing in common. Parents discover this at the worst moment, usually when a revision guide bought on a friend's recommendation turns out to cover the wrong option entirely.

The table below sets out the structure and the options most commonly entered by British-curriculum schools in the emirate. Treat the shape as a planning guide and confirm paper timings and weightings against the live 4HI1 specification on qualifications.pearson.com, because Pearson revises specification documents between series and your child's centre holds the version that applies to them. What does not change is the principle: find the option names first, then build the plan.

Knowing the combination also tells you where the risk sits. A centre entering two political depth studies plus the warfare breadth study has given its students a coherent twentieth-century spine, and revision can be shared across papers. A centre pairing a development study such as medicine with a political depth study has given them two different essay shapes to master, which needs explicit teaching rather than assumed transfer. The Middle East breadth study brings its own demand: enormous contextual familiarity among students in this region, and a corresponding need to convert that familiarity into dated, evidenced argument.

sections.heading: The source questions: what the mark scheme is actually asking for
paragraphs: Source questions are where the clearest, fastest gains sit in 4HI1, because they are marked on a method rather than on the breadth of a student's reading. The method is learnable in a handful of sessions and then applies to any unseen document. What stops students is a reasonable but wrong instinct: they read the source for information, find something true, and write about whether it is correct. The mark scheme is interested in something else entirely, which is what the existence of this particular document, written by this person, at this moment, for this audience, allows a historian to conclude.

Inference questions want a claim the source supports without stating, immediately followed by the words that support it. Students lose marks by paraphrasing the source instead of inferring from it, or by inferring well and leaving the quotation out. Utility questions want a judgement built from nature, origin and purpose, with content used as evidence rather than as the whole answer, and they want the limitation named as specifically as the strength. Cross-referencing questions want the two sources set against each other on a particular claim, not summarised in turn.

The table below is the frame we teach, and students can apply it independently within three or four sessions. The reason it works is that it converts a judgement task into a procedure, which is what a fifteen-year-old needs under exam conditions. The procedure does not substitute for knowing the period, because contextual knowledge is what allows a student to say why a document from 1917 says what it says. But it does stop the most common failure, which is a page of accurate content that answers a question the paper did not ask.

sections.heading: The depth-study and breadth essays: where the top bands are actually lost
paragraphs: Extended history answers fail in three recognisable ways, and the marked scripts from Abu Dhabi students are no different from anywhere else in this. The first is narrative drift: the student tells the story of the period in sequence, with everything correct and nothing argued. The mark scheme cannot credit a chronicle, however accurate, because the question asked why or how far rather than what happened. The repair is structural and quick to teach: every paragraph opens with a claim that answers the question and then uses evidence to support the claim, in that order.

The second is the balanced survey that refuses to decide. Students are often taught, correctly, to consider more than one side, and then conclude with a sentence saying both factors mattered. On a how-far question that caps the mark, because the question explicitly asks for a weighting. A judged conclusion does not need to be bold; it needs to be a decision, with a reason attached, that follows from what the essay has already said. Writing the conclusion first, as a single sentence, and then building the essay towards it is the technique that reliably fixes this.

The third is the breadth essay's particular trap: writing well about two episodes instead of arguing about change across the whole period. The changing nature of warfare, the Middle East between 1917 and 2012, or China across the twentieth century all require a thesis about the shape of change, with episodes used as evidence for that shape. A student who knows two conflicts in depth and the rest thinly will produce a strong-sounding answer that sits in the middle of the mark range. Building a decade-by-decade spine, tested without notes, is unglamorous work and it moves this mark more than anything else we do.

All three failures show up on a timed script and none of them shows up in conversation. That is the argument for making every session produce a written, marked, dated answer: it is the only way for a parent in Abu Dhabi, who is not a historian and should not have to be, to tell whether the essay mark is moving or whether the hour has merely been pleasant.

sections.heading: The India and Middle East options: what students in this region get right and wrong
paragraphs: Two 4HI1 options carry a particular pattern in the UAE. Colonial rule and the nationalist challenge in India is a common choice in Abu Dhabi schools with large South Asian cohorts, and the Middle East breadth study appears on several option lists across the emirate. In both cases students arrive with far more context than their counterparts in a British classroom would have: family memory, community narrative, history that is discussed at home rather than only encountered in a textbook. That is an advantage, and it is also the source of a specific and avoidable loss of marks.

The examined requirement is evidenced argument: named events, dates, figures, and attribution of decisions to the people and institutions that made them. Inherited narrative tends to be strong on significance and weak on sequence. A student may write with real conviction about partition and still misplace the Cabinet Mission, or argue the consequences of a conflict without being able to date it. On the Middle East option the same pattern appears around the mandates, the 1947 partition plan, the 1956, 1967 and 1973 wars, and the later settlement attempts: fluent on meaning, approximate on chronology.

The work, then, is conversion rather than correction. Sessions on these options take what the student already understands and attach the specification's apparatus to it: a dated spine, the named organisations and their shifting strategies, the documents that are routinely set as sources, and a vocabulary that keeps the answer historical rather than argumentative. Handled this way, a student's background becomes exactly the asset it should be, because the detail is memorable to them in a way that a borrowed European example never is. Handled badly, it produces confident essays in the middle of the mark range.
bullets: Build a dated spine before writing anything on either option
Attribute decisions to named bodies, not to nations in general
Keep the register historical: evidenced claims, not inherited position
Use the documents the specification actually sets, and read their attribution lines

sections.heading: What history tutoring costs in Abu Dhabi, and what moves the number
paragraphs: Most tutoring pages in this market publish no price. The published UAE market bands, from provider pages and the Bestimate 2026 rate survey, run roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour at the budget end, AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180 to AED 500 for an in-home visit including travel, and AED 200 to AED 450 or above for an IB or IGCSE specialist. Those are market figures attributed to the sources that published them, not a price list for this page; IB Gram's own rate depends on the booking and is given in a consultation after the trial.

More useful than a band is knowing what moves a quote, because that is what you can negotiate or avoid. The table below lists the variables that actually change a history tutoring rate in this emirate and what each one is worth asking about. Two of them are worth flagging up front: travel, which inflates an in-home rate without buying any teaching, and exam-season timing, when demand concentrates into a few weeks and every provider's availability tightens at once.

There is also a value question separate from price. A student losing marks only on the source section needs a short clinic, not a two-year weekly slot, and a provider who sells the longer commitment anyway is selling you something you do not need. A student with no chronological spine three months before a breadth essay needs more hours than the trial will make comfortable to admit. The diagnostic exists partly so the recommendation can be honest in both directions, including the direction where the recommendation is fewer sessions.

sections.heading: Chronology, terminology and the ninety-minute memory problem
paragraphs: History has a storage problem that other IGCSE subjects do not. A mathematics student who understands a method can reconstruct it; a history student who has forgotten the date of the Enabling Act or the order of the 1917 revolutions cannot reconstruct anything, and under exam pressure the gap is unrecoverable. This is why revision strategy in history is not a matter of effort but of structure, and why a student who has read the textbook three times can still freeze in front of a twelve-mark question.

The structure we build is a spine: a decade-by-decade or event-by-event skeleton for each option, written by the student, tested without notes, and expanded only once the skeleton is secure. Spaced recall over several weeks is what moves this; a single long revision session does not, however sincere. For the breadth options the spine is the whole battle, because a change-over-time essay is literally an argument about the shape of the spine. For depth studies the spine is narrower and denser, and the test is whether the student can place any named event within a year without hesitating.

Terminology sits alongside it and is routinely neglected. Students lose marks writing about dictatorship, nationalism, mandate, detente, apartheid or total war without using the words with precision, and examiners reward precise historical vocabulary because it demonstrates conceptual control. We keep a running glossary in the student's own words, checked each session, which takes three minutes a week and is one of the cheapest mark gains in the subject. The glossary and the spine together are the reason a session ends with something written down rather than with a feeling that things are clearer.
bullets: A written spine per option, tested without notes before content is added
Spaced recall across weeks rather than one long revision block

Timed practice from the start, because recall under pressure is the real test

sections.heading: Permits, ADEK ethics rules and verifying a history tutor in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is a permitted activity with conditions, and a family hiring a tutor in Abu Dhabi is entitled to know what those conditions are. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years through MoHRE, whose own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged fifteen to eighteen, and university students. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule has been published, so no figure should be quoted to you by anyone.

Abu Dhabi adds a professional-ethics layer. ADEK's rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct has been reported as carrying a comparable restriction. Treat that as press-reported rather than quoted wording and verify it against the current ADEK policy document if it matters to your decision. The practical implication is clear enough: a family should not arrange for a child's own classroom teacher to tutor them privately, and any provider who offers that arrangement is not protecting you.

Separately, a tutoring business with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal entity from an individual tutor and requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute. IB Gram operates no premises in the UAE and holds no regulator approval, accreditation or licence from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and you should be sceptical of any tutoring page in this market that implies otherwise. What we do hold is a tutor pool, a marking standard and a stated delivery model: one-to-one lessons over live video. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; that is a service offered only in India.

process.title: Send the option names, not just the subject
process.description: We ask for the board, the code, both depth studies, the investigation topic and the breadth study by name. On an options qualification this single message prevents the most common waste in the subject, which is weeks of revision aimed at a paper your child will never sit.

process.title: Write two answers in the trial
process.description: One source question and one extended answer, both under time. The tutor marks them against the published Pearson scheme and identifies which of the four examined behaviours is missing. You receive both marked scripts and the written diagnosis whether or not you go on to book.

process.title: Set a narrow first target
process.description: We name one question type to move first and agree a weekly slot in Gulf Standard Time that fits the school run. No grade is promised at this stage or any other, and a provider who promises one is telling you something about themselves rather than about your child.

process.title: Write, mark, rewrite, each week
process.description: Every session is paired with a timed answer marked in writing before the next. The student rewrites the same question type a week later so the comparison is like for like. The spine and the glossary grow in their handwriting, which is what makes recall survive the exam hall.

process.title: Review the scripts, then decide
process.description: At six weeks and each term the trial scripts come back out for direct comparison. If the targeted question type has not moved, the plan changes or the tutor does. Pausing, switching or stopping is normal and costs nothing, and a short course that has done its job should end.

whyPoints.title: Options confirmed before planning
whyPoints.description: Two 4HI1 students on the same street can sit different papers. We establish the exact option combination from your child's own materials, because a revision guide bought on a neighbour's recommendation is the commonest wasted purchase in this subject.

whyPoints.title: Technique split by question type
whyPoints.description: Sessions rotate through inference, utility, cross-referencing, explanation and the judged essay rather than through periods. That ordering exists because the mark separation in 4HI1 sits in those behaviours, and because content is what the school is already delivering.

whyPoints.title: Written marking you can audit
whyPoints.description: Timed answers come back marked against the published scheme with the reason for each withheld mark named. A parent who is not a historian can still compare week six with week one, which is the whole point of putting it in writing.

whyPoints.title: Regional context treated as an asset
whyPoints.description: On the India and Middle East options, students in this region arrive with real contextual depth. Sessions convert that into dated, attributed, evidenced argument rather than leaving it as inherited narrative, which is where the marks actually sit.

whyPoints.title: Delivery and permits stated openly
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram runs no UAE premises, holds no regulator approval, and does not provide home visits anywhere in the UAE. The MoHRE permit position is set out on this page so you can check a tutor rather than trust a badge.

whyPoints.title: A recommendation that can be smaller
whyPoints.description: If the marked scripts say your child needs a six-week source clinic, that is what we will suggest, not a two-year slot. The diagnostic is there so the advice can run in both directions, including towards fewer sessions than you expected to buy.

faqs.question: How much does an Edexcel IGCSE History 4HI1 tutor cost in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published UAE market bands put qualified online subject tutors at roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 or more, and budget options from around AED 45. In-home rates run AED 180 to AED 500 because they carry travel. Those figures are attributed to provider pages and the Bestimate 2026 rate survey rather than quoted as ours. What history costs specifically depends on whether written marking of timed essays is included, which is the single biggest variable in a quote. You get a figure for IB Gram in a consultation after the trial lesson.

faqs.question: Which 4HI1 depth studies has my child's Abu Dhabi school entered?
faqs.answer: Only the school can tell you definitively, and it is worth asking in writing. The quickest check at home is the front cover of a past paper in your child's folder, or the contents page of the revision guide the department recommended. Across British-curriculum schools in the emirate the common depth studies are Germany 1918-45, Russia 1905-24, the USA 1918-41, India 1919-47, changes in medicine, South Africa and superpower relations. We ask for the names before the first lesson, because planning against the wrong option wastes weeks that cannot be recovered later.

faqs.question: Why does my son lose marks on source questions when his knowledge is strong?
faqs.answer: Because source questions are not marked on knowledge. Utility is judged on the nature, origin and purpose of the document, and inference is judged on whether a claim the source implies has been stated and then supported with a quotation. A student who reads a source for information and writes about whether it is accurate has answered a different question. The fix is procedural and usually lands within three or four sessions, which is why a source clinic is often a short course rather than a long commitment. A marked script will show the pattern immediately.

faqs.question: What does nature, origin and purpose actually mean in a 4HI1 source answer?
faqs.answer: Nature is what kind of document it is: a speech, a cartoon, a private letter, an official report. Origin is who produced it and when, including the position they held at that moment. Purpose is what they were trying to achieve by producing it, and for whom. A strong utility answer uses all three to decide how far the source helps a historian investigate the issue named in the question, then names a specific limitation. The attribution line above a source is where all three come from, and skipping it is the most common unforced error in the paper.

faqs.question: Is the Middle East breadth study harder than the changing nature of warfare option?
faqs.answer: Neither is inherently harder, but they fail differently. The warfare option covers seven decades of technology, tactics and civilian impact, and students tend to write well on two conflicts and thinly on the rest. The Middle East option between 1917 and 2012 brings the opposite problem for students in this region: strong contextual awareness and approximate chronology, with decisions attributed to nations in general rather than named bodies. Both are won the same way, by building a dated spine first and arguing about the shape of change rather than recounting episodes.

faqs.question: How much does a 4HI1 student actually have to memorise?
faqs.answer: Less breadth than students assume and more precision. For each depth study the working target is a dated spine of the key events, the named individuals and institutions that made decisions, and roughly two developed examples per examinable theme. For a breadth study it is a decade-by-decade skeleton plus evidence attached to each stage. Unlike geography, history gives no credit for reconstructing from method, so recall has to be built by spaced testing across weeks. We keep the spine written in the student's own hand and test it without notes each session.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help if they have not taught our exact depth study?
faqs.answer: On technique, yes, and that is most of what moves marks: inference, utility, explanation chains and judged essay structure transfer across every option. On content, the honest answer is that option experience matters, because knowing which events the specification actually examines saves a student from revising the wrong detail. We match on the option where we can and tell you plainly when we cannot, which is usually the point at which a family decides between waiting for a match and starting on technique now. Both are reasonable choices.

faqs.question: Do tutors travel to homes in Al Reem Island or Saadiyat for history lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not provide home visits in Abu Dhabi, and in-home tutoring is something we offer only in India. Every lesson on this page is one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. For an options qualification that is a genuine advantage: a student entered for the Middle East breadth study is matched with someone who has taught that option rather than with the nearest available humanities graduate, and nobody loses forty minutes to a bridge crossing in each direction.

faqs.question: Does a private history tutor in Abu Dhabi need a MoHRE permit?
faqs.answer: Individuals providing private lessons in the UAE need the private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is issued through MoHRE, granted free of charge for two years, and MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule is published, so treat any specific amount you are quoted with suspicion.

faqs.question: Can my child's own school history teacher tutor them privately in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: You should assume not. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct has been reported as carrying a similar restriction. That is press-reported rather than quoted wording, so verify it against the current ADEK policy document if the question is live for you. Either way, arranging it puts the teacher at professional risk and gives your child a tutor who cannot mark their work independently.

faqs.question: How many past papers should a 4HI1 student sit before the series?
faqs.answer: Quality matters more than volume, and a sensible pattern is one timed section a week from roughly six months out, rising to a full paper every fortnight in the final term. The condition is that each one is marked against the published scheme and the same question type is rewritten the following week; papers sat and self-marked against a model answer teach far less. Pearson publishes past series materials, and we reference and link them at source rather than reproducing them, because redistributing exam board documents is not ours to do.

faqs.question: Does history count as an accredited subject for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: On the British track the sourced requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at E or above or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. History sits inside that count as an accredited subject. One page currently ranking for UAE tutoring queries claims six IGCSE subjects are required, which does not match the sourced rule. Equivalency is a ministry process that IB Gram neither performs nor guarantees; verify current requirements through the ministry's own channel.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a depth study and a breadth study in change?
faqs.answer: A depth study examines a short period intensively, so the questions reward precise causation and explained consequence inside a narrow window. A breadth study in change spans decades and asks what altered across them, so it rewards a thesis about the shape of change supported by evidence drawn from the whole period. They need different essay architectures, and a student who writes a depth-study paragraph structure into a breadth essay will produce an accurate answer that sits mid-range. Teaching the two shapes separately is one of the first things we do.

faqs.question: How do we fit history sessions around a Khalifa City school run and after-school sport?
faqs.answer: By picking the slot last rather than first. School finish times vary across the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor and the mainland communities, and bridge traffic makes anything before 5pm fragile for families who cross. Khalifa City households commonly settle on 6pm, Al Reem on 5.45pm or later, and Yas families often prefer a weekend morning, which suits timed paper practice better anyway. Slots are set in Gulf Standard Time and can be moved week to week because nobody is driving anywhere.

faqs.question: Is there a trial lesson before we book weekly history sessions?
faqs.answer: Yes, one per student, with no card details required and nothing to cancel if you stop there. It is a working session rather than a pitch: your child writes one source question and one extended answer under time, the tutor marks both against the published Pearson scheme, and you receive the marked scripts with a written note on which examined behaviour is missing. If a different tutor would suit better you can ask for one, and if the scripts suggest your child does not need tutoring, we will tell you that.

abu-dhabi/edexcel-igcse-history-4hi1-tut.closingBody: The quickest way to know whether 4HI1 tutoring will help your child is to produce two things: the names of the depth studies and breadth study their Abu Dhabi school entered, and one answer written under time. We mark it against the published Pearson scheme, name which of the four examined behaviours is missing, and tell you how many weeks the repair is likely to take, including when the answer is that a short source clinic will do. Lessons run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, and every week produces a marked script you can read for yourself.

abu-dhabi/edexcel-igcse-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Pearson Edexcel International GCSE subjects to students at Abu Dhabi schools. Each profile names the specification codes covered, the evening hours available on Gulf Standard Time, and whether the tutor has worked with the tier your child is entered for.

intro.heading: What a parent is really asking for when they want a tutor in the house
paragraphs: The request behind this search is rarely about pedagogy. It is about a Tuesday. School finishes, the bus arrives somewhere between a quarter past three and four, there is football or music, and by the time homework starts the useful part of the evening is thinning out. Having an adult physically present at a fixed time solves a supervision problem and a motivation problem at once, and parents who ask for a home tutor in Abu Dhabi are usually solving those first and the subject second.

That is worth taking seriously rather than arguing with. So this page does the home-tuition question properly. What visiting tutors in this emirate actually charge once travel is priced in. How much of a sixty-minute slot survives a crossing from the island to Khalifa City at half past five. Which categories of person are permitted to tutor privately in the UAE at all, and what the Abu Dhabi ethics rules say about a child's own schoolteacher. What a household needs on the desk for the arrangement to work at all, visiting or otherwise.

Then the position, stated once and clearly: IB Gram does not sell home visits in Abu Dhabi. Visiting tuition is a service we run only in India. In the UAE every lesson is one-to-one and live over video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time. We would rather you read that in paragraph three than discover it after a form.

The case for the online format is not that it is a near-enough substitute. It is that on three of the four things a parent is buying it is straightforwardly better. The tutor pool is the whole pool rather than the drivable one, which decides whether your child gets somebody who has taught 4CH1 organic chemistry to Year 11 forty times or somebody who is confident with science generally. None of the hour is spent in a car, so a sixty-minute slot is sixty minutes. And the work leaves a trail: an annotated screen can be saved, a marked PDF can be compared with the one from a month ago, and a parent in another room can read both.

The fourth thing - an adult in the room - online delivery genuinely does not provide. The section on supervision deals with that honestly, because the answer is a household arrangement rather than a feature, and pretending otherwise would be the kind of claim this page is trying to argue against.

Everything below is specific to this emirate rather than to the Gulf in general. Abu Dhabi private schools are licensed and inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which publishes its own inspection outcomes. School bus arrivals cluster earlier in the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor than on the island, which changes which hour a session can realistically occupy. And the emirate carries an ethics rule on school staff tutoring their own students that does not sit in the same place everywhere in the country. Those three facts do more to shape a workable tutoring arrangement here than any statement about teaching philosophy, so they are treated as the starting conditions rather than as background.

abu-dhabi/edexcel-igcse-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Edexcel sits inside a British-curriculum route that Abu Dhabi families join at different points. The stages below are the three where a request for a tutor in the house most often arrives, and each has a different reason behind it.

programmes.name: The year before the specification starts
programmes.description: Requests at this stage are usually about work habits rather than content. A parent wants somebody sitting with a thirteen-year-old for an hour a week so that independent study becomes a thing that happens. The subject work is genuinely secondary, and that is a legitimate purchase, but it is worth knowing it is what you are buying.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi British-curriculum schools begin Edexcel content during Year 9 rather than waiting for Year 10. Ask your head of key stage which applies, because a student already working on 4MA1 material should be practising on real past paper questions from the start, and a habit-building session that never touches a paper will not show up in a mock.

programmes.name: First year of the Edexcel course
programmes.description: The year when codes appear on timetables and content starts accumulating faster than most students revise it. A weekly hour here is the cheapest intervention in the whole British-curriculum route, because it works on topics while they are still current rather than reconstructing them eighteen months later under exam pressure.
programmes.countryNote: Year 10 is also when Abu Dhabi families discover how many subjects their child has taken on. Nine or ten entries is common in this emirate, and a tutor is not a solution to an overloaded timetable. If the real problem is subject count, the conversation belongs with the school before any hours are bought.

programmes.name: Examination year and the series decision
programmes.description: The year where logistics get tightest and where parents most want a physical presence. Work is paper-led: timed questions, question selection, command terms and the two or three topics a marked script actually names. The entry decisions - tier, subject count, whether to sit in November - are made months before the papers.
programmes.countryNote: Entries in Abu Dhabi go through the school's examinations officer, so the deadline that binds your family is the centre's internal cut-off rather than any date Pearson publishes publicly. Ask for it in writing in the autumn term. Families who leave it find that a tier change or an extra subject is no longer available, whatever the tutoring plan says.

abu-dhabi/edexcel-igcse-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the Edexcel codes Abu Dhabi households most often name when they call asking for somebody to come round. The notes say what a session actually works on, because the subject label and the examinable skill are not always the same thing.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (4MA1)
subjects.description: The most requested code in this emirate by a wide margin. Two equally weighted papers, so there is no easier sitting to rely on. Sessions work on method chains that survive to step four, on the difference between a method mark and an accuracy mark, and on the habit of banking straightforward marks before grinding at a hard question.

subjects.name: Physics (4PH1)
subjects.description: Two written papers, the first considerably longer and heavier. Practical skills are examined inside the written papers rather than separately, which is reassuring for an online arrangement and surprising to parents who expect a laboratory. Work concentrates on units, rearranging equations under pressure and the sequencing of extended explanations.

subjects.name: Chemistry (4CH1)
subjects.description: Organic chemistry and moles arithmetic account for most of the recoverable marks in Abu Dhabi cohorts. Both are highly structured, which makes them well suited to short repeated practice rather than long explanatory sessions. A student who can do moles calculations reliably has usually bought back a grade boundary's worth of marks.

subjects.name: Biology (4BI1)
subjects.description: The subject where marks are lost to vocabulary rather than to understanding. Denatured rather than killed, diffusion rather than movement, named example rather than general case. Sessions drill command terms and precise phrasing, and parents are often surprised how much of the gain is linguistic.

subjects.name: English Language A (4EA1)
subjects.description: Non-fiction reading and transactional writing in one paper, poetry and prose with imaginative writing in the other, and a coursework alternative at centres that offer it. The shift that moves marks is from summarising what a writer said to analysing the choices the writer made.

subjects.name: English Literature (4ET1)
subjects.description: Quotation banks, paragraph shape and timing across questions. Strong readers often underperform here because they write appreciation rather than argument. Work is on integrating short quotations into a sentence that is already making a point, which is a technique rather than a talent.

subjects.name: Business (4BS1)
subjects.description: Definitions must be precise and chains of reasoning must be developed rather than listed. The highest-tariff questions ask for evaluation, and evaluation has a teachable structure. A student who writes four unconnected advantages is scoring a fraction of what the same knowledge could earn.

subjects.name: Further Pure Mathematics (4PM1)
subjects.description: Taken alongside 4MA1 or 4MB1 by students heading towards maths-heavy sixth-form routes. Calculus and series arrive early, so the limiting factor is almost always algebraic fluency rather than the new content itself. This is one of the codes with the thinnest local specialist coverage in Abu Dhabi.

abu-dhabi/edexcel-igcse-home-tutor.regionsTitle: What the drive actually costs, community by community
abu-dhabi/edexcel-igcse-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Travel is the whole of the visiting-tutor economics in this emirate. The notes below describe the realistic evening picture in each community rather than a map distance, because a tutor's willingness to take a slot is decided by what the return leg does to their next booking.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Buses land between 15:15 and 16:00, so a 16:30 start is genuinely available here. A tutor coming from the island in the evening peak will often lose fifteen to twenty-five minutes each way, which is why Khalifa City households are quoted at the upper end of the visiting band.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: Villa communities with the emirate's longest island-bound commutes. Parents here report tutors arriving late and leaving early to protect a second booking, which turns a paid hour into something closer to forty-five teaching minutes.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Short school runs, late co-curricular finishes and a willing supply of visiting tutors because the drive is short from the island. The constraint here is the student's calendar rather than the tutor's, and 18:00 and 18:30 slots fill first.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Bridge-dependent in both directions, with high-rise parking and lift time that nobody prices in. A fixed repeating slot survives the week far better than a negotiated one, whichever format you choose.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: Large mainland communities a long way from the island specialist pool. These are the postcodes where a parent looking for a 4PM1 or 4CP0 tutor within driving distance most often finds nobody at all, at any price.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Newer housing with growing Year 10 and Year 11 cohorts. Visiting tutors frequently decline these slots outright in the evening peak, or price them with the return leg included, which is the honest way to do it.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Mushrif
regions.note: The best-served part of the emirate for visiting tuition: short runs, long-established schools and a dense tutor supply. If a household anywhere in Abu Dhabi can make a visiting arrangement work on cost, it is here.

schoolClusters.city: Island schools
schoolClusters.note: Long-established British-curriculum provision with early internal mock calendars. Students from these schools usually reach tuition already holding marked mock scripts, which shortens the diagnostic and means fewer paid hours spent finding out what is wrong.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas
schoolClusters.note: Where most of the emirate's newer British and American provision sits, and where the bulk of visiting-tutor requests originate. Demand concentrates on Mathematics A Higher tier and the sciences, and the request is almost always for a fixed weekday evening slot.

sections.heading: What the Abu Dhabi visiting market charges, and who published the figures
paragraphs: Three of the six most visible tutoring sites serving this market publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars, which is not a currency UAE families transact in. So here are the bands, in dirhams, with the source attached to each. They are market rates gathered in October 2026, not an IB Gram price list.

At the budget end, platforms advertise online tuition from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, with one UAE content site listing its own entry rates from AED 45 to AED 65 and one regional platform from around AED 33 to AED 52. A qualified subject tutor working online sits in the AED 150 to AED 300 band; one UAE agency publishes its own IGCSE rates from AED 150 an hour. An in-home one-to-one visit, travel included, runs from about AED 180 to AED 500, with Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table putting the common range at AED 180 to AED 350 and independent home tutors advertising AED 200 to AED 500. Named examiner-level tutors are quoted up to AED 650 and above.

Monthly packages circulate too. Around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions is a common online shape, while in-home packages of four two-hour sessions appear at roughly AED 1,599 to AED 1,799. Bestimate's own monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour arrangement run AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support.

The pattern in those numbers is the whole argument of this page. Visiting tuition in Abu Dhabi is priced roughly a third higher than equivalent online tuition for the same qualification level, and the difference is not teaching. It is a car. Whether that premium is worth paying depends entirely on whether the thing you are buying is subject expertise or adult presence, and it is worth being honest with yourself about which.

sections.heading: Where a visiting hour actually goes, minute by minute
paragraphs: Parents price a visiting tutor by the hour and then experience something shorter, and the gap is rarely anybody behaving badly. It is arithmetic. A tutor with a 17:00 booking in Al Raha Gardens and an 18:30 in Khalifa City has to protect the second one, which means the first one ends in time to make the drive. Nothing dishonest has happened and the family has still paid for sixty minutes.

Set against that, an online session starts when the clock says so. The difference is not marginal. Across a thirty-week school year, ten lost minutes a week is five hours of teaching, which at the published mid-market rate is a meaningful sum of money for something that produced no marks.

There is a second, quieter cost in the visiting model. A tutor who has driven thirty minutes has an incentive to fill the hour with activity, because activity looks like value to whoever is listening from the kitchen. Sitting a student in silence for twenty-five minutes while they attempt a timed question alone is often the most useful thing that can happen in a session, and it is the hardest thing to do with an audience and a car waiting outside.
