abu-dhabi/experienced-ib-tutor.programmesIntro: Abu Dhabi schools run all three mainstream IB programmes, and some add the Career-related Programme. Experience is programme-specific: the assessment model, the vocabulary and the parent's role change completely between them. Check that a tutor's experience sits in the programme your child is actually enrolled in.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Transdisciplinary, inquiry-led and without external examinations. Progress is judged through teacher observation, portfolios and whatever standardised measures the school chooses to run. A tutor working at this level is building reading fluency, number facts and written structure, and the end point is the Exhibition in the final year rather than a paper.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi IB schools run the PYP on the island and along the Al Raha corridor, with intake drawn from a wide mix of first languages. Tutors with genuine PYP experience talk about reading ages, phonics stages and number fluency; those without it default to worksheets borrowed from a British Year 4 scheme and call it inquiry.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four published criteria, each scored from 0 to 8 and summed before conversion to a 1-7 grade. The vocabulary is criterion descriptors and command terms. The final year carries the Personal Project, supervised inside the school, and some schools add on-screen eAssessment.
programmes.countryNote: MYP experience in Abu Dhabi matters most in Years 10 and 11, when families start comparing the programme against IGCSE and asking whether their child is ready for Higher Level. A tutor who has only taught the Diploma will read an MYP report card as a percentage sheet, which it is not, and will coach for the wrong thing.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject carries an internal assessment marked in school and moderated externally, with the remainder examined by written paper. The grade is a 1-7 per subject against published criteria and boundaries.
programmes.countryNote: This is where most Abu Dhabi requests land, and where the cohort count matters most. A tutor who has taken groups through several May sessions knows how the autumn of the second year collapses under internal assessment deadlines in four subjects at once, and plans the term around that rather than around the textbook order.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A smaller framework combining at least two Diploma courses with a career-related study, a reflective project and a personal and professional skills course. It appears in a handful of UAE schools and is frequently confused with the full Diploma by families and by tutors alike.
programmes.countryNote: If your child is on the Career-related Programme, say so at the first contact. The Diploma subjects inside it are examined identically, but the core is different, the workload profile is different, and a tutor who has never seen a reflective project will quietly treat it as an Extended Essay with fewer words.

abu-dhabi/experienced-ib-tutor.subjectsIntro: Experience is held per subject and per level, not across a programme. The list below shows what each course actually assesses and where Abu Dhabi students most often lose marks, which is the ground a tutor's experience has to cover before the hourly rate means anything.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebraic fluency, calculus and proof, with a non-calculator paper that exposes weak manipulation immediately. Marks go on unjustified steps and on reading the command term as a hint rather than an instruction. A tutor whose experience is entirely in Applications and Interpretation will not see where the proof work is thin.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and technology use throughout, including a calculator-permitted paper in every component. Losses cluster in interpretation: a correct regression followed by a sentence that says nothing about context. Experience here is about exam technique on long multi-part questions rather than algebraic depth.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics, fields, waves and nuclear content, plus a substantial investigation marked against published criteria. Students lose marks on uncertainty treatment and on explanations that restate the question. A tutor needs experience of the investigation specifically; it is a different skill from teaching the written papers.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Structure and reactivity across the whole course, with organic mechanisms and energetics carrying the heaviest Higher Level load. The common failure is memorised mechanisms applied to an unfamiliar substrate. Experienced tutors drill the reasoning behind a curly arrow rather than the arrow itself.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Conceptual breadth with heavy terminology and data-based questions in every paper. Marks disappear in extended response, where students write everything they know instead of what the command term asks for. Experience shows in how quickly a tutor can convert a 4 into a 6 by rebuilding answer structure alone.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Microeconomics, macroeconomics and the global economy, assessed partly through commentaries built on published news articles. The usual loss is diagram work that is drawn correctly and then not referred to in the analysis. A tutor with commentary experience will fix the article choice before the writing starts.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tools, techniques and theory applied to real organisations, with a case study released in advance for one paper. Students underperform by narrating the case rather than applying a framework to it. Experience here means having seen several pre-released cases and knowing how examiners reward application.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Textual analysis across literary and non-literary forms, with an individual oral and a written assessment at Higher Level. The individual oral is the most coachable component in the Diploma and the one most often left until it is too late. A tutor who has prepared orals before will start in the first term.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Language acquisition through five prescribed themes, assessed by reading, writing, listening and an individual oral. Marks are lost on register and task type rather than on vocabulary. Experienced tutors treat the writing paper as a format exercise first and a language exercise second.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Arabic runs as a Diploma language option and, separately, as a federally required subject in UAE private schools. The two jobs are different, and families often buy one when they need the other. State at the outset which one you mean, including whether your child is in the Arab or non-Arab stream.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches, with research methods threaded through, plus an experimental study at both levels. Students lose marks by describing a study without evaluating it. A tutor needs experience of the internal assessment write-up format, which is tightly prescribed.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Systems fundamentals, algorithmic thinking and a developed solution assessed internally. The usual problem is a working program with documentation that does not evidence the criteria. Experience shows in whether the tutor talks about criteria letters or about the code.

Parents here often want an IB tutor for Khalifa City who can start at 17:00 after a long school run, which rules out most visiting tutors and rules in a fixed online slot.

regions.note: Mixed British and IB households, with a steady stream of Year 11 families asking whether their child is ready for Higher Level. The experience they need is MYP-to-Diploma transition experience, which is narrower than general IB teaching.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Requests here skew towards the Diploma core, particularly Extended Essay supervision support and Theory of Knowledge. An IB tutor for Saadiyat Island is more often asked for structural feedback on a draft than for content teaching.

regions.note: Younger cohorts, with PYP and early MYP support more common than Diploma work. Families tend to ask about reading fluency and number facts rather than about grades, and the right experience is primary rather than secondary.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Apartment households with tight evening schedules and frequent mid-year arrivals from other curricula. The recurring question is how much of a Diploma year a new arrival can realistically recover, which only a tutor who has handled a mid-course transfer can answer honestly.

regions.name: Al Bateen and the Corniche
regions.note: Long-established families, often with older siblings who have already finished the Diploma. They compare tutors against a previous one, so the conversation starts with what the last tutor failed to do rather than with the subject.

regions.note: Price-sensitive and volume-driven: two or three siblings across different programmes in one household. The experience question becomes whether one tutor can hold both an MYP and a Diploma brief, which is usually a no.

regions.name: Masdar City and Al Falah
regions.note: Newer communities with smaller school catchments, where the local tutor pool for a rare Higher Level subject is effectively empty. These are the households for whom online delivery is not a compromise but the only route to a specialist at all.

schoolClusters.city: The island and the Al Raha corridor
schoolClusters.note: IB schools here carry the bulk of the emirate's Diploma cohort, and their internal assessment calendars are the thing a tutor has to plan around. Students we support attend schools in this cluster; no school named here has any relationship with IB Gram.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Reef and the mainland communities

abu-dhabi/experienced-ib-tutor.modesIntro: Three ways of buying an experienced tutor's time, each suited to a different problem. The format matters less than the match, but the wrong format wastes a good tutor: a weekly slot cannot fix a crisis six days out, and a crash block cannot build algebraic fluency.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one, same tutor, same slot
modes.description: The default and the only format that produces a usable record. One 60 or 90-minute session each week over live video, with the same tutor holding the subject for the whole term so that the error log carries forward instead of restarting.

modes.title: Coursework feedback cycle
modes.description: Scheduled around your child's own school deadlines rather than weekly. The student submits a draft, the tutor returns criterion-referenced feedback, the student revises it, and the next session is spent on the revision. Feedback only; the work stays the student's throughout.
bullets: Feedback mapped to the published criteria the school will mark against
Comments on structure and reasoning, never rewritten sentences

modes.title: Pre-session intensive block
modes.description: A short, dense run of sessions in the weeks before a written series, built around timed papers rather than teaching. Suits a student whose content knowledge is broadly intact and whose marks are leaking through technique, timing and command-term misreading.

sections.heading: What 'experienced' should prove, and the claims that prove nothing
paragraphs: An experienced IB tutor in Abu Dhabi is one who can name the programme, the subject, the level and the number of cohorts carried through to a final examination series, and who can then show you what they did with a weak script last term. That is the whole test. Everything else on a tutor profile is decoration. The word itself costs nothing to type, nobody verifies it, and it appears on almost every listing in this market, which is precisely why it has stopped carrying information.

The claims that follow it are usually unfalsifiable by design. Ten years of experience could mean ten years of the same Standard Level course, or two years of IB layered on eight years of a different curriculum. Taught at leading IB schools could mean a term of cover teaching. Helped students achieve top grades is not a claim about the tutor at all, since the students who arrive already strong will achieve those grades with or without help. None of these is a lie. None of them is checkable either, and an unfalsifiable claim is worth exactly what you can verify of it.

Three artefacts move the conversation onto solid ground. The first is a marked script with the tutor's own annotations on it, anonymised, so you can see whether they write diagnoses or ticks. The second is a session plan for a real student, which shows whether they think in components and criteria or in textbook chapters. The third is one contactable reference from a parent whose child has already finished the course, not one who is three weeks into it. A tutor with genuine experience produces all three without friction, because they already exist.
bullets: Ask for cohorts completed, not years taught
Ask which level: Higher Level experience does not follow from Standard Level

sections.heading: Experience that transfers between courses, and experience that does not
paragraphs: Teaching experience is not one substance that accumulates. It is a set of specific competences, some of which move between courses and most of which do not. The failure mode this produces is predictable: a strong A-Level Chemistry teacher takes on an IB Chemistry student, teaches the content accurately, and the student's internal assessment mark does not move, because the investigation is marked against criteria the tutor has never read.

The transfers that genuinely hold are within a subject across levels, and within a subject across boards at a content level. A tutor who has taught Higher Level Biology can teach the Standard Level course, because the content is a subset and the assessment model is shared. A tutor who has taught A-Level Physics knows the physics. What does not transfer is anything procedural: the internal assessment criteria, the command-term vocabulary, the oral formats, the moderation process, and the particular way IB examiners reward reasoning over recall.

This is why the level question matters more than it sounds. Higher Level is not Standard Level with extra weeks. It carries additional content, a different weighting profile across the papers, and in several subjects an additional component altogether. A tutor whose Higher Level experience is theoretical will teach the shared material competently and then run out of ground at exactly the point your child needs them, which is usually the back half of the second year. Ask which topics are Higher Level only in that subject; a tutor who has taught the level answers in seconds, and one who has not will reach for the syllabus.

sections.heading: Years, cohorts and hours: three ways of counting the same tutor
paragraphs: Three different numbers get called experience, and they predict different things. Years in post counts elapsed time. Cohorts completed counts how many times the tutor has seen a group from the start of a course to a results day. Hours in the subject counts contact time, which for a private tutor can be far higher per cohort than for a classroom teacher who also carries form duties, cover and reports.

Cohorts completed is the most useful single number, because the back half of a course is where tutors learn their job. Anyone can teach the first term of a Diploma subject from the textbook order. The skill is in the autumn of the second year, when four internal assessments fall due in the same fortnight, predicted grades are being set, and the student has to be persuaded to abandon a weak investigation topic rather than nurse it to a low mark. A tutor who has lived through that several times plans the term differently from the start.

Hours matter for a specific reason: a private tutor sees one student at a time, so a year of private work produces more diagnostic repetitions on individual error patterns than a year of whole-class teaching. That is a genuine advantage, and it is why a four-year private tutor can outperform a fifteen-year classroom teacher on exam technique while losing to them on moderation judgement. The two profiles are complementary rather than ranked, and the right one depends on whether your problem is technique or internal assessment marks.

sections.heading: The three IB programmes are three different jobs
paragraphs: Parents reasonably assume that IB experience is portable across the Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma programmes, because the three share a name, a philosophy and a vocabulary. In practice they share very little that a tutor can use. The PYP has no external examinations at all, so progress is evidenced through portfolios, observation and whatever standardised measures the school chooses. The MYP is scored against four published criteria per subject, each from 0 to 8, summed and then converted to a 1-7 grade. The Diploma is examined by written paper with an internally marked and externally moderated component in every subject.

A tutor moving between these without noticing produces specific, identifiable errors. On an MYP brief they talk about percentages, because percentages are what they know, and the parent is reassured by numbers that the school does not use. On a PYP brief they set past-paper practice for a nine-year-old, because practice papers are their instrument, and the child's reading comprehension does not move. On a Diploma brief after years of MYP work they underestimate the sheer volume of the second year and plan a gentle weekly programme into a term that needs triage.

The useful question is therefore not whether a tutor has IB experience but which programme they have taught this academic year and last. Recency matters as much as depth here, because the three programmes evolve on separate cycles and a tutor who last touched the MYP five years ago is working from a model that may have moved. If your child is in Year 11 and about to choose Diploma subjects, you want somebody who has both sides of that transition in recent memory, which is a narrower group than general IB experience implies.

sections.heading: The first hour, and what an experienced tutor does with it
paragraphs: The trial lesson is the only evidence you will get before you commit money, and it is more informative than any profile. An inexperienced tutor uses it to be likeable: they establish rapport, ask the student what they find hard, agree that the topic is hard, and teach a small piece of it well. The student enjoys it. Nothing diagnostic has happened, and the parent books on the strength of a pleasant forty minutes.

An experienced tutor spends that hour building a diagnosis. They ask for a recent marked script before the session rather than during it. They watch the student attempt a question live, in writing, without prompting, because the gap between understanding a worked example and producing an answer alone is where most lost marks live. They test command-term comprehension directly: give the student the same content under explain, justify and evaluate and see whether the answer changes. By the end they can state, in a sentence, whether the problem is knowledge, method, technique or working speed, and roughly how many sessions each of those takes to shift.

That sentence is what you are buying. The four categories need different treatment and different amounts of time. A knowledge gap is the cheapest to fix and the most visible. A method problem takes a few weeks of corrected practice. An exam-technique problem can move a grade in a month and is the most common single cause of a predicted grade sitting below a student's actual understanding. Working speed is the slowest to shift and the most often misdiagnosed as a knowledge gap, which is why an experienced tutor times the attempt rather than just marking it.

sections.heading: What experience costs around Abu Dhabi, band by band
paragraphs: IB tutor rates in AED vary by a factor of ten across this market, and the variable that moves them most is the kind of experience being sold. The figures below are market rates published by providers and by a rate survey, not IB Gram prices. Each band is attributed, and the point of the table is to let you see what you are buying rather than to recommend a number. Rates were read in October 2026 and providers revise them.

At the budget end, EdFlik publishes online tutoring from AED 45 to 65 per hour and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52, which typically buys a university student or an early-career tutor working from the textbook. Unitors publishes IGCSE tutoring from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. TutorChase quotes around AED 270. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 survey puts in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to 350, home tutors at AED 200 to 500, and IB, IGCSE and A-Level specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above. BartyED publishes AED 650 for a premium named tutor. Monthly packages in the market run around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Two things follow from that spread. The first is that the gap between a budget hour and a specialist hour is not a quality gradient along a single line; they are different products, and a budget hour spent on a Higher Level investigation is usually wasted rather than merely slower. The second is that the top of the range is not reliably better than the middle. Above roughly AED 450 you are often paying for scarcity, a name or examiner framing rather than for additional teaching competence, and scarcity is exactly what online delivery removes. The honest advice is to buy the band that matches the job: technique work at the middle of the range, rare Higher Level content at the upper middle, and nothing at the bottom for anything that will be externally moderated.

sections.heading: ADEK's ethics rule, the permit, and the one tutor to rule out
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi has a rule most families have never been told, and it rules out the tutor they would otherwise choose first. ADEK's professional-ethics requirements for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school. This was reported by Gulf News and should be verified against the current ADEK policy document before anyone states it as ADEK's exact wording, but the direction is unambiguous. The most experienced person available, your child's own subject teacher, is also the one you should not hire.

The reasoning is sound even setting the rule aside. A teacher who is paid privately by a family is also the person setting that student's predicted grade, marking their internal assessment before moderation and writing their reports. That is a conflict a parent cannot manage, and it puts the teacher's employment at risk for the sake of one hour a week. A tutor from outside the school has no stake in the grade and can tell the student plainly that a paragraph is weak.

Separately, private tutoring in the UAE now runs on a permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is applied for through MoHRE's own channels; the service is listed as Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing with a two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you. Ask any UAE-resident tutor whether they hold the permit, and treat an evasive answer as an answer.

sections.heading: Where experience is most tempting to misuse
paragraphs: An experienced tutor knows exactly how marks are awarded against each criterion. That knowledge is what you are paying for, and it is also what makes the academic-honesty boundary sharper here than anywhere else in tutoring. A tutor who can see that a student's investigation will land two marks below a boundary can also see the three sentences that would lift it, and the temptation to supply those sentences rather than teach them is strongest in precisely the tutors who are most capable.

The boundary is not vague. A tutor may teach the content, explain what a criterion rewards, discuss a topic choice, ask questions about reasoning, point out that a section does not evidence what it claims, and comment on a draft the student has written. A tutor may not supply sentences, restructure a draft into their own shape, correct a dataset, choose the research question outright, or edit work to a submission standard. The work has to be the student's own, in the student's own words, through its full draft history. IB academic-honesty rules make the consequence of crossing that line an expulsion risk for the student, not a service-quality question for the tutor.

Two practical safeguards cost nothing. Keep the draft history: dated versions in the student's own account are the clearest evidence of authorship if a question is ever raised, and they also show progress, which is useful for a different reason. Second, ask any tutor directly what they will not do with an internal assessment. A tutor with real experience answers immediately and specifically, because they have had the conversation with a school before. A tutor who treats the question as an obstacle to the sale has told you something important about what happens in week six.

sections.heading: One reference, two questions, and when to stop paying
paragraphs: A single reference, properly asked, is worth more than a page of profile text. Two questions do the work. The first: what was your child's position in this subject when the tutor started, and what was it at the end? The second: what did the tutor do in the first month that you would not have thought of? The first question tests whether anything moved. The second tests whether the tutor had a method or was simply pleasant and available.

Ask for a reference whose child has finished the course rather than one three weeks in. Early-stage families are enthusiastic by default, because the first month of tutoring reliably feels productive: the easy knowledge gaps close fast, confidence returns, and nothing has yet been tested by an external mark. Grade movement is lumpy, and the first month is misleading in both directions. A reference from a completed course has seen what happened when the internal assessment was moderated and the papers were sat.

Set the stopping condition at the start, because it is almost impossible to set later. After six to eight weekly sessions you should be able to see three things: a written record of what each session addressed, an error log that is shrinking in at least one category, and at least one piece of work marked against the published criteria with a band that is moving. If all three are absent after two months, the problem is the match or the plan, not the student's effort, and the right response is to change tutor or stop. An experienced tutor will say that to you unprompted at the review, which is the final test of the word on the listing.

faqs.question: How many years should an experienced IB tutor have behind them?
faqs.answer: Years are the wrong unit. Ask instead how many cohorts the tutor has carried through to a final examination series in your child's subject at your child's level. Four or five completed cohorts at Higher Level is a strong signal; twelve years in a school with two of them touching the IB is not. The reason is that the back half of a Diploma course teaches the tutor their job, when several internal assessments fall due together and predicted grades are being set. A tutor who has lived through that repeatedly plans the term differently from the first week.

faqs.question: Does an experienced IB tutor need to have taught in an Abu Dhabi school?
faqs.answer: No, and insisting on it narrows your options sharply for no gain. What a tutor needs is experience of the programme, subject and level your child is taking, plus an understanding of how UAE school calendars and internal assessment deadlines run. Local school experience is useful for one thing only: familiarity with how a particular school sets its internal deadlines, which a tutor can learn from your child's own timeline in a single session. Since every UAE lesson here is delivered online, the pool is national and international rather than limited to who lives nearby.

faqs.question: Is a former examiner better than an experienced classroom teacher?
faqs.answer: They are good at different things. Examining experience sharpens judgement about where a borderline script sits between two bands, which is genuinely useful when a draft needs an honest read. Classroom experience is better for pacing, relationship management and the long grind of building fluency. Treat any examiner claim carefully: ask which board, which component, which series, and whether the status is current. Nobody should use examiner framing to imply access to marking, grade boundaries or unseen paper content, because that access does not exist and the implication is misleading.

faqs.question: My child's tutor has twenty years of A-Level experience. Is that enough for the IB?
faqs.answer: It covers the content and very little else. The physics, chemistry or mathematics is the same material, so subject knowledge is not the risk. What does not transfer is procedural: the internal assessment criteria and their letter allocations, the command-term vocabulary that decides how an answer must be shaped, the oral formats in the language subjects, and the external moderation process. Ask the tutor to describe your child's internal assessment and what each criterion rewards. If the answer is general rather than specific, the gap will appear in the second year, which is when it is most expensive.

faqs.question: Does experience in IB Maths Analysis and Approaches transfer to Applications and Interpretation?
faqs.answer: Partly, and less than most tutors assume. The two routes share foundational material but reward different things. Analysis and Approaches is algebraically heavy, includes proof, and has a paper sat without a calculator, so weak manipulation shows up immediately. Applications and Interpretation runs modelling and statistics throughout with technology permitted in every component, and marks are lost on interpretation rather than on algebra. A tutor confident in one should say plainly whether they have taught the other through a full cohort. Ask which route, then ask what the difference means for how they would teach your child.

faqs.question: What should an experienced tutor actually do in the first session?
faqs.answer: Build a diagnosis rather than a rapport. They should ask for a recent marked script before the lesson, watch your child write an answer unaided rather than follow a worked example, and test the same content under two or three different command terms to see whether the answer changes. By the end they should be able to say in one sentence whether the problem is knowledge, method, exam technique or working speed, and roughly how many sessions each would take to shift. A pleasant forty minutes with no diagnosis is the commonest weak trial lesson in this market.

faqs.question: Can an experienced Middle Years Programme teacher tutor my child in the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but check it rather than assume it. The two programmes share a philosophy and almost none of the machinery. MYP work is scored against four published criteria per subject, each from 0 to 8, then converted to a 1-7 grade. The Diploma is examined by written paper with an internally marked, externally moderated component in every subject and a far heavier second-year workload. A tutor crossing over without noticing typically underestimates that workload and plans a gentle weekly programme into a term that needs triage. Ask which programme they have taught this year and last.

faqs.question: Is a more experienced tutor worth the higher hourly rate in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the job. Market rates run from around AED 33 to 65 at the entry level, where published figures come from Tutopiya and EdFlik, up to AED 200 to 450 and above for IB specialists according to Bestimate's 2026 survey. For homework supervision, the cheaper hour is adequate. For Higher Level content or anything that will be externally moderated, a budget hour is usually wasted rather than merely slower. Above roughly AED 450 you are often paying for scarcity or a name, and online delivery is precisely what removes the scarcity premium.

faqs.question: Can my child's own schoolteacher tutor them privately in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: They should not, and ADEK's professional-ethics requirements for private and charter school staff prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. That has been press-reported and is worth verifying against the current ADEK policy document, but the direction is clear. The conflict is also obvious without the rule: the same person would be setting predicted grades, marking internal assessment work before moderation and writing reports. A tutor from outside the school has no stake in the grade and can tell a student plainly that a section is weak.

faqs.question: Does a tutor need a permit to teach privately in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is obtained through MoHRE's app, website or e-services system under the service name Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, with a stated two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include school-registered teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat any quoted amount as unsourced.

faqs.question: How long does it take to find a tutor for a rare Higher Level subject?
faqs.answer: Common subjects at either level are usually matched within a couple of days. The narrow combinations take longer, and they are the ones where the local pool in any single emirate thins out quickly: a particular language at Higher Level, Computer Science, Music, Film, or a subject where the internal assessment carries most of the difficulty. We state the position before you book rather than after. If the genuine specialist sits outside the UAE, you are told at first contact, which is the whole practical argument for online delivery over a local search.

faqs.question: Will an experienced tutor edit my child's Internal Assessment to a better standard?
faqs.answer: No, and a tutor offering to is selling your child an expulsion risk. The permitted work is substantial: teaching the content, explaining what each criterion rewards, discussing a topic choice, questioning the reasoning, and pointing out where a section does not evidence what it claims. What is not permitted is supplying sentences, restructuring a draft into the tutor's shape, correcting a dataset, choosing the research question outright, or polishing work to a submission standard. Keep dated drafts in your child's own account; they evidence authorship and they also show progress.

faqs.question: How do I choose between two tutors who both say they are experienced?
faqs.answer: Run the same three requests past both. Ask for the cohort count in your child's exact subject and level. Ask for one anonymised marked script carrying the tutor's own annotations, so you can see whether they write diagnoses or ticks. Ask for a contactable reference from a family whose child has finished the course, not one three weeks in. The tutor with real experience produces all three without friction because they already exist. Differences in the quality of those three artefacts will tell you more than an hour of conversation.

faqs.question: Do lessons for Abu Dhabi families happen at our home or online?
faqs.answer: Online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. That is stated plainly because it changes what you get rather than limiting it: a household in Masdar City or Al Falah is matched on who has actually taught the subject at the level required, instead of on who is willing to drive there at 17:00. Sessions are timed to Gulf Standard Time and fixed around your school run.

faqs.question: How soon should I expect to see a grade move?
faqs.answer: Expect the record to move before the grade does. The first month of tutoring reliably feels productive because easy knowledge gaps close quickly, and that early improvement flatters every tutor. A fairer review point is six to eight weekly sessions, where you should see session notes naming what was addressed, an error log shrinking in at least one category, and one piece of work marked against published criteria with a band that has moved. If none of those three exists after two months, change the plan or the tutor. No honest tutor promises a particular grade.

abu-dhabi/experienced-ib-tutor.closingHeading: Audit the experience, then book the trial
abu-dhabi/experienced-ib-tutor.closingBody: Ask the four questions: which programme, which subject, which level, how many cohorts completed. Ask for the three artefacts: an annotated script, a session plan, a reference from a finished course. Then take the free trial lesson and judge it on whether you end the hour with a one-sentence diagnosis of what is actually wrong. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time, with no in-home visits anywhere in the UAE. Send the subject, the level and one recent marked script, and we will tell you honestly whether a tutor with the right experience is available for your child.

abu-dhabi/experienced-igcse-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IGCSE subjects to Abu Dhabi families over live video. What we match on is narrower than a job title: which board, which specification version, which tier and which practical route a tutor has actually prepared candidates for, because those are the facts that make long service useful rather than merely long.

intro.heading: Experience is a measurement, and most pages never take it
paragraphs: Every tutoring site in this market uses the word experienced and almost none of them say what is being counted. Fifteen years of teaching a national curriculum GCSE is not fifteen years of IGCSE. A decade of A Level chemistry is not a decade of 0620 Paper 6. Four years with one board tells you little about the other two a family in this emirate might meet. The word is doing the work of a credential while carrying none of the information, which is why a parent looking for an experienced IGCSE tutor in Abu Dhabi usually ends up comparing adjectives.

There are better units. Examination series prepared for, because each series teaches a tutor something about how questions are set and where candidates go wrong. Specification versions read, because boards revise syllabuses on published cycles and a tutor working from an old version will teach content that has moved or been removed. Boards worked, because Cambridge, Pearson Edexcel and OxfordAQA structure the same subject differently. Tiers taught, because Core and Extended are different jobs. And practical routes covered, because a tutor who has only ever prepared alternative-to-practical candidates has not prepared anybody for a timed practical.

The useful thing about those units is that they are checkable in a free trial. A tutor who has prepared candidates across several series will tell you, unprompted, which topics recur and which the examiner reports keep flagging. A tutor who has read the current specification will know which formulae are given and which are assumed. A tutor who has worked both main boards will describe the differences in paper structure without being prompted. None of that requires taking anybody's word for anything.

Experience is also visible in an artefact, which is the part of this page most worth reading. Hand a tutor a marked script and watch what they do with it. An experienced marker annotates against criteria, identifies the line where a chain broke rather than the wrong final answer, distinguishes a method loss from a knowledge loss, and flags the questions the student answered to a different command word. An inexperienced one ticks what is right, crosses what is wrong and writes 'more detail needed'. The gap between those two sets of annotations is the gap you are paying for.

Two statements of fact. IB Gram delivers one-to-one tuition over live video to families across the emirate and does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, where ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools; visiting tutors are a service available only in India. And IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform with no approval from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, Cambridge or Pearson and no premises in the UAE. Every AED figure below was published by another organisation and is attributed to it.

abu-dhabi/experienced-igcse-tutor.programmesIntro: Abu Dhabi families meet more than one international GCSE family, sometimes inside the same school timetable, and experience with one does not automatically carry to another. These are the four qualification families most often in play here, with what experience in each actually consists of.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: The most widely entered family in the emirate, with syllabuses numbered in four digits and grading on either an A* to G or a 9 to 1 scale depending on the code. Experience here means knowing the paper set per syllabus, which practical route a school has chosen, and how the tiering of a subject changes the question style rather than only the difficulty. Cambridge runs a June and a November series, with Checkpoint tests for younger years in March, May and October.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the zone, since it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong timetable was used. An experienced tutor in this emirate knows to ask which zone the school sits in before building a revision sequence from a timetable found online.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: A separate specification family with its own codes, graded 9 to 1, and with paper structures that differ from Cambridge's for the same subject. Experience here includes knowing where Pearson places the marks within a specification and how its assessment model differs, which is the kind of detail a tutor either has from preparing candidates or does not have at all.
programmes.countryNote: Pearson International GCSE exams are available in May/June and November each year; the November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so any plan should be built from the live official document rather than a restated date.

programmes.name: OxfordAQA International GCSE
programmes.description: A smaller third family in the region, offered by some schools and available through approved examination centres for private candidates. Experience with it is genuinely scarcer, and a tutor who claims it should be able to describe the specification structure in the same detail they would for Cambridge. Where a school enters this board for one subject only, that subject is the one to ask about specifically.
programmes.countryNote: For Abu Dhabi families this most often matters when a private candidate entry is being arranged through a centre that offers one board rather than another. The centre's own subject list and internal deadlines should drive the tutoring plan, because centre deadlines sit ahead of the board's and vary between centres in the same emirate.

programmes.name: Cambridge O Level
programmes.description: Still entered by some schools in the region alongside or instead of IGCSE, and frequently confused with it by families comparing notes. The two are related but not interchangeable: syllabus content, available components and coursework provision can differ. Experience here means knowing which of the two a cohort is actually entered for and not assuming from the subject name.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge runs O Level in the same June and November series as IGCSE, which means the entry deadlines and timetable-zone rules apply in the same way. Where a school enters O Level in some subjects and IGCSE in others, an experienced tutor checks the statement of entry rather than the timetable on the school's website, because the two have been known to disagree.

abu-dhabi/experienced-igcse-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Abu Dhabi families most often ask for an experienced tutor in, described by what experience specifically buys in each one. In some subjects it buys content depth; in others it buys knowledge of where a paper sets its traps, which is a different thing and often the more valuable one.

subjects.name: Mathematics (0580, 0980, Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Experience shows in question recognition. A tutor who has worked several series knows which topics recur in which paper, which questions students habitually misread, and where method marks are routinely available and unclaimed. Content knowledge in school mathematics is common; knowing what the paper does with it is not.

subjects.name: Physics (0625, 0972, Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: The practical route is the experience test. A tutor who has prepared candidates for the timed practical talks about apparatus discipline and recording conventions; one who has prepared alternative-to-practical candidates talks about observation language and justified conclusions. A tutor who does not distinguish the two has prepared nobody for either in particular.

subjects.name: Chemistry (0620, 0971, Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Experience is audible in how a tutor handles moles. The inexperienced version teaches the formula; the experienced version insists the relative formula mass is written out first, every time, because that single habit removes the error that corrupts every later step in a calculation chain.

subjects.name: Biology (0610, 0970, Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: A content-heavy subject where experience buys triage: knowing which strands reward revision and which reward technique. Extended-response marking is the clearest signal, because a tutor who has marked many answers awards against the criteria rather than rewarding fluent writing that misses the command word.

subjects.name: English First Language (0500, 0990)
subjects.description: Experience here is almost entirely in the criteria. A tutor who has marked directed-writing tasks across several series can say in a sentence why an articulate answer scored in the middle band, usually because audience and form were ignored. A less experienced tutor praises the prose and suggests more detail.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (0510, 0511)
subjects.description: The experienced question is which variant the school entered, because the handling of speaking differs between the two codes. Experience also shows in the note-making tasks, where candidates lose accuracy marks by writing beyond the task, and a tutor who has seen this pattern teaches to the limit rather than to the page.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (0606)
subjects.description: Experience is scarce in this code, which is why matching matters more here than in any other subject on the page. The specific thing to look for is a tutor who can describe how the course's calculus and trigonometric work differs in presentation from the main syllabus, rather than one who simply knows the mathematics.

subjects.name: Computer Science (0478)
subjects.description: A subject where experienced teaching and competent programming are different skills. The marks sit in pseudocode conventions, completed trace tables and the validation against verification distinction, none of which a strong developer necessarily teaches well. Ask what the paper rewards, not what languages the tutor writes in.

subjects.name: Economics (0455) and Business Studies (0450)
subjects.description: Experience shows in diagram discipline and in how evaluation bands are described. A tutor who has marked these papers knows that an unlabelled axis costs marks a well-argued paragraph cannot recover, and that evaluation requires a judgement reached rather than a balanced list, which is the single most common misunderstanding in both subjects.

subjects.name: Geography (0460) and History (0470)
subjects.description: Source-handling subjects where experience buys knowledge of what counts as using evidence. Quoting a figure from a resource, attributing a source and answering the printed command word are the habits that separate bands, and a tutor who has marked these papers corrects them in minutes rather than describing them in general terms.

abu-dhabi/experienced-igcse-tutor.regionsTitle: Local supply of experienced subject tutors, by community
abu-dhabi/experienced-igcse-tutor.regionsIntro: Experience is unevenly distributed across the emirate, and it does not follow income. It follows where long-established schools sit, because that is where tutors with several series behind them tend to live. These notes describe what families in each community can realistically find within a drive.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: Close to several of the emirate's longest-running schools, so the local pool of tutors with multiple series behind them is relatively deep. Families here usually have a recommendation in hand already; the useful work is testing the claim rather than finding a name.

regions.name: Al Rawdah and Al Wahda
regions.note: Central and well connected, with group tuition widely available. Experienced individual supply narrows sharply at the top of the Extended tier in the separate sciences, which is where families in these districts most often widen the search beyond the drive.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Strong school provision and a mobile cohort, so a tutor here may have experience of three school systems and one examination board. The specific question to ask is how many series they have actually prepared candidates for, which is a different number from years taught.

regions.name: Al Jubail Island
regions.note: A small and relatively new residential community with no concentration of tuition supply of its own. Travel to the island or the corridor is a real cost in the evening, so the online format changes what is available rather than what is convenient.

regions.name: Al Samha and Al Rahba
regions.note: Northern communities on a long commute from the central island. Published in-home rates for this stretch carry the most travel inside them, and a travelling tutor cannot reliably hold an early evening slot. Sessions from 6.30pm onwards are the realistic window.

regions.name: Al Ghadeer
regions.note: On the emirate boundary, where families often look towards Dubai supply as well as Abu Dhabi. That widens the pool but also widens the drive, and it introduces a second regulator's school system into the comparison, which is worth noting when reading school reports.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Heavy British-curriculum enrolment and predictable Year 11 demand for maths and the separate sciences. Experienced tutors here book out early in mock season, typically from November, so a family planning a January start is usually choosing from what is left.

schoolClusters.city: Al Bateen, Al Rawdah and the western island
schoolClusters.note: Long-established island schools, several running IGCSE through to A Level, with inspection outcomes published by ADEK. An inspection report describes the school's provision rather than your child's performance, so read it beside their own marked work. Students we support attend schools across this cluster.

schoolClusters.city: Saadiyat, Al Jubail and Al Reem
schoolClusters.note: Newer international schools with mobile cohorts and mixed board entries. A student transferring mid-course may have been taught a different specification for the same subject name, which is why an experienced tutor asks for the statement of entry before building a plan rather than after the first session.
schools: The British International School Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: Al Reef, Al Samha and the northern communities
schoolClusters.note: Enrolment in these communities has grown faster than local tutor supply, and the distance from the central island is what makes experienced individual provision hardest to find here locally. Demand concentrates on Extended science and Additional Mathematics in Year 11.

modes.title: A single script review
modes.description: One session spent entirely on a marked paper the school has already returned, with the mark scheme beside it, producing a written analysis of where the marks went and what kind of work recovers them. This is the purest test of experience available, because an experienced tutor produces a diagnosis in an hour and an inexperienced one produces encouragement.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one with work marked between sessions
modes.description: Sixty or ninety minutes a week plus a question set marked before the next lesson, so the student's own attempts are the material rather than a textbook exercise. The marking between sessions is where experience is visible and where quotes in this market differ most: two providers at the same hourly rate may include it or not.

The work is built from the mock scripts as they come back, which makes this the most efficient period of the year to buy tuition and the most commonly missed one.

sections.heading: Specification versions, not years: the count that actually matters
paragraphs: Boards revise their syllabuses, and a revision is not cosmetic. Content moves between papers, topics are added or withdrawn, assessment weightings change, and in some cases the number of components a candidate sits changes with them. A tutor who learned a subject from a previous version and has not re-read the current one will teach confidently and partly wrongly, and the student will not know which parts. This is the most common form of stale experience and the hardest for a parent to detect, because nothing about the teaching sounds uncertain.

The check is simple and takes a minute. Ask which version of the specification your child's cohort is being examined on, where that document lives, and what changed from the previous version. A tutor who has read it answers with specifics: these two topics moved, that component's weighting changed, this formula is now given rather than assumed. A tutor who has not will answer in generalities about covering the syllabus. The specifications are published on the boards' own sites for anyone to read, which means there is no excuse for working from memory and no need for a tutor to supply copies.

There is a related and more granular version of the same point about formulae and data sheets. Whether a relationship is printed on the paper or expected from memory changes how a topic should be taught, and it varies by board, by subject and sometimes by version. A tutor who knows which formulae are given has read the paper's front matter; one who teaches every relationship as something to memorise is wasting the student's revision time on recall that carries no marks. That is a small thing and it is exactly the kind of small thing several series of experience produces.

sections.heading: Reading experience off a marked script
paragraphs: The fastest way to assess a tutor is to watch them annotate. Hand over a marked paper in the trial session and ask what they see. The answer separates experience from service length more cleanly than any question about qualifications, because annotation is a skill that only accumulates by doing it to many scripts against a published scheme.

An experienced annotation does four things. It names the criterion a mark was awarded or withheld against, rather than marking by impression. It locates the line at which a multi-step chain broke, rather than marking the final answer wrong. It distinguishes a method loss from a knowledge loss, because those need different work. And it flags where the student answered a different command word from the one printed, which is invisible unless you are looking for it and accounts for a large share of avoidable loss.

An inexperienced annotation ticks, crosses and adds a comment about showing more working. It is not dishonest and it is not useless, but it cannot support a plan, because it does not say what kind of problem the student has. If a tutor hands back a script with four ticks and 'needs more detail', you have bought marking rather than diagnosis, and the difference will show up in March as a term of pleasant sessions with no measurable change. Ask for one answer to be re-annotated with the criterion named; a tutor who marks to the scheme can do it immediately.

sections.heading: What several series teach a tutor that one cannot
paragraphs: Series experience is cumulative in a specific way. Each cycle a tutor sees which topics were set and how, which questions a cohort collectively misread, which command words produced the widest spread of answers, and what the board's own examiner report said about it afterwards. Over several series that becomes a working knowledge of a paper's behaviour, and it is the reason an experienced tutor can look at a question and say what the common wrong answer will be before the student writes it.

That foresight has practical uses. It changes the order of revision, because the topics with the widest spread deserve the most time rather than the ones the student likes least. It changes what gets practised under timed conditions, because the questions that eat time are known. And it changes how a mock is interpreted, since an experienced tutor knows which mock questions were unusually hard and which were unusually generous, and therefore how much of a disappointing mark is signal.

What series experience does not give anybody is access to anything unreleased, and this is worth stating plainly because the market blurs it. Examiner reports, past papers, mark schemes and grade threshold information are published by the boards after a series on their own sites. Nobody has advance sight of a paper, nobody knows the boundaries before they are set, and a tutor who implies otherwise is either misrepresenting their position or offering something that should end the conversation. Experience is about pattern recognition in published material, which is valuable and entirely legitimate.

sections.heading: Experience with boards, not only with subjects
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi schools do not all enter the same board, and some enter more than one across their subject offer. A family can therefore have one child sitting Cambridge in the sciences and Pearson in mathematics, graded on different scales with different paper structures. A tutor experienced in one and unfamiliar with the other will teach the subject competently and the paper wrongly, and the student will meet the difference for the first time in the examination hall.

The differences that matter are structural rather than philosophical. How many papers a candidate sits for the subject. Whether tiering exists and how it is handled. Which grade scale applies. Where the assessment weight sits across the components. How practical science is assessed, and whether the school has a choice about it. Whether coursework forms part of the subject at all. Each of those changes what a revision plan should look like, and none of them can be inferred from the subject name.

The honest position for a tutor is to say which boards they have prepared candidates for and to decline the others, and the honest question for a parent is to ask it directly rather than asking whether they can teach the subject. Almost any qualified teacher can teach IGCSE chemistry. Rather fewer can tell you, without looking it up, how the paper set your child is entered for differs from the one the school next door uses, and that is the knowledge you are paying a premium for when you pay for experience.

sections.heading: Experience with the Abu Dhabi school year, month by month
paragraphs: A tutor experienced with this emirate specifically knows the shape of the year, and that knowledge is worth more than it sounds. The school calendar, the mock window, Ramadan and the examination series interact, and a plan built without them drifts. Families usually discover the problem in the third week of a block that cannot now be completed before a paper.

The pattern most Abu Dhabi families recognise runs roughly like this. September and October are for diagnosis, while teaching is still ahead of revision and nothing is urgent. November into January is mock season, which is when the most useful evidence of the whole year arrives and when experienced tutors stop having free slots. February and March are the repair window, where the mock scripts are turned into targeted work and where Ramadan may shift session timing. April is final timed practice, and May and June are the series itself for most candidates.

Ramadan deserves its own sentence because it reliably breaks plans made in January. School days shorten, routines move, and evening study happens at different hours. An experienced tutor asks about it in advance rather than discovering it, and the workable arrangements are usually a shift to post-Iftar timing, shorter and more frequent contacts, or a deliberate pause with set work instead. None of those is a problem if it is planned; all of them are a problem if the plan assumed a fixed 5pm slot all year.

sections.heading: The experience that does not transfer
paragraphs: Four kinds of long service look like IGCSE experience and are not, and each produces a predictable failure. The first is national-curriculum GCSE experience applied to IGCSE. The subjects are close relatives and the assessment is not identical, and the tutor who assumes otherwise will be confident about paper structures that do not apply.

The second is A Level or post-16 experience applied downwards. A tutor used to teaching sixth-formers often pitches above the specification, teaching the mechanism behind a result the paper does not ask for while the student still loses marks on the question that is set. Depth is not the problem at IGCSE; precision against the command word is. The third is single-tier experience. A tutor who has only taught Extended candidates may not know what the Core papers contain, and Core candidates have a different failure mode, usually incompleteness rather than error.

The fourth is subject-adjacent experience, where a strong practitioner teaches a related school subject: a developer teaching Computer Science, an accountant teaching Business Studies, an engineer teaching Physics. The content is safe and the marks are not, because the marks sit in conventions, command words and presentation that only come from preparing candidates. None of these four is disqualifying, and each can be fine with a tutor who knows what they do not know and says so. The warning sign is a tutor who treats the transfer as obvious.

There is a practical way to test any of the four in a few minutes. Ask the tutor to describe one thing about your child's paper set that would surprise somebody who knew the subject but not the specification. A tutor whose experience genuinely transfers has an answer ready, usually about a component weighting, a practical route or a formula that is printed rather than memorised. A tutor whose experience sits elsewhere will answer about the content instead, which is the tell. That is a fair question rather than a trap, because the honest answer is sometimes that they would need to read the current syllabus first, and a tutor who says so and then does it is a better bet than one who improvises.

sections.heading: The examiner claim and how to handle it
paragraphs: Examiner status is the most used credential in this market and the least verifiable. Marking for a board is real work that genuinely sharpens a teacher's understanding of how criteria are applied, so the claim is worth something when true. The problem is that a parent cannot check it, that it is often stated in the past tense without a date, and that it is frequently used to imply something it cannot deliver.

The implication to reject is access. Marking a paper does not give anybody advance sight of a future paper, knowledge of boundaries before they are set, or the ability to influence a result. Boundaries are set by the board after a series is marked, which is precisely why no tutor can promise a grade. If an examiner claim is accompanied by any suggestion of inside knowledge, the right response is to end the conversation, because the claim has stopped being a credential and become a sales device.

The way to handle it fairly is to treat it as one signal among several and test what it should have produced. Someone who has applied a mark scheme professionally can mark an answer aloud, name the criteria, and explain why a fluent response scored in the middle band. They can describe how two candidates with the same content reach different marks. That demonstration is worth more than the title, and it is available in a free trial lesson. For our part, we do not describe tutors as examiners for the examination boards, because current examiner status is not something we can evidence for an individual, and a credential we cannot evidence should not be on a page.
bullets: Marking experience is genuine and sharpens how criteria are applied
It confers no access to unreleased papers, boundaries or results
Test it by asking the tutor to mark an answer aloud against the criteria
Any hint of inside knowledge is a reason to walk away

sections.heading: Week by week: what an experienced tutor will and will not predict
paragraphs: Parents ask how quickly a grade will move, and the answer separates experience from salesmanship faster than any credential. An experienced tutor will make predictions about process and refuse them about outcomes, because the process is in their control and the outcome is decided by a board after the papers are marked.

What can reasonably be forecast: that the component losing marks will be named after the first session; that a timed repeat attempt on the same question type will exist by the fourth; that method errors on a targeted question type should begin falling within three to four attempts; and that on the Extended tier method improvement usually precedes mark improvement by two to three weeks, because those papers reward chains that complete. Those are claims a parent can hold a tutor to, and they are the ones to ask for.

What cannot be forecast is a grade, a number of grades, or a point at which a boundary will be crossed. Grade thresholds are set per series after marking, and a student near a boundary is near it in a way nobody can resolve in advance. A tutor who offers to guarantee an improvement is making a claim about a process they do not control; several providers in this market do it, and it should reduce rather than increase your confidence. The honest version is a measurable process with an unpromised outcome, which is less comfortable to read and considerably more useful to buy.

sections.heading: What an experienced tutor should refuse to do
paragraphs: Experience shows as much in refusals as in teaching, and the refusals are specific. An experienced tutor will not promise a grade, for the reasons above. They will not distribute copied folders of specifications, past papers, mark schemes or grade threshold tables, because those are the boards' copyright and are published on the boards' own sites for anyone to read. They will not claim an approval or accreditation from a board or a regulator, because those are issued to institutions under defined conditions and not to individuals teaching privately.

The most important refusal concerns assessed work. Where an IGCSE subject carries an internally assessed component, the work must be the candidate's own. A tutor may teach the skills, explain the criteria, discuss a plan, question a draft and give written feedback on what the student has produced. Supplying text, or editing a draft until the sentences are no longer the student's, is malpractice, and the consequence falls on the candidate. An experienced tutor states that boundary at the first session rather than negotiating it during a deadline week, and says it to the student directly, because the student is the person who stands to lose the qualification.

There is one more refusal that is specific to this emirate. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff, as reported in the press, bar teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that also addresses serving students affiliated with the teacher's own school. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on a summary. The practical reading is unchanged either way: a teacher offering to tutor their own student privately is offering something they should be declining, and an experienced tutor knows it.
bullets: No grade promises, because boundaries are set after the series is marked
No copied board documents; they are published for anyone to read
No claimed approval from a board or a regulator for an individual tutor
