sections.heading: Which Arabic A course is your child sitting, and what is each component worth?
paragraphs: There are two Arabic A courses and four versions of them, and an alarming number of parents do not know which one their child is on. Arabic A: Literature reads literary works only. Arabic A: Language and Literature splits the course between literary works and non-literary texts, which in Arabic means newspaper columns, speeches, advertising copy, cartoons and social-media posts. Each exists at Standard and Higher Level. The reading list, the Paper 1 task and the HL essay all change depending on which pair your child is in.

The component weightings matter more than the course name, because they tell you where an hour of tutoring buys the most grade. At Standard Level, both papers carry 35% and the individual oral carries 30%. There is no HL essay at SL. At Higher Level, Paper 1 stays at 35%, Paper 2 drops to 25%, the HL essay takes 20% and the oral takes 20%. That redistribution is the single most useful fact on this page for an HL family: at Higher Level, 40% of the grade sits in two pieces of work produced over months, under no time pressure, with feedback available throughout. Most students spend their tutoring hours on the timed papers, which are the half of the grade they can least control.

The practical reading of the table below is that an HL student in DP2 who has not started thinking about the HL essay is carrying a fifth of their grade as unfinished business while paying someone to practise unseen analysis. We generally recommend an HL family spends the first block of sessions on the essay and the oral, then moves to the papers once both are banked. For an SL student, the oral at 30% deserves the same treatment: it is the largest single component and it is almost never rehearsed to time.

One more distinction worth holding. The Paper 1 task is a guided analysis of a text the student has never seen, supported by a guiding question. At HL Language and Literature there are two texts to analyse rather than one, in 2 hours 15 minutes rather than 1 hour 15. That is not a harder version of the same task, it is a pacing problem, and the fix is a timing drill rather than more content.

sections.heading: Reading a marked Arabic A script: what each criterion letter is telling you
paragraphs: Ask the school for the marked script with the criterion marks visible. Not the grade, not the percentage — the four numbers. Once you have those, the diagnosis takes about two minutes and it is the same diagnosis a tutor would charge for an hour to produce.

A low criterion A with a reasonable B means the student is analysing confidently but has misread the text. In Arabic that is often a vocabulary problem in a specific register: a classical construction in a pre-modern text, or an idiom in a column written in a Gulf newspaper's house style. The fix is targeted reading in that register, not more essay practice. A reasonable A with a low B is the commonest pattern of all, and it means the student is explaining what the text says and calling it analysis. The fix is mechanical: every paragraph must name a technique, quote it, and say what effect it produces on a reader. Students who learn that one move routinely gain two or three marks a paper.

A low criterion C means the essay has no spine. The student knows things and says them in the order they occurred to him. This is the fastest criterion to improve and the one most often ignored, because an essay plan feels like a waste of exam minutes until a student has lost five marks for not having one. A low criterion D in a fluent Arabic speaker is almost always register rather than accuracy. The student writes the way they speak, and the Diploma expects formal written Arabic with controlled syntax and precise literary vocabulary. That takes a term, not a session, and it is the gap that surprises bilingual families most.

The table below is the version we use in a first session. It is not a secret and nothing stops you using it yourself at the next parents' evening. The point of writing it down is that it converts a grade into a job list, and a job list is something you can watch being completed.

Healthy A, low B: description masquerading as analysis, the commonest pattern
Low C: no plan, the fastest criterion to move
Low D in a fluent speaker: written register, a term's work

sections.heading: The HL essay needs a draft history, not a rescue
paragraphs: The HL essay is 1,200 to 1,500 words on one work or body of work the student has studied, developed from a line of inquiry the student chooses. It is worth 20% of the Higher Level grade and it is marked out of 20 on the same four criteria as everything else. It is also the component where the boundary between teaching and malpractice is thinnest, so it is worth being precise about what a tutor is for.

A tutor may discuss which of the works studied has analytical potential. A tutor may ask why a proposed line of inquiry is too broad and keep asking until the student narrows it. A tutor may read a draft the student has written and point out that paragraph four asserts something the quotation does not support. A tutor may explain how citations work and check that the referencing matches what the school requires. All of that is teaching and all of it is normal.

A tutor may not supply the sentences. Not an outline the student has not reasoned through, not a model paragraph to adapt, not a rewritten conclusion. The IB's academic-honesty regulations put the consequences of crossing that line on the student, not the tutor, which is the strongest practical argument for keeping the boundary visible. There are services in this market selling finished assessed work. That is a malpractice trigger and the student carries the risk, so we say clearly what we will and will not touch.

What protects a student is a draft history. Version one with the student's own argument, a set of tutor questions rather than corrections, version two responding to those questions, a feedback note, version three. If anyone later asks how the essay came to exist, the answer is on the page. This is also how a parent sees progress on a component that otherwise produces nothing visible for eight weeks: there is a dated chain of drafts, each one better than the last for a reason you can read.
bullets: 1,200-1,500 words, 20% of the HL grade, 20 marks on criteria A to D
A tutor's job on the essay is questions and feedback, never sentences
Keep every draft dated — the chain is the student's own evidence

sections.heading: Diploma Arabic A and the mandatory Arabic stream are two different subjects
paragraphs: This is the single most common confusion in Abu Dhabi parents' evenings, and it costs families money. Private schools in the UAE are required to teach Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies regardless of which international curriculum they are licensed to deliver. That requirement comes from federal rules and is implemented by each emirate's regulator. In Abu Dhabi, private and charter schools are supervised by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which handles the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection ratings.

The mandatory Arabic stream and Diploma Arabic A are not the same subject, are not marked the same way, and frequently are not taught by the same teacher. The regulators' guidance for the mandatory subjects is explicit about separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, specified instructional time, and the language of instruction for each group. The Dubai regulator's published guidance, for instance, calculates mandatory-subject time in 40-minute lesson units and prohibits combined classes for Arab and non-Arab students because the curriculum expectations differ. It also states that additional or different content for those subjects requires prior permission from the Ministry of Education.

So when a student's school Arabic mark is strong and their Diploma Arabic A mark is weak, nothing contradictory is happening. One assesses progress against a Ministry curriculum. The other assesses literary analysis in Arabic against four IB criteria. A tutor who treats them as one subject will spend your hour on the wrong thing. When we take an Arabic A student in Abu Dhabi, we ask which stream the school Arabic sits in and then set it aside, because the Diploma grade is the one that reaches a university admissions office.

The practical consequence for a family in Mohammed Bin Zayed City or Al Shamkha is simple. If the problem is the mandatory stream, the school's own department is the right first stop and the fix is usually free. If the problem is Arabic A criterion B, the school's Arabic specialist may have one Diploma group and little time, and that is where outside one-to-one work earns its rate.
bullets: ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of Abu Dhabi private schools
Mandatory Arabic is a Ministry curriculum requirement, not a Diploma course
Regulator guidance requires separate Arab and non-Arab classes for these subjects
A strong school Arabic mark and a weak Arabic A grade are not a contradiction

sections.heading: What eight weeks of Arabic A sessions should actually show you
paragraphs: Tutoring that cannot be audited is tutoring you have to take on faith, and eight weeks is long enough to stop guessing. The table below is the shape of a first block for an Arabic A student, written as evidence rather than as topics. Each row names the artefact that should exist by the end of that week and what the criterion marks should be doing. If those artefacts are not appearing, the honest conclusion is that the sessions are not working and you should change something.

Week one produces a diagnosis and nothing else: two pieces of existing work read, criterion marks recorded, the set works confirmed, the level and route confirmed. We write down a baseline because a baseline is what makes week eight meaningful. Weeks two to four attack the single weakest criterion. One criterion, repeatedly, on short pieces rather than full papers, because the point is to make one behaviour automatic. By week four there should be two or three short pieces showing the same criterion scoring higher than it did in week one.

Weeks five and six widen to a full component under timed conditions — a complete Paper 1 or a full-length oral rehearsal, marked properly. This is usually where a mark dips, because timing exposes a skill that was fine when there was no clock. That dip is information rather than failure and it is why the block runs eight weeks rather than four. Weeks seven and eight consolidate: a second full component, the criterion marks from week one placed next to the ones from week eight, and a written decision about what the next block should be or whether there should be one.

Not every student moves in eight weeks. A fluent speaker fixing criterion D register is working on a habit laid down over fifteen years, and the realistic timeline is a term. We say so at the start rather than at week nine. What should always be visible after eight weeks, regardless of grade movement, is a stack of marked scripts with dated criterion marks on them, which is a different thing from a report that says the student is engaging well.

sections.heading: What Arabic A tuition costs in Abu Dhabi, and how to audit a quote
paragraphs: No competitor page in this market publishes an AED rate table, which makes it difficult for an Abu Dhabi parent to tell a fair quote from an opportunistic one. The bands below come from published UAE sources and from competitor pages that state their own rates. They are market figures, not IB Gram's price list, and they are given so you can hold any quote — ours included — against something.

At the budget end, platforms advertise online tutoring from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour, and one regional platform lists from around AED 33 to 52. Those rates buy a university student or an early-career tutor, which is a reasonable purchase for primary homework support and a poor one for Arabic A Higher Level. A qualified subject tutor working online sits in the AED 150 to 300 band, with one UAE agency publishing IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. Specialist IB, IGCSE and A-Level tutors run AED 200 to 450 and above; a UK-based agency publishes AED 270, and a UAE rate survey puts specialists at AED 200 to 450 plus. In-home one-to-one, with travel inside the rate, runs AED 180 to 350 by one survey and up to AED 500 on home-tutor listings. Named or examiner-led premium tuition reaches AED 650 at one Dubai provider.

Monthly packages circulate too: around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions, and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. A UAE cost survey estimates monthly spend for weekly one-hour sessions at AED 240 to 600 at the budget tier, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-tier, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 plus for specialist exam-year support. Set those against school fees, which in Abu Dhabi are regulated by ADEK and reviewed on application rather than frozen by decree, and tutoring is usually a single-digit percentage of the annual education bill.

The audit questions are more useful than the number. Does the rate include marking of work submitted between sessions, or is marking billed separately? Is it per hour or per lesson, and how long is a lesson? Does the tutor hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, and will they say so? What happens if the match is wrong after two sessions? Is VAT inside the quoted figure? A provider who answers those five cleanly at AED 280 is better value than one who answers none at AED 180.

sections.heading: Counting back from the May session in an Abu Dhabi school year
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi Diploma students sit the May examination session, and the useful planning exercise is to count backwards from it rather than forwards from today. The IB sets the session dates and publishes them; we do not restate them here because the IB's own site is the only place they should be read from, and dates circulating on secondary sites have not been confirmed against it. Ask your school's IB coordinator for the current session timetable and the school's internal deadlines, which are the ones that actually bind your child.

What does not change is the order of events, and the order is where families get caught. The school's internal deadlines for the HL essay and the individual oral fall months before the written papers, usually in DP2's first two terms. By the time a family starts worrying about Arabic A in the spring, 40% of a Higher Level grade is already submitted and moderated. That is why an HL student who comes to us in DP2 term one gets the essay and the oral first, and the papers afterwards. A student who arrives in March gets the papers, because that is all that is left.

The UAE calendar adds two constraints worth planning around. Ramadan shifts the school day and household routines, and the sensible response is to move sessions later in the evening rather than to pause for a month during a Diploma year. Families who plan post-Iftar slots in advance keep continuity; families who improvise lose three or four weeks. The second is the long summer break between DP1 and DP2, which is the best uninterrupted block of study time in the two-year course and is the one most often wasted. An Arabic A student who reads the DP2 set works properly over that summer starts the year ahead by a term.

For Cambridge and Pearson students in the same household, published board dates are available and show how far ahead entries sit: Cambridge's March 2027 series, for example, has an exam period of 3 February to 4 March 2027 with final entries due 27 November 2026, and results on Direct from 13 May. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November series, with June 2026 results reaching centres on 19 August 2026. Those are the boards' own published figures and they illustrate the same lesson: the deadline that matters is months before the paper.

sections.heading: Permits, ethics rules and what happens if no Arabic A specialist is free
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is a permitted activity rather than an unregulated one. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through MoHRE. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. MoHRE's own service page for it is 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing', applied for through the ministry's smart app, website and e-services system, with a stated two-working-day completion time and no fee listed.

Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No schedule of amounts is published, so we do not quote one, and you should be sceptical of any page that does. What a parent can reasonably do is ask. A tutor who holds the permit will say so without hesitation; one who changes the subject has told you something. Abu Dhabi adds a further constraint: press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff indicates that teachers may not provide paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct points the same way. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it, but the direction is clear and it rules out the arrangement some families ask for first.

The last piece of honesty on this page concerns availability, because nobody else in this market discloses it. Arabic A Higher Level, Literature route, is a narrow specialism. There are weeks when no UAE-based Arabic A specialist has a slot that matches a DP2 student's 18:00 Tuesday. When that happens we say so, and we offer the alternatives explicitly: wait for a named slot to open, take a different time with the specialist who is available, or work with a specialist based outside the UAE teaching on Gulf Standard Time. We do not quietly substitute a general Arabic tutor for an Arabic A specialist and let you find out in week three.

A trial lesson comes first in every case, with one trial per subject, booked before any payment is taken, so you can judge whether the tutor can read your child's script before you commit to a block. If the match is wrong after it, nothing has been spent and we try a different specialist.

process.title: Send the marked work, not the grade
process.description: Before anything is booked, send two pieces of marked Arabic A work with the criterion marks visible, plus the set works and the level. A photograph of the examiner's annotations is worth more than a summary of the report. This is what makes a first session a diagnosis rather than an introduction.

process.title: Match on the component, not the subject
process.description: We match on the specific need: an HL essay supervisor, an oral coach, a criterion B specialist, a register and syntax specialist. Arabic A is four jobs under one name. We tell you which Arabic A route and level the tutor has taught and how recently, and name a second option where there is one.

process.title: Take the trial lesson and set a baseline
process.description: One trial lesson per subject, booked before payment, in which the tutor reads the submitted work and writes down baseline criterion marks. You should finish the trial knowing which criterion is costing the grade and what the first four sessions will target. If that is not clear, the match is wrong.

process.title: Agree the block and the artefacts
process.description: Sessions are booked as a defined block with a stated focus, a session length and a day. Agree in writing what artefact each session produces — a marked script, a recorded rehearsal, a dated draft. Marking of work submitted between sessions is agreed up front rather than discovered on an invoice.

process.title: Review at week eight against week one
process.description: At the end of the block, the week-one baseline sits next to the week-eight marks and we write down what moved and what did not. Then one of three decisions: continue on a new target, change tutor, or stop because the job is done. Open-ended tutoring with no review point is how families end up paying for habit.

whyPoints.title: Every session leaves a marked script behind
whyPoints.description: The output of an Arabic A hour is a piece of the student's own work, annotated against criteria A to D, with the four marks written on it and saved. Three of those side by side answer the only question a parent actually has, which is whether this is working.

whyPoints.title: Specialists, not the nearest available Arabic speaker
whyPoints.description: Online delivery means the Arabic A HL Literature specialist is chosen for having taught the course, not for living near Khalifa City. For a subject this narrow, that is the whole difference between a diagnostic hour and an hour of conversation practice.

whyPoints.title: The academic-honesty line is stated, not implied
whyPoints.description: Our tutors teach, question and give feedback on the student's own work. They do not supply sentences for an HL essay or any assessed component. We put that in writing because the risk of the alternative falls on your child, not on us.

whyPoints.title: Sourced numbers or no numbers
whyPoints.description: Every AED band on this page is attributed to the survey, agency page or platform that published it. Where a date or figure could not be verified from the primary source, this page says so instead of filling the gap. That includes IB session dates, which belong to the IB.

whyPoints.title: Timed to the Abu Dhabi school day
whyPoints.description: Sessions are scheduled in Gulf Standard Time around the real constraint, which is the school run and the mainland commute. Al Reem Island and Khalifa City students generally start later than Al Bateen students, and Ramadan slots are planned before Ramadan rather than during it.

whyPoints.title: Availability is disclosed
whyPoints.description: When no UAE-based Arabic A specialist matches your slot, you are told and given the options, including a specialist outside the UAE teaching on Gulf Standard Time. No substitution happens quietly, and no page here implies a bench depth we cannot evidence.

faqs.question: What does an IB DP Arabic A home tutor in Abu Dhabi cost per hour?
faqs.answer: Published UAE market bands put budget online tutoring at roughly AED 33-65 an hour, a qualified subject tutor online at AED 150-300, and IB specialists at AED 200-450 and above. In-home visits run AED 180-500 because travel sits inside the rate. Diploma Arabic A at Higher Level realistically needs the specialist band. Those are market figures from published sources rather than our price list. When you compare quotes, ask whether marking of work submitted between sessions is included, whether the rate is per hour or per lesson, and whether VAT is inside the figure, because those three answers move the real cost more than the headline rate does.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send an Arabic A tutor to our address in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. Arabic A support for Abu Dhabi families is one-to-one live video, with the student's script shared on screen, annotated during the hour and saved afterwards. For this subject the trade works in your favour: the number of people who have taught Arabic A Literature at Higher Level and marked comparative essays to the Diploma criteria is small in any emirate, and online delivery removes the requirement that one of them lives near your area and is free at the hour your child is.

faqs.question: My child speaks Arabic fluently at home but scores 4 in Arabic A. How is that possible?
faqs.answer: Arabic A is a literary-analysis qualification, not a fluency test. The commonest pattern in a fluent speaker is a healthy criterion A with a low criterion B: the student understands the text and then describes what it says rather than analysing how it works. The second commonest is a low criterion D, which in a fluent speaker is register rather than accuracy — writing in the rhythms of spoken Arabic where the Diploma expects controlled formal syntax and precise literary vocabulary. Neither is a language problem. The first is a technique that takes four sessions; the second is a habit that takes a term.

faqs.question: Should my child be on Arabic A Literature or Arabic A Language and Literature?
faqs.answer: Usually the school decides, and the practical question is whether your child knows which one they are on. Literature reads literary works only and asks for a guided analysis of an unseen literary passage. Language and Literature splits the course between literary works and non-literary texts: columns, speeches, advertising, cartoons. Students who read novels confidently sometimes struggle with Language and Literature because analysing a newspaper column needs a different vocabulary of techniques. If your child is choosing, the deciding factor is which kind of text they can already say something intelligent about under time pressure.

faqs.question: How much of the Higher Level Arabic A grade is finished before the exams?
faqs.answer: Forty per cent. At Higher Level the HL essay carries 20% and the individual oral carries 20%, and both are completed and internally assessed during DP2, months before the written papers. That is the most useful planning fact on this page. An HL family that starts tutoring in DP2 term one should spend the first block on the essay and the oral, because those are the components where unlimited time and feedback are available. By March, only the timed papers remain, and they are the half of the grade a student can least control on the day.

faqs.question: What are the four Arabic A criteria worth on each paper?
faqs.answer: On Paper 1 the four criteria carry 5 marks each out of 20: A understanding and interpretation, B analysis and evaluation, C focus and organisation, D language. On Paper 2 the split changes to A 10, B 10, C 5, D 5 out of 30. The individual oral is marked out of 40 with all four criteria carrying 10 marks. The HL essay is out of 20 with 5 each. Those allocations are the reason to ask the school for criterion marks rather than percentages: the same grade can hide four completely different problems with four different fixes.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Arabic A HL essay without breaking IB rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor may discuss which studied work has analytical potential, push the student to narrow a line of inquiry until it is answerable, read a draft the student has written and point out where a claim is not supported by its quotation, and check that citation matches what the school requires. A tutor may not supply sentences, model paragraphs or an outline the student has not reasoned through. Keep every draft dated, because that chain is what demonstrates the work is the student's own if anyone later asks.

faqs.question: How long is the Arabic A individual oral and what is actually assessed?
faqs.answer: Fifteen minutes: a 10-minute analysis followed by 5 minutes of questions from the teacher. The student examines a global issue through an extract from a literary work and, depending on the course, a second work or non-literary text. It is marked out of 40, with 10 marks each for understanding, analysis, organisation and language. It carries 30% at Standard Level and 20% at Higher Level, which makes it the largest single component at SL. It is also the component least often rehearsed to time, which is why a recorded full-length rehearsal usually gains marks faster than anything else available.

faqs.question: Is the Arabic my child studies for school the same as Diploma Arabic A?
faqs.answer: No. UAE private schools must teach Arabic alongside their licensed international curriculum, and in Abu Dhabi those schools are supervised by ADEK. That mandatory stream follows a Ministry curriculum with specified instructional time and separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students. Diploma Arabic A is a Group 1 literary-analysis course assessed against IB criteria. Different content, different marking, often a different teacher. A strong school Arabic report and a weak Arabic A grade are not contradictory, and a tutor who conflates the two will spend your hour on the wrong curriculum.

faqs.question: What evidence should I expect after eight weeks of Arabic A sessions?
faqs.answer: A stack of marked work with dated criterion marks on it. Specifically: a week-one baseline from two existing pieces, two or three short marked responses showing the targeted criterion moving, one full component sat under timed conditions and marked, and a week-eight comparison against the baseline with a written decision about what comes next. Grade movement in eight weeks is realistic for criterion B or C and unrealistic for criterion D register work, which takes a term. What should always exist is the evidence, separate from whether the grade has moved yet.

faqs.question: Which Abu Dhabi areas do your Arabic A students usually come from?
faqs.answer: Requests cluster in three places. The island — Al Bateen, Al Mushrif, Al Khalidiyah — where Arabic-first households are concentrated and short school runs allow a 16:00 start. The Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor, which generates the most Diploma enquiries in the emirate and where the mainland commute pushes first sessions to 17:00 or later. And the newer island communities, Saadiyat and Al Reem, where Diploma cohorts are small and HL essay support is the common request. Delivery is online in every case, so the area affects timing rather than availability.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in Abu Dhabi need a permit, and can I check it?
faqs.answer: Yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. Tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no schedule of amounts is published, so treat any page quoting a figure with caution. You can simply ask a tutor whether they hold it; the answer, and how readily it comes, tells you most of what you need.

faqs.question: Can my child's own school Arabic teacher tutor them privately for a fee?
faqs.answer: In Abu Dhabi that is the arrangement to avoid. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff indicates teachers may not provide paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct points the same way. Confirm the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it. Practically, it also creates a conflict you do not want: the person marking your child's internal assessment should not be paid separately to improve it.

faqs.question: Can Arabic A sessions move during Ramadan or around school mock weeks?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the families who plan for it keep their continuity. The usual adjustment is a later evening slot, often post-Iftar, agreed before Ramadan begins rather than improvised in the first week. Pausing for a month during a Diploma year is the expensive option, because the HL essay and oral deadlines do not move. Mock weeks are different: we normally keep the session but switch it to marking the mock paper the student has just sat, which is the most useful thing available in that fortnight and costs no extra preparation.

faqs.question: What if no Arabic A specialist is free at the time we need?
faqs.answer: You get told. Arabic A at Higher Level on the Literature route is a narrow specialism, and there are weeks when no UAE-based specialist has a slot matching an 18:00 Tuesday. The options are stated openly: wait for a named slot to open, move to a different time with the specialist who is available, or work with a specialist based outside the UAE teaching on Gulf Standard Time. What does not happen is a general Arabic tutor being substituted for an Arabic A specialist without anyone mentioning it.

faqs.question: Does taking Arabic A affect a UAE university application?
faqs.answer: It can help, but tutoring is not required for any of it. Arabic A alongside an English A course is the usual route to the bilingual diploma, which needs grade 3 or above in both Language A courses; confirm the current conditions with your school's IB coordinator. For Ministry of Education equivalency, the published British-track rules require five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one A-Level at E or two AS-Levels. No IB points threshold has been verified from the ministry's own pages, so verify any figure you are given directly with the authority.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-a-home-tutor.closingHeading: Send the script and we will tell you what it says
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-a-home-tutor.closingBody: The fastest way to find out whether Arabic A tutoring will help your child is to send two pieces of marked work with the criterion marks visible, the set works, and the level and route. Then take a trial lesson, one per subject, booked before any payment, and judge the tutor on whether they can read the script in front of them. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time around the Abu Dhabi school day. If no specialist matches your slot, we will tell you that too.

Arabic A specialists are thinner on the ground than English or Maths tutors, and we tell you what we have before you meet them.

intro.heading: Which Arabic are you paying for?
paragraphs: There are at least three different Arabic lessons in the life of a Diploma student at an Abu Dhabi private school, and the first useful thing a tutor can do is tell a parent which one is causing the problem. The federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, which means every private school in the emirate teaches Arabic regardless of the international curriculum it is licensed for. That is the mandatory stream, it is in the school fees, and it is not the Diploma course.

Arabic A is something else: a Group 1 Diploma course for a student working in Arabic as a best language, taken at Standard or Higher Level, and offered either as Literature or as Language and Literature. It is assessed against the same kinds of criteria as any other Language A course, with a guided analysis of unseen text, a comparative essay on studied works, an individual oral and, at Higher Level, an essay. A strong Arabic speaker can struggle with it, because speaking Arabic at home and writing literary analysis in Modern Standard Arabic are not the same skill.

The confusion costs money. Parents in Al Mushrif or Khalifa City who are told their child is behind in Arabic frequently buy general Arabic tuition when the problem is Diploma literary commentary, or buy Diploma commentary tuition when the problem is the mandatory stream's assessment and the school's own expectations. Those two purchases look identical on an invoice and produce very different results. Establishing which lesson is failing is a conversation with the school and costs nothing.

The regulatory detail here is unusually specific, and it is worth reading because no competitor page in this market covers it. Dubai's regulator, KHDA, publishes the most detailed public guidance on mandatory Arabic: separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes strictly prohibited due to different curriculum expectations and language of instruction; Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Arabic as a first language and for Islamic Education for Arabs; instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with any mandatory subject lesson advised to run at least 25 minutes; and a rule that the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. Those are KHDA's published requirements for Dubai schools. Abu Dhabi private schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, so confirm the emirate's own current requirements with your child's school.

What follows is the money, with its sources. Published AED bands and the honest observation that almost nobody in this market publishes a rate for Arabic specifically. The cost difference between Literature and Language and Literature, and between Standard and Higher Level. Whether a bilingual diploma is worth the extra hours. Why Arabic is excluded from the Ministry of Education's five-subject count for British-track equivalency, which surprises most families. And where Arabic A marks actually go.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-a-tutor.programmesIntro: Arabic appears at several points in an Abu Dhabi student's schooling, and only one of them is a Diploma Group 1 course. These are the three a family is most likely to be weighing, and what each actually costs to support.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Arabic A
programmes.description: A Group 1 course for a student working in Arabic as a best language, available as Literature or as Language and Literature, at Standard or Higher Level. Components follow the Language A pattern: guided analysis of unseen text, a comparative essay on studied works, an individual oral, and at Higher Level an essay. Everything is written and spoken in Modern Standard Arabic rather than in a dialect.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools vary in whether they offer Arabic A at both levels and in both courses, and some offer only one combination. A family planning a bilingual diploma should establish what their school actually runs before DP1 subject choices close, because the option cannot be assembled afterwards.

programmes.name: MYP Language and Literature in Arabic
programmes.description: Arabic can be taken as a Language and Literature subject in the MYP for students working in it as a best language, reported against four criteria. The transferable habit is analytical writing in Standard Arabic rather than vocabulary breadth, and students who have only ever written descriptively find the Diploma's commentary demands abrupt.
programmes.countryNote: Where an Abu Dhabi continuum school has reported MYP criterion scores in Arabic, keep them. They distinguish a student who has always found written Standard Arabic difficult from one whose difficulty began with Diploma-level commentary, and those two profiles need different and differently priced help.

programmes.name: Mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies
programmes.ageRange: All year groups in private schools
programmes.description: A federal requirement rather than an IB course. Private schools must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum. KHDA's published guidance for Dubai schools requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in these subjects and sets instructional time against a 40-minute lesson unit; the Ministry of Education must approve any different or additional content.
programmes.countryNote: This stream is paid for in school fees, and tutoring it is a separate decision from tutoring Arabic A. Parents told their child is weak in Arabic should ask which stream is meant, because the answer determines whether they need a Diploma specialist or a general Arabic teacher at a different rate.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-a-tutor.subjectsIntro: What an Arabic A family actually buys hours against, with the skill each component tests and an honest note on how scarce the right teacher is.

subjects.name: Guided analysis of unseen text
subjects.description: An unseen passage in Arabic with a guiding question, analysed against four criteria. The dominant failure is paraphrase: retelling the passage in better Arabic without making a claim about how it works. Scarce teaching skill, and the component where a specialist is worth the rate.

subjects.name: Comparative essay on studied works
subjects.description: An unseen general question answered through two studied Arabic works. Knowledge and comparative analysis dominate the mark allocation, so the choice of pairing matters as much as the writing. Students often pair works by theme and find nothing structural to compare.

subjects.name: Individual oral
subjects.description: A timed oral in Modern Standard Arabic examining a global issue through set material, followed by questions. Dialect interference under pressure is the most common and most fixable problem, and it responds to recorded practice rather than to more content teaching.

subjects.name: Higher Level essay
subjects.description: An essay developing a line of inquiry about one work or body of work, drafted over weeks under school supervision. The only component that leaves a dated documentary trail, which makes it the clearest evidence a parent gets that hours are producing something.

subjects.name: Modern Standard Arabic register
subjects.description: Fusha is the language of assessment, and a fluent Emirati, Levantine or Egyptian speaker may still write with dialect structures or vocabulary. Register correction is unglamorous, quick to teach and worth a disproportionate number of marks across every component.

subjects.name: Classical and modern Arabic literature
subjects.description: Works span poetry, drama, the novel and classical forms, and the periods are genuinely distant from a teenager's reading. Context teaching matters more here than in most Language A courses, and it is the part a non-specialist tutor cannot improvise.

subjects.name: Arabic poetry and prosody
subjects.description: Metre, rhyme and the conventions of classical forms are technical knowledge, not sensibility. A student who cannot hear a metre is at a disadvantage in unseen analysis that no amount of general reading repairs, and this is one of the narrowest specialisms in the market.

subjects.name: Literature or Language and Literature
subjects.description: The two Arabic A courses differ in whether non-literary material is studied alongside literary works. Students sometimes do not know which course they are enrolled on, which is worth checking before buying hours, because the reading and the papers differ.

subjects.name: Writing commentary under time
subjects.description: Papers are handwritten in Arabic under time pressure. Students who produce strong untimed commentary and weak timed work have a planning problem, visible in one marked script, and drills fix it far more cheaply than additional content teaching.

subjects.name: The learner portfolio
subjects.description: A required record of the student's own work across the course, feeding the oral and the Higher Level essay. A thin portfolio in DP1 becomes expensive in DP2, because the oral and essay then have to be built from scratch under deadline pressure.

sections.heading: Five Arabic lessons, and which of them you are already paying for
paragraphs: A parent in Abu Dhabi can reasonably be confused about what Arabic their child is studying, because a private school may be delivering several things under the same word. The federal baseline is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, so those run alongside whatever international curriculum the school is licensed for. On top of that sits whatever Diploma language course the student has chosen.

The distinctions are not pedantic; they change who you should hire. Arabic as a first language in the mandatory stream is taught to Arab students in Standard Arabic and is a school obligation. Arabic as an additional language is taught to non-Arab students with different curriculum expectations. Islamic Education is separate again, and KHDA's published guidance for Dubai schools states that separate classes must be organised for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Diploma Arabic A is a Group 1 academic course with its own assessment, and it is the only one of these that an IB grade comes from.

The practical test for a family is simple. Ask the school which lesson the concern relates to, and ask for a marked piece of work from it. A weak mark in the mandatory stream is addressed with the school and, where tutoring helps, with a general Arabic teacher at the lower end of the published bands. A weak Diploma commentary is a specialist problem at the higher end. Buying the wrong one is the most common way money is wasted in this subject, and it is entirely avoidable in one conversation.

One further KHDA requirement is worth knowing because it shapes what good teaching looks like: for the mandatory subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. That is a real constraint on how mandatory-stream material may be taught and described, and it is another reason the mandatory stream and the Diploma course should not be run together by one tutor improvising across both.

sections.heading: What an Arabic A tutor costs when the market barely publishes a rate
paragraphs: Published pricing in this market is built around English, Maths and the sciences. Across the competitor pages examined for this project, Arabic appears mostly as a subject label rather than as a priced service, and none of the rate tables found breaks out an Arabic rate. So the honest position is that the AED bands below are general Diploma bands, and an Arabic A quote may land outside them in either direction because supply is thin.

The general bands are these, each the provider's own published figure read in October 2026. Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45, both at the entry end. Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. TutorChase quotes AED 270. Bestimate's rate table shows in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350 and subject specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with monthly estimates for a single weekly hour running AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. BartyED publishes AED 650 at its premium tier.

For Arabic A, scarcity rather than seniority is what moves a quote. An experienced Diploma Arabic A teacher who can mark literary commentary in Modern Standard Arabic and teach classical prosody is a narrow specialism, and a family that finds one should expect to pay in the specialist band and should book earlier in the year than they would for English. A general Arabic teacher who is excellent with the mandatory stream may be unable to help with unseen commentary at all, and will often say so, which is a sign of a good tutor rather than a limitation.

The other variable is format, and it behaves the same way as in every subject: in-home pricing carries travel inside the hour, with Bestimate's in-home band sitting above comparable online figures and independent home tutors quoting up to AED 500. For a scarce specialism that premium is doubly expensive, because it also restricts the pool to people who live near your address. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; tutoring here is delivered one to one over live video, and visiting tutors are a service we run only in India.

sections.heading: Literature or Language and Literature, Standard or Higher: what each choice costs
paragraphs: Arabic A exists as two different courses, and a surprising number of students cannot say which one they are enrolled on. Literature studies literary works only. Language and Literature studies literary works alongside non-literary material such as journalism, speech and advertising, and the papers differ accordingly. Both run at Standard and Higher Level, and both lead to the same Group 1 credit, so the choice is about fit rather than prestige.

The cost implications are real. Language and Literature brings non-literary analysis into the course, which many Arabic-speaking students find more approachable than classical poetry, and that tends to reduce the hours needed. Literature leans harder on classical and modern literary works, where context teaching and prosody matter, and that is the narrower specialism and therefore the more expensive one to support properly.

The level decision is the larger financial one. Higher Level in either course adds works, adds an essay drafted over weeks, and adds reading volume at a point in DP2 when every other subject is also competing for time. A student who takes Arabic A at Higher Level because it feels like their strong subject, and then needs paid support for the Higher Level essay in the same term as an Extended Essay and three Internal Assessments, has made an expensive scheduling decision rather than an academic one. Standard Level in a best language is an entirely respectable choice.

The one case for Higher Level that survives scrutiny is a student intending to use Arabic academically or professionally, or one assembling a bilingual diploma where the Arabic side needs depth. Before committing, ask the school which of the two courses and which levels they actually run, because not every Abu Dhabi school offers all four combinations, and a plan built on an unavailable combination collapses late.

sections.heading: The bilingual diploma, and whether the extra hours earn their keep
paragraphs: A candidate who completes two Language A courses can be awarded a bilingual diploma, and for an Arabic-speaking family in Abu Dhabi that is an appealing prospect: formal recognition on the certificate that the student works at a literary level in both Arabic and English. It is a real distinction and it is also a workload decision with a price attached, so it deserves arithmetic rather than enthusiasm.

The cost is straightforward to estimate. Two Language A courses means two sets of works, two sets of unseen papers, two individual orals and, if both are at Higher Level, two essays drafted in the same academic year. A student who would otherwise take English A and a Group 2 language is swapping a language acquisition course for a second literature course, which is a substantial increase in reading and in written output. If both courses then need support, the tutoring bill is close to double for the language half of the Diploma.

The sensible version is asymmetric. Most students taking two Language A courses are genuinely stronger in one of them, and the support should follow the weaker one rather than being split evenly out of fairness. A student who writes excellent English commentary and struggles with fusha register needs an Arabic commentary block and no English tutoring at all, and the reverse is just as common. Spending equally on both is how a bilingual diploma becomes expensive without becoming more likely.

Whether it is worth it depends entirely on where the student is going. For a university or career path where Arabic literacy at an academic level matters, the recognition is valuable. For a student applying to programmes that will never ask, a strong single Language A grade plus a comfortable Group 2 language may produce a better overall points total for less money and less stress. That is a conversation with the Diploma coordinator and a university adviser rather than with a tutor, and it should happen before DP1 choices close rather than in DP2.

sections.heading: Why Arabic does not count towards the Ministry's five-subject equivalency rule
paragraphs: This is the fact that surprises most Arabic-speaking families in Abu Dhabi, and it is sourced rather than inferred. For equivalency on the British track, the Ministry of Education requires proof of five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade no less than E or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for that count.

Read carefully, that is a statement about which certificates satisfy a specific administrative requirement, not a judgement about the value of Arabic. A student still studies Arabic because federal rules require private schools to teach it, and an Arabic A grade still counts fully towards the Diploma points total and towards university applications that value it. What the rule means is narrower: a family cannot assume Arabic fills one of the five slots in the British-track count, and planning a subject portfolio on that assumption produces an unpleasant discovery at attestation.

One ranking competitor in this market publishes the claim that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects. The sourced rule is five, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded from that five. Getting this right is a genuine accuracy advantage over a page currently ranking, and it matters to a family making subject choices in Year 9 or 10.

For the IB specifically, no points threshold is published on this page, because none has been read on an official Ministry source, and an unsourced figure on a page like this would be worse than silence. Equivalency is a Ministry process that IB Gram neither performs nor guarantees, and tutoring is not required for it. Verify the current requirements on moe.gov.ae or through your emirate's attestation channel before making any decision that depends on them.

sections.heading: Where Arabic A marks actually go: fusha, paraphrase and the unseen passage
paragraphs: Fluent Arabic speakers lose Arabic A marks in a small number of recurring places, and none of them is vocabulary. The first is register. Modern Standard Arabic is the language of assessment, and a student who speaks Emirati, Egyptian or Levantine Arabic at home will import structures and words that read as colloquial in a written commentary. Under time pressure this gets worse, not better. Collecting a student's own recurring register slips into a personal checklist is cheap, unglamorous and produces visible improvement within two or three marked pieces.

The second is paraphrase. Asked to analyse an unseen passage, a strong Arabic speaker will often retell it elegantly. The retelling can be more fluent than the passage and still score in the middle band, because nothing has been claimed about how the text works on a reader. The remedy is the same one that works in any Language A course: a required claim before any device is named, and a required consequence after every observation. Students generally find this easier in Arabic than their teachers expect, once it is explicitly asked for.

The third is classical material. Pre-modern Arabic poetry and prose are genuinely distant from a seventeen-year-old's reading, and metre and rhyme conventions are technical knowledge rather than something to be felt. A student who cannot hear a metre is at a measurable disadvantage in unseen analysis, and this is the narrowest teaching specialism in the subject. It is also the clearest case for paying specialist rates for a small number of hours rather than general rates for many.

The fourth is the oral, where dialect interference and structure cost more marks than content gaps. Recording a full timed run in fusha is uncomfortable and effective: students hear their own code-switching, discover their opening is too long, and usually cut it themselves. Because the words spoken in the examination are the candidate's own, this is work a tutor can support with no authorship question arising at all.

sections.heading: Scarcity, permits and what happens when no Arabic A specialist is free
paragraphs: Honesty about supply is more useful to a parent than a claim of universal coverage, and in this subject supply is the binding constraint. Diploma Arabic A teachers who can mark literary commentary in Modern Standard Arabic and teach classical prosody are a narrow group, and the number available at a particular hour on a weeknight is smaller still. Any platform promising an immediate local match for Higher Level Arabic A Literature is describing a pool it does not have.

Our position is that delivery is online for exactly this reason. The match is made from specialists across our network rather than from whoever lives near your address, and where nobody suitable is free for the level and course your child is sitting, you are told with a realistic date rather than given a general Arabic teacher in the slot. You see the matched tutor's actual teaching background before the trial lesson, which in this subject is the question that decides whether the hour is worth its rate.

The permit position applies to Arabic tutors exactly as it does to any other. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount quoted at you is verifiable.

Two emirate-specific points close this out. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct reflects the same restriction, so your child's own Arabic teacher is not an available option here. And KHDA's guidance for Dubai schools requires that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the relevant approval from KHDA to teach those subjects, which is a school staffing requirement rather than a tutoring one. IB Gram holds no regulator licence or accreditation of any kind and operates no office or centre in the UAE.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the Abu Dhabi calendar and when Arabic work actually happens
paragraphs: Scheduling matters more in this subject than in most, for two reasons. The reading is heavy and it is in a register the student does not use conversationally, so it needs unbroken time rather than snatched twenty-minute blocks. And the Arabic A cohort in Abu Dhabi overlaps substantially with households whose rhythm changes significantly during Ramadan.

School days shorten across the UAE during Ramadan and household evenings reorganise around Iftar, which moves the usable working window later and compresses it. Long timed commentary practice does not fit a post-Iftar slot well; short focused work does. The practical response is to front-load reading and timed papers into the weeks before, and use the Ramadan weeks themselves for oral practice, register work and feedback on drafts already written. Sessions after Iftar at 60 to 75 minutes are productive when the task is specific.

Internal deadlines are the thing to map in advance. If a school's Higher Level essay deadline or internal oral assessment window falls during or immediately after Ramadan, the available working hours in those weeks are genuinely fewer and a draft that slips is unlikely to recover quietly. Identifying those dates in the first term, and moving the drafting earlier rather than hoping, is free and removes most of the pressure.

The wider calendar point applies to every Diploma subject and is worth stating once. Abu Dhabi candidates overwhelmingly sit the May session, and schools build their internal deadlines backwards from the IB's own upload windows, which fall well before the examination period. We do not publish specific IB session or results dates on this page, because they are set and revised by the IB and an out-of-date date is worse than none; your child's Diploma coordinator holds the current calendar and is the right source for it.

process.description: Ask the school whether the concern is the Diploma Arabic A course or the mandatory Arabic stream, and ask for a marked piece from whichever it is. Mapping them in the first term lets the drafting move earlier, which is the cheapest form of insurance available in this subject.

faqs.question: What does an IB Arabic A tutor cost per hour in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No provider found in this market publishes an Arabic-specific rate, so the honest answer uses general Diploma bands and admits the gap. Published figures read in October 2026 run from Tutopiya at AED 33 and EdFlik at AED 45 at the entry end, through Unitors IB from AED 200 and TutorChase at AED 270, to Bestimate's specialist band of AED 200 to AED 450 and above and BartyED at AED 650. For Arabic A expect the specialist band, because scarcity rather than seniority sets the price. IB Gram quotes after a free trial lesson rather than from a list.

faqs.question: Is Diploma Arabic A the same as the Arabic my child already studies at school?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the most expensive confusion in the subject. Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum, and that mandatory stream is already covered by school fees. Diploma Arabic A is a Group 1 academic course chosen by the student, assessed through unseen commentary, a comparative essay, an oral and at Higher Level an essay. A weak mark in one tells you nothing about the other, so ask the school which lesson the concern refers to before hiring anyone.

faqs.question: My daughter speaks Arabic at home. Why is she struggling with Arabic A?
faqs.answer: Because conversational fluency and written literary analysis in Modern Standard Arabic are different skills. A student who speaks Emirati, Levantine or Egyptian Arabic at home will import dialect structures and vocabulary into written commentary, and under time pressure that increases rather than decreases. The second common gap is paraphrase: retelling a passage elegantly instead of making a claim about how it works on a reader. Both are diagnosable from one marked piece, and both respond to a short specialist block rather than to general Arabic conversation practice.

faqs.question: Is Arabic A counted in the Ministry's five-subject equivalency total for the British track?
faqs.answer: On the British track it does not. The Ministry's published requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. A separate requirement covers Advanced Level or Advanced Subsidiary Level subjects. This does not reduce Arabic's value in the Diploma or in university applications, but a family planning a subject portfolio should not assume Arabic fills one of the five slots. Verify the current rule on moe.gov.ae before relying on it.

faqs.question: Which Arabic A course should my son be on, Literature or Language and Literature?
faqs.answer: Literature studies literary works only, across forms and periods, and leans harder on classical and modern Arabic literary material. Language and Literature studies literary works alongside non-literary material such as journalism, speech and advertising, and the papers differ accordingly. Both carry Group 1 credit and both run at Standard and Higher Level. Many Arabic-speaking students find the non-literary strand more approachable than classical poetry, which can reduce the hours needed. Check which course your child is actually enrolled on, because a surprising number cannot say.

faqs.question: Should my son take Arabic A at Higher Level if it is his strongest subject?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Higher Level adds works, adds an essay drafted over weeks, and adds reading volume in the same DP2 term as an Extended Essay and several Internal Assessments. A student who chooses Higher Level because the subject feels comfortable and then needs paid essay supervision alongside everything else has made a scheduling decision rather than an academic one. Standard Level in a best language is entirely respectable. Higher Level makes clear sense where Arabic literacy matters for the intended university or career, or where a bilingual diploma needs depth on that side.

faqs.question: How does a bilingual diploma work, and does it double the tutoring bill?
faqs.answer: A candidate completing two Language A courses can be awarded a bilingual diploma, which is genuine recognition that they work at a literary level in both languages. The workload is real: two sets of works, two orals and, at Higher Level, two essays in the same year. It need not double the bill, because almost every student is stronger in one of the two languages and the support should follow the weaker one rather than being split evenly. Decide before DP1 choices close, since the combination cannot be assembled later.

faqs.question: Can a general Arabic teacher help with Diploma commentary?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and a good one will tell you honestly when they cannot. Teaching the mandatory Arabic stream well is a different skill from marking literary commentary against Group 1 criteria and teaching classical metre and rhyme conventions. A tutor who says the commentary is outside their experience is demonstrating judgement rather than weakness. Where only general Arabic support is available, it can still help with register and fluency while the school's own teacher carries the commentary, and that split is sometimes the most cost-effective arrangement available.

faqs.question: Why does classical Arabic poetry cause so much trouble?
faqs.answer: Because metre and rhyme conventions are technical knowledge rather than something a reader feels, and pre-modern Arabic is genuinely distant from a teenager's everyday language. A student who cannot hear a metre is at a measurable disadvantage in unseen analysis, and no amount of general reading repairs it. This is the narrowest teaching specialism in the subject and the clearest case for buying a small number of specialist hours rather than many general ones. Ask directly whether a prospective tutor has taught classical material at Diploma level.

faqs.question: How many hours does an Arabic A student in Abu Dhabi usually need?
faqs.answer: The common shape is a diagnostic session, a commentary block of four to six hours, two or three recorded oral sessions in Modern Standard Arabic, and for Higher Level candidates four to six sessions of essay supervision. That is roughly ten to seventeen paid hours across the two Diploma years, concentrated around internal deadlines rather than spread weekly. A standing weekly slot across twenty-four months is rarely the right structure here, and a tutor proposing one without asking about deadlines has not read the course.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Arabic A Higher Level essay?
faqs.answer: Yes, inside a firm boundary. A tutor may teach what each criterion rewards, discuss whether a line of inquiry is answerable at the required length, read a dated draft and name where the argument stalls or where words are spent badly, correct recurring register problems, and teach cutting as a technique. A tutor may not supply sentences, rewrite a paragraph into final form, choose the line of inquiry, or hand over a previous candidate's essay to adapt. The test is whether the student could have produced that version unaided and can explain why it is stronger.

faqs.question: Can my child's Arabic teacher at school tutor him privately?
faqs.answer: Not in Abu Dhabi. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition permit carries a code of conduct reflecting the same restriction. It is a regulatory position rather than a school preference, so asking does not help. What the school's teacher can do is explain what the marks mean and which component is weak, which is useful and free, and an independent tutor can then work from that information.

faqs.question: Do Arabic A sessions work during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, with a change of content rather than frequency. School days shorten across the UAE and household evenings reorganise around Iftar, which moves the usable window later and compresses it. Long timed commentary practice is a poor fit for a post-Iftar slot; oral practice in fusha, register work and feedback on drafts already written all work well at 60 to 75 minutes. The sensible plan front-loads reading and timed papers into the weeks before and identifies any internal deadline falling in or just after those weeks during the first term.

faqs.question: What happens if no Arabic A specialist is available when we need one?
faqs.answer: You are told, with a realistic date, rather than matched to someone who cannot do the work. Diploma Arabic A teaching is a narrow specialism and the pool available at a given weekday hour is small, so we would rather disclose the limit than fill a slot. Where only partial coverage exists we will say what it covers: a tutor who can handle register and oral practice but not classical prosody, for instance. Lessons are delivered one to one over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India.

intro.heading: Eighteen months, no Arabic, and a Group 2 grade to produce
paragraphs: Arabic ab initio is the Diploma's beginner language course, offered at Standard Level only, for students with little or no prior experience of the language. In Abu Dhabi it is usually chosen by one of two students: a new arrival who joined an international school in Year 11 or 12 and needs a Group 2 subject, or a student who has sat through years of school Arabic without ever becoming literate in it and has been placed, honestly, at the beginning. Both have the same problem. The course assumes nothing, which means everything has to be built inside the Diploma's own timetable while five other subjects run alongside it.

The thing that makes Arabic ab initio different from French or Spanish ab initio is that the first obstacle is not grammar or vocabulary. It is the writing system. Twenty-eight letters, most with four different shapes depending on where they sit in a word, written right to left, joined in cursive, with the short vowels that would tell a reader how to pronounce a word normally left off the page entirely. A beginner in Spanish can read a word on day one and mispronounce it. A beginner in Arabic cannot find the word.

That single fact reorganises the whole teaching plan. Reading fluency is not a prerequisite to be cleared in a fortnight; it is a term's structured work, and it is the term that decides the grade. Every mark in Paper 2 depends on reading unvocalised text at speed. Every mark in Paper 1 depends on producing it. Students who are rushed through the script in three weeks so the course can get on to vocabulary spend the next eighteen months guessing at words, and their listening score never explains why.

The second organising fact is the prescribed content. Arabic ab initio covers five themes — identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet — and twenty prescribed topics distributed across them. Unlike Arabic B, where themes are broad territories, the ab initio topics are a finite list, and that makes coverage auditable. A student three months from the examination session can be shown exactly which of the twenty they have working vocabulary for and which they do not. Most families have never seen that list. It is the most useful document in the course.

On delivery, we are plain: IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses in Abu Dhabi, or anywhere in the UAE. Home visits are a service we run only in India. Arabic ab initio sessions are one-to-one over live video, which suits a beginner better than most subjects: handwriting is corrected on a shared screen while the student forms the letter, audio is played and replayed from the same window, and every session leaves a saved record of which letters, words and topics were covered. For a course that is essentially an eighteen-month build, that record is the plan.
