abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-home-tu.programmesIntro: Ab initio students have usually not come up through an IB language pathway, which is why they are in it. Understanding what the surrounding programmes do explains who ends up here and when.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic ab initio is a Group 2 language acquisition course at Standard Level, designed for genuine beginners. It assesses productive, receptive and interactive skills across five themes and twenty prescribed topics. There is no literature requirement and no Higher Level option, so the whole course is a controlled build from the writing system upwards to short, accurate communication.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools place students into ab initio on evidence of prior experience, and the IB sets the eligibility principle. A student who has had years of effective Arabic teaching cannot simply move down to ab initio for an easier grade, and schools in the emirate are generally careful about this because the course is intended for beginners.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language Acquisition runs in phases, and a student finishing MYP5 in phase 1 of Arabic is close to the ab initio starting point rather than the Arabic B one. The phase a school records at the end of MYP5 is the single best piece of evidence for which Diploma course fits, and it is worth asking for explicitly.
programmes.countryNote: Students arriving in Abu Dhabi from outside the region in Year 10 or 11 often have no MYP Arabic phase at all, which is the cleanest route into ab initio. Schools on Saadiyat and Al Reem with high international mobility see this pattern most, and their ab initio groups are correspondingly larger.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Primary Arabic for non-Arab children builds spoken familiarity and recognition of vocalised text, usually without systematic work on reading unvocalised Arabic. A child can leave the PYP able to greet, count and recognise words on a flashcard, which is a long way from reading a short paragraph.
programmes.countryNote: Families who arrive in Abu Dhabi during primary and expect school Arabic to produce literacy by Year 12 are frequently surprised. The useful checkpoint is whether the child can read an unfamiliar unvocalised word aloud, because that, not vocabulary count, separates an ab initio candidate from an Arabic B one.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme includes a language development component with a portfolio rather than an examined course. For a student staying in the UAE for work, practical spoken Arabic with no examination is sometimes a better fit than ab initio, and it carries no script-fluency requirement.
programmes.countryNote: CP is rare in Abu Dhabi relative to the Diploma, but it is worth knowing it exists before committing a reluctant beginner to an examined course. Where a family's goal is workplace Arabic rather than a Diploma grade, the honest recommendation is sometimes not ab initio at all.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-home-tu.subjectsIntro: Beginners in Arabic rarely need a second language tutor, but they often need support in the subjects where unfamiliar technical English and heavy reading loads collide with a Group 2 course that is eating their evenings. These are the requests that arrive alongside ab initio.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: Beginner Diploma Arabic: the script, the twenty prescribed topics, two short writing tasks, a listening and reading paper worth half the grade, and a visual-stimulus oral. The limiting factor for almost every student is reading speed in unvocalised text, which is why the first term matters more than the last.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: The next course up, for students with real prior Arabic. Ab initio students sometimes ask about moving across after a strong first year; it is rarely sensible mid-course, because Arabic B assumes a reading range and a vocabulary base that eighteen months of beginner work does not produce.

subjects.name: French ab initio
subjects.description: The alternative beginner course at several Abu Dhabi schools, with the same component structure and weightings. French looks easier because the alphabet is familiar, which misleads students: its listening paper is harder than the script makes it look, while Arabic's difficulty is visible from day one.

subjects.name: Spanish ab initio
subjects.description: Also structurally identical, and the beginner course most often chosen for its transparent spelling. A family comparing Arabic ab initio with Spanish ab initio is really comparing a front-loaded difficulty with an evenly distributed one, and local exposure in the UAE favours Arabic.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Taken by students for whom English is an additional language, with the same three-skill architecture as every Group 2 course. Students doing both English B and Arabic ab initio get a structural discount: learning how a receptive-skills paper works once helps in both.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The commonest companion request. The exploration is 20% of the grade and is a written piece produced over weeks, which makes it schedulable around a language build. Students new to a UK or IB system often lose marks on presentation conventions rather than mathematics.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Reading-heavy with a pre-release case study, which competes directly with Arabic reading practice for evening time. Sequencing matters: the case study has a fixed release window, and the Arabic build does not, so the Arabic can bend around it.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: A popular interdisciplinary choice with strong local material on water scarcity, energy and urban growth in the UAE. The practical investigation is internally assessed, and the write-up skills overlap with the structured planning an ab initio student needs anyway.

subjects.name: Digital Society
subjects.description: Concept-led and discussion-heavy, with an internal assessment built around a real-world inquiry. Students who find Arabic reading slow often do well here because the course rewards argument rather than recall, and Arabic-language source material is available for the inquiry.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Portfolio-based, with the comparative study and process portfolio taking most of the two years. It is the subject most often paired with a demanding language build, because studio time is flexible and can give way in a heavy Arabic term.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The exhibition and the 1,600-word essay contribute up to 3 points with the Extended Essay. Beginners in a new writing system often write unusually well on knowledge and language, since the experience of being illiterate in a language they hear daily is a live example.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: A 4,000-word independent research essay in a subject the student is studying. An ab initio student would not write it in Arabic, and should not be encouraged to; the right choice is a subject where their reading is fast. Support is question narrowing and feedback on the student's own drafts.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-home-tu.regionsIntro: Arabic ab initio requests come disproportionately from the parts of Abu Dhabi with the most international movement, because a mid-school arrival is how most students end up in a beginner language course. Timing, not geography, is what the area changes.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach

regions.name: Al Maryah Island

regions.name: Al Zahiyah

regions.name: Al Bandar

regions.name: Shakhbout City

regions.name: Al Jubail Island
regions.note: Low-density community between the mainland and Yas, with families spread across several school catchments. Long drives mean an evening slot is usually more reliable than a late-afternoon one.

schoolClusters.note: Campuses with high international turnover, which is why their beginner language groups exist at all. A student joining in Year 11 from outside the region is the typical ab initio candidate here.

schoolClusters.city: Al Raha, Khalifa City and the mainland corridor
schoolClusters.note: The emirate's largest IB continuum belt. Most students here have followed MYP language acquisition, so ab initio groups are smaller and made up mainly of recent arrivals rather than continuing students.

schoolClusters.city: Central island schools

sections.heading: What a beginner Arabic tutor in Abu Dhabi is actually being asked to do
paragraphs: The job has a defined shape, which is unusual in tutoring. A student who cannot read Arabic needs to reach a Group 2 Standard Level grade in roughly eighteen months, with five other Diploma subjects running at the same time and no possibility of the deadline moving. Everything about an ab initio plan follows from that: what gets taught first, what gets cut, and what is honestly out of reach.

The order is not negotiable. Reading and writing the script come first, because every other component depends on them. Working vocabulary across the twenty prescribed topics comes second, built topic by topic rather than as word lists. Examination technique comes third and takes surprisingly little time once the first two exist. Students who are taught in the reverse order — technique and phrases first, script somehow absorbed along the way — plateau at a level where they can produce memorised sentences and cannot read an unfamiliar question.

What is honestly out of reach is worth stating too. Eighteen months of beginner Arabic does not produce a student who can watch Arabic news comfortably, read a novel or hold an unstructured adult conversation. It can produce a student who reads a short unvocalised paragraph on a familiar topic, writes 70 to 150 words accurately, follows clearly spoken Modern Standard Arabic on a prescribed theme, and talks about a photograph for four minutes with structure. That is what the course asks for, and it is achievable. Promises beyond it should be treated with suspicion.

Delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; that service exists only in India. For a beginner the online format earns its place rather than merely being acceptable: handwriting is corrected on a shared screen as the letter is being formed, audio replays from the same window without anyone fetching a device, and each session leaves a saved record of exactly which letters, words and topics were covered. For an eighteen-month build, the record is the curriculum.
bullets: Fixed deadline, defined syllabus, no Higher Level to worry about
Order: script, then the twenty topics, then paper technique
Realistic outcome: short accurate writing and structured speech on familiar topics
Not realistic: comfortable news comprehension or unstructured adult conversation

sections.heading: The Arabic writing system is a term's work, and it is the term that decides the grade
paragraphs: Twenty-eight letters, most taking four shapes depending on whether they stand alone, open a word, sit inside it or end it. Written right to left and joined in cursive, so word boundaries have to be learnt rather than seen. Several letters differ only in the number and position of dots. And the short vowels that tell a reader how a word is pronounced are written only in children's books, the Qur'an and language textbooks — in ordinary Arabic they are simply absent, so reading means recognising a word's consonant skeleton and supplying the vowels from knowledge.

That last point is the one that catches teaching plans out. A beginner course that keeps the short vowels on the page indefinitely produces a student who reads fluently in a system the exam does not use. The vowels have to go, deliberately and early, and the removal has to be planned: fully vocalised text for the first few weeks, partially vocalised for the next few, unvocalised familiar words soon after, unvocalised unfamiliar words last. Students who are moved off vocalised text at the right time read unfamiliar Arabic by month five. Students who are not are still guessing in DP2.

Letter order matters as well. Teaching the alphabet alphabetically means a student meets letters that look nothing alike while waiting weeks for the ones that share a shape. Teaching by shared skeleton — the group that differs only by dots, the group with the same tail, the non-joining letters together — lets a student read actual words in week one and makes the confusable pairs explicit instead of accidental. It also front-loads the mistakes, which is where a tutor is most useful.

Handwriting is not a decorative skill here. Paper 1 is handwritten and a letter formed wrongly can read as a different letter, which costs message marks as well as accuracy. This is the single strongest practical argument for the online format in this subject: the student writes on a shared screen and the tutor sees the stroke order as it happens, rather than inspecting the result and guessing how it was produced. sections.heading: Five themes, twenty prescribed topics, and why the list should be on your wall
paragraphs: Arabic ab initio content is prescribed rather than suggested. Five themes — identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet — carry twenty topics between them, and the examination draws on that list. For a beginner course this is a gift, because it converts an open-ended language into a finite syllabus. Twenty topics, each needing perhaps forty to sixty usable words and a handful of structures, is a countable job.

Most ab initio students have never seen the list laid out. They experience the course as a sequence of unrelated lessons: a week on family, a week on food, a week on the environment, with no sense of how many weeks there are or whether anything has been missed. By DP2 nobody can say which topics are secure. The fix is a ledger: twenty rows, each marked as covered, revisited or open, updated every session. It takes a minute a week and it is the difference between revising and worrying.

The ledger also makes triage possible. A student four months from the session with eight topics open cannot do all eight properly, and pretending otherwise wastes the four months. The sensible move is to secure the topics with the widest vocabulary overlap first — the ones whose words reappear elsewhere — and accept thin coverage on the most specialised. That is a decision a family should make consciously with the evidence in front of them, not one that happens by default because time ran out.

Vocabulary load differs more between topics than students expect. Topics about daily life recycle words the student already has; topics about technology, the environment or social organisation introduce abstract nouns that appear nowhere else in the course. A tutor who teaches the topics in list order rather than in overlap order makes the course harder than it needs to be. The table below groups them by what they actually cost.

sections.heading: What Arabic ab initio actually examines, and in how long
paragraphs: There are three components and no coursework. Paper 1 is the productive paper: one hour, two short written tasks, 25% of the grade. Paper 2 is receptive: a 45-minute listening section and an hour of reading, 50% between them. The individual oral is conducted and marked by the school and moderated by the IB, worth the remaining 25%, and it starts from a photograph linked to one of the five themes. Standard Level is the only level, so there is no second syllabus to worry about and no literary works to read.

Half the grade in receptive skills is the headline, and for a beginner it is the right place for most of the work to go. A student cannot write what they cannot read, and the listening section exposes gaps in vocabulary that writing practice hides, because in writing the student simply chooses the words they know. In listening they get the words the examiner chose. A student who scores well on writing and badly on listening has a vocabulary breadth problem, not a technique problem, and the honest response is more topic coverage rather than more past papers.

Paper 1's two tasks ask for short, controlled pieces within stated word ranges printed on the paper. For a beginner, the discipline is writing less rather than more. A student who attempts complex sentence structures they do not control produces errors in every line; a student who writes short accurate sentences with correct agreement and a couple of connectives scores better and finishes in time. This is counter-intuitive to ambitious students and is one of the most reliable mark gains available in the course.

The oral is where beginners most often outperform expectations, because four minutes of structured speech about a photograph is a trainable performance rather than a test of range. A reliable structure — what is in the image, where and when it is, what the people are doing, what the student thinks about it — carries a candidate through even when vocabulary runs short. The marks reward language, message and interaction, and interaction credits things like asking for a question to be repeated, which beginners are often too embarrassed to do.

sections.heading: How a beginner practises listening when they only know four hundred words
paragraphs: Advice to listen to Arabic radio is useless to an ab initio student. Unfiltered Arabic at native speed with unlimited vocabulary is noise, and twenty minutes of noise teaches nothing except that Arabic is impossible. Beginner listening practice has to be graded, topic-linked and short, and it has to be built around the words the student actually has.

What works is narrow and repetitive. Audio on a prescribed topic the student has already covered, spoken in clear Modern Standard Arabic, thirty to ninety seconds long. Listened to twice, as the exam does, with answers written. Then — and only then — the transcript, read against the answers, with every word that was known on the page but not recognised in the ear written down. That gap between reading knowledge and listening recognition is the whole problem, and the list of words that live on the wrong side of it is usually short and highly repetitive.

Numbers, dates and times deserve their own treatment, because they defeat beginners more reliably than anything else and they appear in almost every listening section. Arabic numerals in speech involve agreement patterns that are genuinely irregular, and a student who has learnt to read numbers on a page may not catch them at speed. Fifteen minutes a week on numbers alone, for a term, is disproportionately valuable and almost never done.

The other half of the fix is deliberate exposure to different voices. A student who has only ever heard their teacher's Arabic has calibrated to one accent, one pace and one set of habits. The examination audio will not sound like that. Three or four different speakers across a term is enough to break the dependency, and it is far easier to arrange in an online session where any clip can be played from the same screen than it is in a classroom with one teacher and a speaker on the wall.
bullets: Graded, topic-linked audio of thirty to ninety seconds — not Arabic radio
Twice only, under time, transcript afterwards
Keep the list of words known by eye but not by ear — it is the real gap
Numbers, dates and times: fifteen minutes a week for a term
Deliberately vary the speaker so the student is not calibrated to one voice

sections.heading: The individual oral: a photograph, four minutes, and a structure to fall back on
paragraphs: The ab initio oral begins with a visual stimulus, a photograph connected to one of the five themes. The student has supervised preparation time, then describes and discusses the image, then answers questions, with the conversation widening beyond the image before the end. It is marked out of 30 on language, message and interactive skills, and it is worth a quarter of the grade. For most beginners it is the component with the most available upside.

The reason is that it is a performance with a predictable shape. Vocabulary range is limited for every ab initio candidate, so the differentiator is not range but structure. A candidate who describes everything in the photograph and stops has given the examiner four minutes of inventory and earned message marks accordingly. A candidate who names what is there, places it in a context, says what the people are doing and then offers a view with one reason has produced an actual response, using no more words than the first candidate did.

We teach four moves and drill them until they survive nerves: what the image shows, where and when this is happening, what is being done and by whom, and what the student thinks about it with one reason attached. The moves are deliberately mechanical because the student will be under pressure in a second language they have had for eighteen months. Mechanical is an advantage in that situation. Fluency is not what is being tested; communication is.

The interactive marks are the ones beginners give away out of embarrassment. If a question is not understood, the credited behaviour is to ask for it to be repeated or rephrased, in Arabic. Beginners instead guess, answer the wrong question, and lose message marks as well as interaction marks. Teaching three fixed phrases for asking for a repeat, and insisting the student use them in rehearsal, is a two-minute intervention with a measurable payoff. Recording rehearsals is what makes it stick, because the student hears themselves guessing and recognises it.
bullets: Four moves: what, where and when, who is doing what, and a view with a reason
Mechanical structure beats improvised range under exam pressure
Three fixed phrases for asking a question to be repeated, used in every rehearsal
Record the rehearsals — the student has to hear the guessing to stop it

sections.heading: Arriving mid-course in Abu Dhabi: two honest timelines
paragraphs: A large share of ab initio students in this emirate did not plan to take Arabic. They arrived at an Abu Dhabi school partway through, needed a Group 2 subject, and ab initio was the only honest placement. How much can be done depends entirely on how many months are left, and the answer is better stated as a plan than as encouragement.

A student starting at the beginning of DP1 has the full build available and should finish comfortably. The script goes in over the first term, the twenty topics spread across the remaining four, and the final months go to paper technique and oral rehearsal. Twice-weekly sessions during the script phase and weekly thereafter is the usual shape, with the summer between DP1 and DP2 used for reading volume rather than new content. This is the only version of the course with no compromises in it.

A student starting in DP2 is on a different plan and should be told so. There is not time for a leisurely script phase, so reading goes in intensively over six to eight weeks while topic work runs alongside it, and coverage is triaged: the topics with the widest vocabulary overlap first, the specialised ones last or not at all. A reasonable Group 2 grade is still achievable; a strong one depends on how much of the evening the student can genuinely commit, and that is their decision to make honestly.

A student starting after the winter of DP2 is in salvage territory, and the honest conversation names that. The work becomes examination survival: enough reading to attempt the passages, reliable structures for the two writing tasks, a drilled oral structure, and ruthless prioritisation of the topics most likely to recur. We will take that work on and we will not pretend it produces the same outcome as eighteen months. Families who are told otherwise are being sold the comfortable answer rather than the useful one.

sections.heading: Eligibility, permits, and what ab initio does for a UAE application
paragraphs: Eligibility first, because it is asked constantly. Arabic ab initio is for students with little or no previous experience of the language, and the judgement is made by the school within the IB's framework. A student who has had years of effective Arabic teaching cannot move down into ab initio to secure an easier grade, and Abu Dhabi schools generally police this carefully given how many of their students have had mandatory Arabic for a decade. Where a student has sat in Arabic lessons for years without becoming literate, the honest position is a conversation with the school about evidence rather than an assumption either way.

Private tutoring in the UAE needs a permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page calls it 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing' and lists a two-working-day completion time with no fee. Tutoring without it attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no schedule of amounts is published, so no figure is quoted here. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools, and its reported professional-ethics rules bar school staff from paid tutoring of students enrolled at their own school.

On university applications, the useful position is a narrow one. Ministry of Education equivalency rules for the British track require five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count of five, plus one accredited A-Level at E or two AS-Levels at the same grade. The American track specifies SAT Math of at least 450 and English evidence through IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or SAT reading and writing of 450. No IB points threshold has been verified from the ministry's own pages, so we publish none, and neither should anyone else. Equivalency is a process the authority runs; it is not something a tutoring provider performs, guarantees or accelerates, and tutoring is not required for it.

What ab initio does do is give a student a credited Group 2 subject, a beginner's working Arabic in the country they live in, and a genuine foundation if they continue the language later. What it does not do is make them a bilingual candidate or substitute for Arabic A on any bilingual-diploma route. Anyone suggesting otherwise should be asked for the IB regulation that says so.

process.title: Tell us how much Arabic there genuinely is
process.description: Can the student read the alphabet? Read a vocalised word? Read an unvocalised one? Write their name unaided? Those four answers place a beginner precisely and take two minutes to collect. Vague answers like 'a bit from school' produce the wrong plan, so we ask for the four specifics instead.

process.title: Fix the deadline before anything else
process.description: Which session is the student sitting, and how many months is that from today? The plan for eighteen months and the plan for eight are different plans, not the same plan at different speeds. We write the number down first because it decides whether the script phase can breathe or has to be compressed.

process.title: Match a tutor who teaches beginners by choice
process.description: Teaching the script well is a specific skill and not every strong Arabic teacher enjoys it. We match tutors who teach ab initio deliberately, say how recently they have taken a beginner through a full cycle, and name a second option where one exists.

process.title: Take the trial lesson on the alphabet
process.description: One trial per subject, before any payment, spent on actual letters rather than on introductions. By the end the student should be able to read and write a short vocalised word, and you should have a week-by-week outline of the script phase. If neither exists, the match is wrong.

process.title: Run the script phase twice weekly, then slow down
process.description: Letter recall decays quickly at the start, so the opening block is twice weekly for six to twelve weeks. Once unvocalised familiar words are being read, sessions drop to weekly and move onto topics. Front-loading intensity is cheaper over the full course than spreading it evenly.

process.title: Keep the twenty-topic ledger visible
process.description: Twenty rows, each marked covered, revisited or open, updated every session and shared with you. It takes a minute a week and it is what makes triage possible when time gets short. A course without this ledger cannot tell you what has been missed until the exam does.

whyPoints.title: The script is treated as the main event
whyPoints.description: Reading unvocalised Arabic is the limiting factor on every component, so it gets a planned build with stages and weeks attached rather than a fortnight at the start. Short vowels are removed deliberately and on schedule, not left on the page because it feels kinder.

whyPoints.title: Handwriting is corrected as it happens
whyPoints.description: Paper 1 is handwritten, and a letter formed wrongly reads as a different letter. On a shared screen the tutor sees stroke order as the student writes, which is something an inspected finished page cannot show.

whyPoints.title: Coverage is countable
whyPoints.description: Twenty prescribed topics, logged every session as covered, revisited or open. When four months remain and eight topics are open, that is a decision to be made with evidence rather than a discovery to be made in the exam hall.

whyPoints.title: Listening practice is graded, not aspirational
whyPoints.description: Thirty to ninety seconds of clear Modern Standard Arabic on a topic already covered, heard twice, then checked against the transcript. Advice to watch Arabic news is not a plan for a student with four hundred words.

whyPoints.title: Timelines are stated before you book
whyPoints.description: Eighteen months, twelve, eight or five all produce different realistic outcomes, and we name which one applies. A late start can still be worth doing; it is not worth being told it is the same as an early one.

whyPoints.title: Sessions fit an Abu Dhabi evening
whyPoints.description: Slots are set in Gulf Standard Time around the school run and the mainland commute, with Ramadan timings agreed in advance rather than improvised. Beginners need concentration, so we avoid the slots where a student is already finished for the day.

faqs.question: Can my child take Arabic ab initio if they have had school Arabic for years?
faqs.answer: That depends on evidence, and the school decides within the IB's framework. Ab initio is for students with little or no previous experience of the language, so a student who has had years of effective Arabic teaching is not an ab initio candidate even if the grades were poor. The grey area in Abu Dhabi is real, though: many students sit in mandatory Arabic lessons for a decade without becoming literate. The right move is a conversation with the school using a reading sample rather than an assumption, and it needs to happen before subject choices are locked.

faqs.question: Is there a Higher Level option in Arabic ab initio?
faqs.answer: No. Ab initio exists at Standard Level only, in Arabic and in every other language that offers it. A student who wants a Higher Level Group 2 subject needs Arabic B, which assumes genuine prior experience of the language and requires two literary works at HL. This surprises families who are planning a subject grid around three Higher Levels, so it is worth checking early. The absence of an HL route is also part of why ab initio is a cleaner build: there is one syllabus, one set of components, and no second tier of content.

faqs.question: How long does it take to read Arabic from nothing?
faqs.answer: Functional reading of familiar unvocalised words takes about twelve weeks of structured twice-weekly work. Reading unfamiliar words from their consonant skeleton and context takes about sixteen. Reading at the pace the examination requires is ongoing and improves across the whole course. Those numbers assume the short vowels are removed on a planned schedule rather than kept on the page indefinitely, and that the student reads a little most days. A course that keeps fully vocalised text going into DP2 produces a student who reads fluently in a system the exam does not use.

faqs.question: Why are the short vowels taught and then taken away?
faqs.answer: Because ordinary written Arabic does not show them. Short vowels appear in children's books, the Qur'an and language textbooks; a newspaper, a sign in Abu Dhabi or an examination reading passage does not mark them. A beginner needs them at first to learn pronunciation and word shape, then has to be weaned off deliberately: fully marked for a few weeks, partially marked for a few more, then familiar words unmarked, then unfamiliar ones. Done on schedule, this is unremarkable. Skipped, the student arrives at the reading paper unable to decode anything they have not memorised.

faqs.question: What do the two Arabic ab initio Paper 1 tasks ask for?
faqs.answer: Two short written pieces, produced in one hour, worth 25% of the grade between them. The word ranges are printed on the paper and staying inside them matters. The discipline for a beginner is writing less: short accurate sentences with correct agreement and a couple of connectives score better than ambitious structures the student does not control, and they finish in time. Each task also has a text type and an audience implied by the prompt, and showing awareness of those is part of what is credited, not an optional flourish.

faqs.question: How many topics does the Arabic ab initio course actually cover?
faqs.answer: Twenty prescribed topics across five themes: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. That finite list is the best feature of the course, because it makes coverage auditable. Each topic needs roughly forty to sixty usable words plus a few structures, which is a countable job rather than an open-ended one. Ask the school for the list and keep it visible, marking each topic as covered, revisited or still open. Most students have never seen it set out, and by DP2 nobody can say which topics are secure.

faqs.question: How should a beginner practise Arabic listening at home?
faqs.answer: With graded, topic-linked audio, not Arabic radio. Thirty to ninety seconds of clear Modern Standard Arabic on a topic already covered, heard twice as the exam does, answers written under time, then the transcript read against the answers. The words that were known on the page but not recognised in the ear go on a list — that gap is the whole problem and the list is usually short. Numbers, dates and times deserve separate weekly attention, because they defeat beginners more reliably than anything else and appear in nearly every listening section.

faqs.question: What happens in the ab initio oral and how is it marked?
faqs.answer: The student is given a photograph linked to one of the five themes, has supervised preparation time, then describes and discusses it before answering questions that widen beyond the image. It is marked out of 30 on language, message and interactive skills, and carries 25% of the grade. The school conducts and marks it and the IB moderates. Beginners often do better here than they expect, because the component rewards structure over range: naming what is there, placing it in context, saying what is happening and offering a view with one reason.

faqs.question: What should my child say in the oral if they do not understand a question?
faqs.answer: Ask for it to be repeated or rephrased, in Arabic. This is credited behaviour under interactive skills, and beginners almost never do it because it feels like an admission of failure. Instead they guess, answer a different question, and lose message marks as well as interaction marks. Three fixed phrases for requesting a repeat, drilled until they come out automatically, is a two-minute intervention with a real payoff. Recorded rehearsals are what make it stick, because the student hears themselves guessing and recognises the habit immediately.

faqs.question: Is living in Abu Dhabi an advantage for a beginner learning Arabic?
faqs.answer: Less than families hope, and in a specific way. The Arabic a student hears around them in Abu Dhabi is Gulf, Levantine or Egyptian dialect; the Arabic examined is Modern Standard. Hearing dialect daily builds confidence and a feel for rhythm, which is worth something, but it does not supply the forms the exam credits and can introduce habits that cost accuracy marks. The real local advantage is written: shop signs, road signs, menus and official notices are in Modern Standard Arabic, which makes Abu Dhabi an excellent place to practise reading if a student is pointed at it.

faqs.question: Will a tutor come to our villa in Abu Dhabi for beginner Arabic lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. Ab initio sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For a beginner this format earns its place rather than merely being tolerable: handwriting is corrected on a shared screen as the letter is formed, audio replays from the same window, and each session leaves a record of exactly which letters, words and topics were covered. In-home Arabic tuition is available in this market at roughly AED 180-500 an hour by published UAE surveys and listings, with travel inside the rate.

faqs.question: How often should a complete beginner in Arabic have lessons?
faqs.answer: Twice a week during the script phase, which runs six to twelve weeks, then weekly once unvocalised familiar words are being read. Letter recall decays quickly at the start, and a single weekly session means half the previous lesson is spent recovering ground. Front-loading the intensity costs less across the full course than spreading it evenly. After the script phase, weekly sessions with daily short reading between them is the pattern that works, and the daily reading matters more than the length of the session.

faqs.question: My child joined their Abu Dhabi school in DP2. Is ab initio still possible?
faqs.answer: Possible, with the plan stated honestly. Starting at the beginning of DP2 leaves about eight months, so reading goes in intensively over six to eight weeks with topic work running alongside, and coverage is triaged towards the topics whose vocabulary reappears elsewhere. A workable Group 2 grade is achievable if the student genuinely commits evening time. Starting after the winter of DP2 is salvage work: examination survival, reliable writing structures, a drilled oral and ruthless prioritisation. We will do it, and we will not describe it as equivalent to eighteen months.

faqs.question: Does Arabic ab initio count as speaking Arabic for a university application?
faqs.answer: It records a credited Group 2 beginner language, which is what it is, and no more than that. It does not make a student a bilingual candidate and it is not a route to the IB bilingual diploma, which involves two Language A courses rather than a Group 2 course. On Ministry of Education equivalency, the published British-track rules require five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count. No IB points threshold has been verified from the ministry's own pages, so verify any figure directly with the authority rather than with a tutoring website.

faqs.question: Is Arabic ab initio harder than French or Spanish ab initio?
faqs.answer: It is harder at the start and not obviously harder overall. Arabic front-loads its difficulty into the writing system: twenty-eight letters with multiple positional forms, cursive joining and unwritten short vowels, which is a term's work before normal language learning begins. French and Spanish beginners read on day one, then meet their difficulty later, in listening comprehension where familiar spelling conceals unfamiliar sound. Students who get a properly planned script phase in Arabic often end up in a stronger position than French beginners who never addressed the gap between how the language looks and how it sounds.

faqs.question: What will the first month of Arabic ab initio sessions actually produce?
faqs.answer: By the end of four weeks at twice weekly, a student should read and write any letter in all its positional forms, write a short dictated vocalised word correctly, read familiar vocalised words without hesitation, and have working vocabulary for the first prescribed topic used in spoken sentences. You should also have a week-by-week outline of the remaining script build and the twenty-topic ledger started. If after a month the student is still reciting the alphabet in order and has written nothing, the teaching sequence is wrong and should be challenged.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-home-tu.closingHeading: Four questions and we can tell you what the plan looks like
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-home-tu.closingBody: Can your child read the Arabic alphabet, read a vocalised word, read an unvocalised one, and write their own name unaided? Those four answers, plus the examination session they are sitting, are enough for us to set out a week-by-week script phase and a realistic outcome. Then take a trial lesson — one per subject, booked before any payment — spent on actual letters rather than introductions. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, twice weekly during the script build and weekly afterwards. If the timeline is too short for the outcome you want, we will say so before you book rather than after.

intro.heading: Starting Arabic from zero in Year 12, in the city where Arabic is everywhere
paragraphs: Arabic ab initio exists for Diploma students with little or no prior experience of the language. In Abu Dhabi that describes a very particular student: someone who has lived in the emirate for years, can greet a neighbour, reads a shop sign slowly, and has never written a paragraph. The course is offered at Standard Level only, runs across the two Diploma years, and ends in three assessed components. The distance between hearing Arabic daily and producing it under timed conditions is the whole problem on this page, and it is a solvable one if the work starts in the right place.

The first obstacle is mechanical. Letters change shape depending on whether they open a word, sit inside it or close it. Short vowels are usually absent from the page, so a reader supplies them from pattern recognition rather than from sight. A student who cannot write the alphabet fluently has no spare attention left for planning a written task inside the hour, which makes handwriting speed a rate limiter on every mark in Paper 1 rather than a presentational nicety. Six to eight weeks spent here is time banked, not time lost.

The second obstacle is register. Your child hears Gulf dialect in the taxi, in the mall and in the school corridor, while the course assesses Modern Standard Arabic. Words used confidently every day can be the wrong words on the page, and the leak is slow enough that nobody notices it until a mock comes back. Separating the two explicitly, in the first month, prevents a term of marks disappearing under the language criterion for a reason that reads as carelessness and is not.

The third thing a parent needs is evidence. School reports on a language acquisition subject tend to arrive as adjectives, and an adjective cannot be compared with last term's adjective. This page is built around the opposite habit. Every fortnight the tutor returns one piece of your child's own work with the criterion letter written beside each comment, keeps the error log from the baseline diagnostic, and shows the same task type twice so movement is measured on one scale instead of two. Your child's DP coordinator can read that file.

Delivery is online, one to one, over live video with a shared screen for the script work. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home tutoring is a service we run only in India. For a language starting from zero that is a straightforward advantage rather than a compromise: an Arabic ab initio specialist who has taught the visual-stimulus oral dozens of times is worth more than whoever is free to drive to Khalifa City at five o'clock, and the screen is where the script practice naturally lives anyway.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-tutor.programmesIntro: Arabic sits in a Diploma student's timetable twice over in this emirate: once as the Group 2 language acquisition subject, and once as the Arabic every licensed private school teaches under the federal curriculum rules. The programmes below are where we pick that up.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic ab initio is a Group 2 subject at Standard Level, taken by students beginning the language. Three components carry the grade: a writing paper, a listening and reading paper, and an individual oral assessed inside the school. Tutoring here is narrow and technical - script fluency, the five prescribed themes, text-type conventions, and timed production - because the grade is decided by what the student can produce unaided in an hour.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi Diploma cohorts are small, and a school may run ab initio with a handful of students across both years in one timetabled block. That gives very little individual oral rehearsal time, which is the single most common reason an Abu Dhabi family looks for a tutor in this subject rather than in a science.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language Acquisition places Arabic learners in phases rather than year groups, and a student can sit in phase 1 or 2 for several years without the school treating it as a problem. That is where the ab initio decision is really made: a phase 2 leaver has the vocabulary base to start the Diploma course comfortably, while a student who has drifted will spend DP1 catching up on script.
programmes.countryNote: Mid-year arrivals into Abu Dhabi MYP classes are common, and phase placement often reflects the term a student joined rather than what they can do. A diagnostic before DP subject selection is worth more here than in almost any other subject.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Primary Arabic in an IB school in the emirate is usually split between the school's own language provision and the Arabic required of every licensed private school. Early script work, letter-form handwriting and listening confidence are what carry forward; vocabulary learned in a themed unit rarely does. Support at this stage is about building the reading habit before the Diploma raises the stakes.
programmes.countryNote: Families who intend to stay in Abu Dhabi through secondary school get the most from primary Arabic, because the student who can read an unvowelled word at eleven is the one choosing between Arabic B and ab initio at sixteen rather than having the choice made for them.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-tutor.subjectsIntro: Arabic is not one subject in an Abu Dhabi school. It is a cluster of routes with different syllabuses, different regulators and different purposes, and parents are frequently told their child is doing two of them without being told how they differ. Here is the map we work from.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: For Diploma students beginning the language. Five prescribed themes, three assessed components, and an emphasis on controlled accuracy rather than range. Most tutoring time goes on script fluency, text-type conventions and the visual-stimulus oral.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: The route for students with real previous experience. Higher Level adds two literary works and the individual oral is built on an extract from one of them, which is a different oral task from the ab initio one and needs different preparation entirely.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: A Group 1 subject for students working in Arabic as a language of instruction. Assessment turns on literary analysis and commentary rather than language acquisition, so a student moved here from Arabic B usually needs reading-volume support, not grammar drills.

subjects.name: Ministry of Education Arabic for non-native speakers
subjects.description: The Arabic required of students in licensed private schools under the federal curriculum rules. It is graded by the school, reported to the regulator, and does not form part of the Diploma. Its syllabus and the ab initio syllabus overlap only loosely.

subjects.name: Ministry of Education Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: The stream for students classified as Arab under the regulator's own rules. Content and language of instruction differ from the non-native stream, and the two are kept as separate classes rather than combined groups.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the licensed international curriculum, taught in separate groups for Arab and non-Arab students. Support here is about comprehension and recall in the taught language, and it is a different teaching job from language acquisition.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies and Moral Education
subjects.description: Delivered alongside the school's own curriculum. For a non-Arab student the school's licensed-curriculum language is normally the medium, so the demand is reading comprehension and structured written answers rather than Arabic itself.

subjects.name: MYP Language Acquisition: Arabic, phases 1-2
subjects.description: Where a future ab initio student usually sits. The target is the alphabet, high-frequency vocabulary and simple present-tense production. A student who leaves phase 2 able to write unaided enters DP1 with the mechanical work already done.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in Arabic
subjects.description: Possible but demanding for an ab initio student, because the essay must be written in the target language in some categories. We coach question framing, source selection and the supervision conversations; the student produces every word themselves.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-tutor.regionsIntro: Abu Dhabi is not one commute. The island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor and the newer mainland communities each generate a different realistic start time for a weekday language session, and a slot that fights the school run gets cancelled by week five.

regions.note: Cranleigh Abu Dhabi sits here, and island families can usually make a 15.45 start work. Straight off the bus is the wrong moment for new grammar, so early slots are better spent on script drills and vocabulary retrieval.

regions.note: Repton Abu Dhabi draws from the island and the towers around it. Parents here often want to sit in for the last ten minutes of a session, which pushes the useful slot to after 18.00 and makes oral rehearsal the natural content.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Raha International School, Al Yasmina Academy and GEMS American Academy Abu Dhabi all pull from this area. Activity blocks finish late, so 16.30 is realistic and 16.00 is not, and the Saturday morning review slot is popular here.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: A short run to the Khalifa City schools and a longer one to the island. Villa households tend to have a quiet study room available, which matters more for a listening paper than most parents expect.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one over live video

sections.heading: What an Arabic ab initio tutor actually does in the first month
paragraphs: An IB DP Arabic ab initio tutor in Abu Dhabi spends the first month on two things: measuring what your child can already do, and fixing the mechanics of the script. The measurement is a short diagnostic - copy a sentence, read ten words aloud, listen to a ninety-second clip and answer three questions, write five lines about a photograph. It takes twenty minutes and it produces a baseline you can keep. Without it there is nothing to compare week eight against, and improvement becomes an opinion rather than a reading.

The mechanics come next. Letter families are drilled by shape rather than by alphabetical order, because the pairs that cost marks are the ones that look alike: baa, taa and thaa differ only in dots, and jeem, haa and khaa differ only in one. Joins are taught alongside the non-connecting letters, so a student stops guessing where a word ends. Reading aloud is recorded and timed, not to add pressure but because words per minute is the one number in this subject that moves visibly inside a month.

By the end of week four the session shape settles. Fifteen minutes of retrieval on the previous fortnight's vocabulary, twenty-five minutes of new material tied to one of the five prescribed themes, then twenty minutes on a timed written task or an oral rehearsal. Your child writes the task; the tutor marks it against the published criteria and returns it with the criterion letter beside each comment. That marked page, kept in order with the ones before it, is the evidence this page keeps promising, and it is what a DP coordinator will actually engage with.

sections.heading: The ab initio course: five themes, three components, one grade
paragraphs: Arabic ab initio runs at Standard Level only across the two Diploma years. Three components carry the whole grade. Paper 1 is the writing paper and is externally marked. Paper 2 holds listening and reading and is also externally marked. The individual oral is assessed inside the school by your child's teacher and then moderated by the IB. There is no written coursework component, which surprises parents arriving from a British curriculum where a language qualification usually carries one.

The content is organised around five prescribed themes: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation, and sharing the planet. Each carries recommended topics, and a school will choose which to teach in depth. For a tutor this matters practically rather than theoretically: a student who can talk fluently about daily routine and food but has never built vocabulary for travel or the environment will meet a stimulus photograph in the oral that they simply cannot describe, and no amount of grammar rescues that.

Exact task counts, word ranges and the current criterion wording live in the IB subject guide, which your child's school holds. We reference it and work from it, and we do not reproduce or supply IB documents, past papers or mark schemes - those are the school's to give you and the IB's to publish. Ask the DP coordinator for the component breakdown in writing at the start of DP1; schools give it willingly and it ends most of the confusion families arrive with.

sections.heading: Learning the Arabic script when you start at zero
paragraphs: Script work is the part of ab initio that looks like primary school and decides a Diploma grade. Twenty-eight letters, each with initial, medial and final forms, a group that refuses to join to the left, and short vowels that the reader supplies rather than sees. A student who decodes slowly spends the reading paper running out of time on question four, and spends Paper 1 writing simple sentences because complex ones take too long to form on paper.

The sequence below is the one we use with Abu Dhabi students starting in DP1 with no prior Arabic, and it is deliberately boring. Each stage has a check that produces a number, because a number from week two can be set beside the same number from week ten. Alphabet dictation scored out of twenty-eight. Joins checked on ten copied words. Reading aloud timed in words per minute. Legible output counted in a fixed fifteen minutes.

Twelve weeks is a realistic figure for a student working one hour a week with homework, and six to eight weeks for a student who already reads some letters from a school Arabic class. Families who skip this phase in favour of starting the themes immediately almost always come back to it in DP2, under exam pressure, with less time. The script is not a warm-up for the course; it is the course's foundation and the cheapest marks on the paper. It is also the one phase where a parent can see progress without understanding any Arabic at all, because the numbers speak for themselves.

sections.heading: Where ab initio marks are actually lost
paragraphs: The losses in this subject are repetitive and diagnosable, which is good news for anyone keeping an error log. The largest single one is dialect leaking into written work. A student writes the word they say at home, it is not the Modern Standard form, and the language criterion absorbs the damage quietly across a whole paper. The fix is a substitution list built from the student's own marked work rather than from a textbook, because the words that leak are personal to the household.

Second is text-type convention. Paper 1 asks for a specific kind of text, and a blog, a letter and a set of instructions each carry layout, salutation and register expectations that are worth marks independent of the Arabic. Students who have only ever written continuous prose lose these marks without knowing they existed. Third is the visual-stimulus oral, where candidates describe the photograph accurately and then stop, never linking it to a prescribed theme, which is where the conceptual marks sit.

Fourth is reading-paper pacing. The questions are not ordered by difficulty in a way that rewards working front to back at a constant speed, and a slow decoder spends disproportionate time early. Fifth, and most avoidable, is wasting the second hearing of a listening item by trying to write full answers during the first. Each of these is a habit rather than a knowledge gap, and habits move faster under one-to-one attention than content does.

sections.heading: Ab initio and the Arabic your Abu Dhabi school already requires
paragraphs: Parents routinely assume the Arabic class on the school timetable is preparation for the Diploma course. It is usually not. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry of Education's general regulations, as the federal government sets out on u.ae. That requirement produces a graded Arabic class with its own syllabus, sitting alongside the Diploma rather than inside it.

In this emirate the Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools, and ADEK publishes its own inspection ratings. The most detailed public guidance on how mandatory Arabic is organised comes from Dubai's regulator: KHDA's mandatory-subjects document sets instructional time against a forty-minute lesson unit, requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students on the grounds that curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ, and states that the use of different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is not allowed. Abu Dhabi families should confirm their own school's arrangements with ADEK or the school directly rather than assuming Dubai's wording applies.

The practical consequence is worth stating plainly. A student can be doing well in school Arabic and badly in ab initio, or the reverse, because the two assess different things. Equivalency adds a further wrinkle: for the British track, the Ministry's published requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among those five. No IB points figure for equivalency has been read on an official source for this page, so verify that one on moe.gov.ae rather than taking any tutoring site's number, including ours.

sections.heading: The evidence file: what you see every fortnight
paragraphs: The promise on this page is narrow and checkable: you see your child's own marked work on a fixed rhythm, and the same measurement is repeated so movement can be read rather than asserted. The file opens with the baseline diagnostic from lesson one, which carries no grade at all - only an error log. A grade at that point would be meaningless and would also set an expectation the student has done nothing yet to earn.

From fortnight two the pattern repeats. One artefact, marked against the published criteria, with the criterion letter written next to each comment so you can see whether the problem is language, message or the conversational element in the oral. Reading sets are marked by question type rather than as a single total, because a student losing marks consistently on inference questions needs different work from one losing them on vocabulary. Oral rehearsals are recorded and played back with the criteria open on screen.

What makes this useful at report time is that the same task type comes back. A Paper 1 task in fortnight two and the same text type in fortnight eight, marked by the same person against the same descriptors, is a comparison. Two different tasks marked by two different people is not. We do not publish aggregate statistics about student outcomes anywhere on this site, because we could not show you the data behind them; what we can show you is your own child's file.

sections.heading: The week that actually exists: scheduling a language session in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: A tutoring plan that ignores the school run collapses by week five. Abu Dhabi's geography makes this sharper than parents expect: an island school finishing at 15.15 and a Khalifa City activity block ending at 16.15 produce different realistic slots for the same family, and a sibling in a third school narrows the window further. Online delivery helps here in a way that is purely practical - no tutor is sitting in bridge traffic, so a 16.15 start is a 16.15 start.

Language sessions also have a content-to-energy problem that a maths session does not. New vocabulary and new grammar need a student who is awake; script drills, retrieval and reading aloud survive tiredness much better. So the slot determines the lesson plan rather than the other way round, and a family with only an early weekday window should expect mechanics on weekdays and new material at the weekend.

Ramadan shifts the whole pattern. School hours shorten, households run late, and the useful study window for a DP2 student often sits after iftar. Lessons can move to a post-iftar slot for the month and move back afterwards, and the one thing worth protecting through it is the fortnightly marked task, because that is the thread that keeps the evidence file comparable across the term. Families who tell us in advance which weeks will be lighter get a plan that absorbs them, rather than a month of cancellations followed by a scramble in April. Eid week is usually written off entirely, and that is sensible.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: what a tutor may and may not do with ab initio work
paragraphs: This is a live question in language subjects, because the individual oral is assessed inside the school and because translation tools make the boundary blurry for students who are not yet confident. The position we hold is simple and we state it to the student in lesson one. The tutor teaches, questions, models and gives feedback. Every mark-bearing word submitted to the school is produced by your child, unaided, in the conditions the school sets.

In practice that means a tutor may rehearse oral technique against unfamiliar stimuli, may mark a practice task to the published criteria and explain the descriptors, may build a vocabulary list from a student's own errors, and may teach the text-type conventions a Paper 1 task expects. A tutor does not sit in on an assessed recording, does not supply sentences for the student to reproduce in an assessed task, and does not polish a piece of assessed work into something the student could not have produced alone.

For the Extended Essay the same line applies with sharper consequences. We coach question framing, source selection and how to use the supervision meetings, and the essay is the student's own from first question to final footnote. Machine translation deserves its own conversation: a paragraph that reads several levels above a student's spoken ability is visible to any experienced examiner, and the risk sits with the candidate. Teaching a student to write at their actual level, well, is both the honest route and the one that scores.

faqs.question: What is IB Arabic ab initio, and which students is it for?
faqs.answer: Arabic ab initio is the Diploma's Group 2 course for students with little or no prior experience of Arabic. It runs at Standard Level only, across the two Diploma years, and is assessed by a writing paper, a listening and reading paper, and an individual oral marked inside the school and moderated by the IB. It suits a student who can greet people and recognise a few words but has never written or read Arabic with any independence. Students with real previous study belong in Arabic B, and your child's school decides the placement.

faqs.question: My child has lived in Abu Dhabi for years and speaks some Arabic. Is ab initio still the right course?
faqs.answer: Possibly, and the answer should come from a diagnostic rather than a conversation. Spoken exposure in the emirate builds listening confidence and a dialect vocabulary while leaving reading and writing untouched, which is a very different profile from a student who has studied the language formally. The school makes the placement decision and will consider prior school Arabic too. What we can give you is twenty minutes of evidence - copying, reading aloud, listening, writing - to take into that conversation so it is based on what your child can actually do.

faqs.question: Why can my child not take ab initio Arabic at Higher Level if they want the challenge?
faqs.answer: No. Ab initio courses in the Diploma are offered at Standard Level only, and that applies to Arabic as it does to the other ab initio languages. A student who needs a Higher Level language acquisition subject takes a language B course at HL instead, which assumes genuine previous experience and adds literary works to the syllabus. For most Abu Dhabi beginners this is not a limitation worth worrying about: the Diploma requires a certain number of HL subjects overall, not an HL language, so the HL load usually sits elsewhere in the timetable.

faqs.question: How is the Arabic ab initio grade actually divided up?
faqs.answer: Three components. Paper 1 is writing and carries a quarter of the grade. Paper 2 holds listening and reading together and carries half. The individual oral carries the remaining quarter and is assessed by your child's teacher in school, then moderated by the IB. Papers 1 and 2 are externally marked. There is no written coursework component in this subject, which catches out families arriving from curricula where a language qualification normally includes one. Ask your DP coordinator for the component breakdown in writing at the start of DP1.

faqs.question: Does the compulsory Arabic class at my child's school cover the ab initio syllabus?
faqs.answer: Generally not. Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum and follow the Ministry of Education's general regulations, and that class has its own syllabus and its own report line. The Diploma course is set by the IB subject guide. The two overlap in vocabulary and script but assess different things in different ways, so a student can be comfortable in one and struggling in the other. Treat them as two subjects that happen to share an alphabet.

faqs.question: How long does it take a complete beginner to read the Arabic script properly?
faqs.answer: For a DP1 student working an hour a week with homework between sessions, twelve weeks is a realistic figure to reach confident reading of familiar unvowelled words and legible writing at speed. A student who already recognises letters from a school Arabic class usually needs six to eight. The checks matter more than the timeline: alphabet dictation out of twenty-eight, joins checked on copied words, reading aloud timed in words per minute. Those numbers move early and visibly, which is useful when a student needs to see that the work is doing something.

faqs.question: Should my child write in Modern Standard Arabic or the Gulf dialect they hear every day?
faqs.answer: Modern Standard Arabic is the assessed variety, and this is the quietest source of lost marks for students living in the emirate. Words used confidently at home or in a shop can be the wrong form on the page, and the language criterion absorbs that across a whole paper without the student noticing. The fix is a substitution list built from your child's own marked work, because the leaks are personal. Dialect listening exposure is still an asset - it just needs the written register taught explicitly alongside it.

faqs.question: What does Arabic ab initio tutoring cost per hour in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published UAE market rates, mostly quoted for Dubai, give the shape of it. Budget online providers advertise from around AED 33 to AED 65 an hour; Unitors lists IB tutoring from about AED 200; TutorChase quotes around AED 270; Bestimate's 2026 tutoring-cost table puts specialist exam-year support at roughly AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with in-home visits from AED 180 to AED 500 once travel is priced in. Rare language specialisms sit at the upper end of the online band. Those are market figures from those sources, not our price list - ask us for a quote and take the free trial first.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does a DP1 ab initio student usually need?
faqs.answer: One hour a week is the common starting point and is enough if homework actually happens between sessions, because the script phase depends on daily short practice rather than long weekly bursts. Two hours a week makes sense in two situations: a student who started the course late and is behind on mechanics, or a DP2 student with an internal oral deadline close. More than two hours a week on a Standard Level language rarely pays for itself against the rest of a Diploma workload, and we will say so.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the individual oral without breaking IB rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the boundary is clear. A tutor may rehearse the task against unfamiliar stimuli, time the description, teach the phrases that link a photograph to a prescribed theme, record a practice attempt and play it back against the published criteria. A tutor may not be present for the assessed recording, may not supply sentences for a student to reproduce in it, and may not shape an assessed response into something the student could not produce alone. Everything submitted is your child's own work, and we say that to the student in lesson one.

faqs.question: What evidence will I actually see that my child is improving in Arabic?
faqs.answer: A file, kept in order. It opens with the lesson-one diagnostic, which carries an error log and no grade. From fortnight two you receive one piece of your child's own marked work each cycle, annotated with the criterion letter beside each comment, plus reading sets marked by question type rather than as a single total and oral rehearsals recorded. The same task type returns later in the term, marked by the same person against the same descriptors, so the comparison is real rather than rhetorical.

faqs.question: Do lessons carry on through Ramadan in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the timing moved. School hours shorten, households run later, and for most DP2 students the useful study window sits after iftar. Lessons shift to a post-iftar slot for the month and move back afterwards. The one thing worth protecting through Ramadan is the fortnightly marked task, because dropping it breaks the thread that makes the evidence file comparable across the term. Tell us early which weeks your family wants lighter, and we will plan the content around them rather than cancelling and catching up later.

faqs.question: Can we start ab initio tutoring in DP2 with six months to go?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the plan looks different. There is no time to rebuild the script from scratch, so the first fortnight is spent finding out exactly which letter pairs and question types are costing marks, then working only on those. Text-type conventions and the oral come next, because they return marks faster than vocabulary breadth at that stage. Nobody can promise a particular grade from a six-month start, and anyone who does should worry you. What a late start reliably buys is fewer avoidable losses on the paper.

faqs.question: Is my child's tutor legally permitted to give private lessons in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Private tuition in the UAE is permitted through a specific route rather than unregulated. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents and university students. MoHRE's own service page lists a two-working-day completion time and applications through its app, website and e-services. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Ask any tutor about their status - it is a fair question.

faqs.question: Will my child's Arabic result matter for Ministry of Education attestation later on?
faqs.answer: For the British track the Ministry's published rule is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, plus one subject at Advanced Level at E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level, and Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five. For the IB we have found no official points threshold on a Ministry source, so no figure appears on this page and you should verify that on moe.gov.ae or with the attestation authority directly. Equivalency is a process you deal with through the official channel, not something a tutoring service performs for you.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach Diploma Arabic B at Standard and Higher Level and work from the component upwards: the writing task, the listening and reading paper, or the individual oral. Sessions are one-to-one, over live video, on Gulf Standard Time.

intro.heading: Arabic B hands half the grade to the skills nobody practises
paragraphs: Arabic B is a Group 2 language acquisition course, and its mark scheme is unusually blunt about where the grade comes from. Paper 1, the writing task, is 25%. The individual oral is 25%. Paper 2, which is listening and reading, is 50%. Half of an Arabic B grade is earned by understanding Arabic that somebody else produced, under time pressure, with no dictionary. Almost every Arabic B student in Abu Dhabi spends their revision time writing practice paragraphs, because writing is the skill you can see yourself getting better at.

That imbalance is the single most useful thing to know about this subject. A student at 4 who writes competently is very often a student whose Paper 2 listening section is scoring under half. The audio plays twice and then it is gone, the speakers use unfamiliar vocabulary in Modern Standard Arabic, and the question types change without warning between multiple choice, short answer and matching. None of that is fixed by more writing practice. It is fixed by listening to a great deal of Arabic in a structured way, with the transcript used afterwards rather than during, which is tedious and is exactly why students avoid it.

The second structural fact concerns the three criteria. Paper 1 is marked out of 30: Criterion A for language carries 12 marks, Criterion B for message carries 12, and Criterion C for conceptual understanding carries 6. Those last six marks are the cheapest on the paper and the most commonly thrown away. Conceptual understanding means the student has chosen the right text type for the audience, context and purpose the task describes, and has used its conventions. A blog post with no title and no sign of a reader, or a formal letter that opens like a text message, loses marks that have nothing to do with the student's Arabic.

Arabic also brings a problem no other Language B subject has in quite the same form. The variety assessed is Modern Standard Arabic. The variety a student hears in Abu Dhabi — in the car, in the mall, from friends at a school in Al Reef or Al Shamkha — is Gulf, Levantine or Egyptian dialect. A student can be comfortably conversational and still lose marks on every component, because the exam does not test the Arabic they are good at. Separating the two explicitly, rather than hoping exposure will do it, is a large part of what Arabic B tutoring is for.

On delivery: IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi, and no tutor will come to a UAE address. Arabic B sessions are one-to-one over live video, with audio played and paused on a shared screen and the student's own written work annotated live. For a listening-heavy subject that is a practical advantage, because the material and the transcript sit in the same window and the session leaves a record of what was heard, misheard and fixed.

Paper 2: listening plus reading, 50%, 1h45 at SL and 2h at HL
Individual oral: 25%, visual stimulus at SL, literary extract at HL
