abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Arabic B students in Abu Dhabi arrive from several different places, and the route in tells you a great deal about which component will cause trouble. These are the programmes that feed it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic B is the Group 2 course for students with prior experience of Arabic, taken at Standard or Higher Level. It assesses three skills — receptive, productive and interactive — across five prescribed themes, and at Higher Level adds two literary works studied in Arabic. The conceptual understandings of audience, context, purpose, meaning and variation run through every component.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi students taking Arabic B typically fall into two groups: non-Arab students who have had mandatory school Arabic for years without using it outside class, and heritage speakers whose spoken Arabic outstrips their reading. The two groups need opposite session plans, and a tutor who treats them alike wastes half the hours.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language Acquisition Arabic runs in phases rather than years, and the phase a student reaches by MYP5 is the best predictor of how Arabic B will go. Students finishing in phase 3 or 4 generally cope with Arabic B SL; those still in phase 2 are being asked to read unfamiliar Arabic at speed within eighteen months.
programmes.countryNote: Because MYP phases are not year groups, two Abu Dhabi students in the same DP1 Arabic B class can be two phases apart. In a small cohort at a Yas Island or Al Reem Island school there may be one teacher covering that spread, which is the usual reason a family starts looking outside school.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Arabic in the PYP is taught as an additional language for non-Arab children, with inquiry-led vocabulary rather than systematic grammar. Children usually leave primary able to read vocalised text slowly and recognise familiar words. Reading unvocalised text at speed — the Paper 2 requirement — is rarely begun before MYP.
programmes.countryNote: For Abu Dhabi families planning ahead, the useful primary checkpoint is whether the child can read a short unvocalised sentence aloud by Year 6. That one skill, more than vocabulary size, determines whether Arabic B later feels manageable or relentless.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme carries a language development component with a portfolio rather than an examined Language B course. Arabic there is practical and workplace-facing, which suits a student staying in the UAE for work, without the receptive-skills load of Arabic B Paper 2.
programmes.countryNote: Few Abu Dhabi schools run CP alongside the Diploma, so transfers between the two are rare. Where a student moves from CP language development into Arabic B, the gap is almost always reading speed rather than vocabulary, and it needs planning before DP1 rather than during it.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Arabic B rarely travels alone. The requests that arrive with it from Abu Dhabi families follow a predictable pattern, and several of these subjects share the skill that Arabic B is short of.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: Three skills, five themes, two literary works at HL. Paper 2 carries half the grade and is where most of the lost marks are. The conceptual understanding criterion on Paper 1 is worth 6 marks and is the quickest available gain for a student who can already write accurate Arabic sentences.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: The beginners' Group 2 course, for students with little or no prior Arabic. Standard Level only. Students sometimes ask to move down from Arabic B into ab initio; eligibility is set by prior experience, not by preference, and the school and the IB decide, not the family.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Group 1 course for students working at first-language level, assessing literary and non-literary analysis rather than language acquisition. Heritage speakers placed in Arabic B who score 7 without effort are often in the wrong course, and this is where they belong.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: The same assessment architecture as Arabic B — identical component weightings, the same three criteria, the same five themes. Skills transfer almost completely, so a student who learns how Paper 2 listening works in one language gains in the other without extra hours.

subjects.name: French B
subjects.description: Commonly taken alongside Arabic in Abu Dhabi schools with a francophone intake. Students juggling two Group 2 languages need their oral preparation separated clearly, because the structure is identical and the content is not, and blending them produces confident answers in the wrong language.

subjects.name: Spanish B
subjects.description: The third Group 2 option at several Abu Dhabi schools. Spanish B students share the Arabic B problem of a listening paper that moves faster than classroom audio, and the fix is the same: unfamiliar voices at natural speed, transcript used afterwards rather than alongside.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The commonest subject request from Arabic B families, usually for the exploration or for statistics. The internal assessment is 20% of the grade at both levels and is marked on criterion letters, so the planning discipline carries over directly from Arabic B coursework.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study heavy, which rewards exactly the reading-under-time-pressure skill Arabic B Paper 2 demands. Students who improve their Arabic reading speed frequently report that the business pre-release case study became easier at the same time.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Command-term discipline decides the grade: 'describe', 'explain' and 'evaluate' each require a different answer shape. Bilingual students often know the studies and lose marks on structure, which is the same failure pattern as Arabic B criterion B.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Resource-based questions and a fieldwork internal assessment worth 20-25% depending on level. The UAE offers unusually good local fieldwork material on water, urban growth and energy, and the write-up is process coaching on the student's own data.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The 1,600-word essay and the exhibition contribute up to 3 points alongside the Extended Essay. Arabic B students often write strongly on TOK's knowledge-and-language theme, because translation between dialect and Modern Standard Arabic is a live example they already understand.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Four thousand words of independent research. A Group 2 Arabic category essay is possible and demands a supervisor who reads academic Arabic. Support is narrowing the research question and giving feedback on the student's own drafts, never supplying text.

regions.name: Masdar City

sections.heading: Receptive, productive, interactive: where the Arabic B marks actually sit
paragraphs: Arabic B assesses three skills and pays for them unevenly. Receptive skills — listening and reading, examined together in Paper 2 — take half the grade. Productive skills, meaning the single written task in Paper 1, take a quarter. Interactive skills, assessed through the individual oral conducted and marked by the school and moderated by the IB, take the remaining quarter. There is no separate reading paper, no separate speaking exam and no coursework essay, which makes Arabic B structurally simpler than most Diploma subjects and much easier to plan around.

The durations are worth knowing because they shape practice. Paper 1 is 1 hour 15 minutes at Standard Level and 1 hour 30 at Higher Level for one task. Paper 2 is 1 hour 45 at SL, split into a 45-minute listening section and an hour of reading, and 2 hours at HL with an hour for each. A student who has never sat the listening section to time has no idea how fast it moves: the audio plays, plays again, and the paper moves on regardless of whether an answer was written.

The criteria then tell you what to work on inside each component. Paper 1 is out of 30, split language 12, message 12, conceptual understanding 6. The individual oral is also out of 30, with language 12, message 12 and interactive skills 6. Two things follow. First, language accuracy is never worth more than 40% of any component, so a student obsessing over grammar perfection is optimising the wrong variable. Second, the 6-mark criteria at the end of each component — conceptual understanding on the paper, interactive skills in the oral — are small, specific and routinely ignored, which makes them the best value hour of tutoring available in this subject.

What this adds up to for an Abu Dhabi family is a session order rather than a general programme. Sit the listening section to time and see the real score. Mark a writing task with the three numbers shown separately rather than as a total. Run one full oral rehearsal. After three sessions you know which component is costing the grade, and the rest of the block has a target instead of a subject.

sections.heading: Diglossia: the Arabic B problem no other language subject has
paragraphs: Arabic exists in two registers at once. Modern Standard Arabic is the written and formal variety, used in news, literature, official communication and the Diploma examination. Spoken Arabic in Abu Dhabi is Gulf, Levantine, Egyptian or one of several other dialects, differing from Modern Standard in vocabulary, verb forms, negation, question structure and pronunciation. A French B student who improves their conversational French improves their exam French. An Arabic B student who improves their conversational Arabic may improve nothing the examiner will see.

This explains a result that confuses Abu Dhabi families every year. A student who chats comfortably with the family driver, follows an Arabic film without subtitles and has lived in the emirate for a decade scores 4. Nothing has gone wrong. They are fluent in a variety the exam does not assess, and partially literate in the one it does. The reverse happens too: a student with almost no spoken confidence can score 6 on reading and writing because their classroom Arabic has always been Modern Standard and they have never been asked to produce it casually.

The fix is not to suppress the dialect. It is to make the switch conscious. A student needs to know that the dialect negation they use daily is not the form Paper 1 wants, that the verb they say every day has a different standard conjugation, and that colloquial vocabulary slipping into a formal letter costs Criterion A marks even when the meaning is perfectly clear. Most students have never had anyone list those differences for them, because their school Arabic teacher is teaching Modern Standard and their family is speaking dialect, and nobody owns the comparison.

In sessions this takes the form of correction on the student's own language rather than generic grammar exercises. The student writes or speaks, the tutor marks each colloquial form, and the standard equivalent goes on a list that belongs to that student. Lists of this kind run to twenty or thirty items, not hundreds, and they tend to stop being a problem within a term because the student is finally being told which half of what they know the exam is looking for.

sections.heading: Paper 2 is half the grade and the hardest half to revise alone
paragraphs: Ask an Arabic B student how they revise and the answer is usually vocabulary lists and past writing tasks. Ask them when they last sat the listening section to time and the answer is often never, or once in a mock. This is the central problem in the subject, and it is a behavioural problem rather than a linguistic one, because listening practice done properly is unpleasant and produces no visible product.

Done properly looks like this. Unfamiliar audio in Modern Standard Arabic, on a theme from the syllabus, at natural speed. Played twice and no more, exactly as the exam does it. Answers written during and after, under the clock. Only then the transcript, read against the answers, with every mis-heard word written down. The list of mis-heard words is the revision product — it is almost always the same twenty or thirty items appearing again and again, usually numbers, dates, connectives and the formal verbs that carry the meaning of a sentence.

The reading section fails differently. Students who lose reading marks usually understood the passage and ran out of time, because reading unvocalised Arabic at speed is a skill built by volume and most Diploma students read almost no Arabic outside class. The practical answer is uncomfortable and effective: twenty minutes of Arabic reading a day, from material the student finds interesting rather than from past papers, with speed measured rather than comprehension quizzed. Reading speed improves on a measurable curve over about eight weeks, and comprehension follows it rather than leading it.

Paper 2 also rewards question-type literacy. The paper mixes multiple choice, short answer, true or false with justification, matching and gap-filling, and each type has a technique. A true-or-false answer with no justification scores zero even when the judgement is right. A short answer copied as a whole sentence from the text often scores when a paraphrase would not. These are not language skills and they can be taught in two sessions, which makes them the cheapest marks available in the component carrying half the grade.

sections.heading: The six conceptual marks on Paper 1 that students hand back
paragraphs: Criterion C on Paper 1 is worth 6 of 30 marks and tests conceptual understanding: whether the student has grasped the audience, context and purpose the task sets, chosen an appropriate text type, and used that text type's conventions. It is the smallest criterion and the most forgiving, because it does not require better Arabic. It requires the student to notice what they have been asked to write and for whom.

Here is what losing those marks looks like. The task asks for a blog post for other students about an environmental initiative. The student writes four accurate paragraphs of general prose with no title, no sign of a reader, no personal voice, no closing invitation to comment. The Arabic may be excellent. The language and message marks hold up. Criterion C collapses, because nothing about the piece is a blog post. The same student, told once that a blog post needs a title, a first-person voice, direct address to a reader and a closing hook, produces all four next time at no cost in accuracy.

Arabic B expects familiarity with a range of text types across personal, professional and mass-media categories: emails and letters, blog posts and diary entries, articles and reports, speeches and interviews, reviews, brochures and proposals. Each has three or four surface conventions that signal what it is. Students do not need to memorise a taxonomy, they need a one-page reference and three practice attempts, and the conceptual marks stop leaking.

The register question sits alongside it. A letter to a school principal and a message to a cousin are both correspondence and the Arabic they require is not the same. In Arabic the formality gap is wider than in English, because the formal register draws on classical structures that a student may only have met in reading. This is why the text-type drill is also a register drill, and why it belongs early in a block rather than in the final weeks before an exam.

sections.heading: The individual oral at SL and HL are two different exams
paragraphs: Both levels call it the individual oral, both are worth 25%, both are marked out of 30 on language, message and interactive skills, and both are run by the school and moderated by the IB. There the similarity ends. At Standard Level the student works from a visual stimulus linked to one of the five prescribed themes: they describe and interpret the image, connect it to the theme, and then answer questions, first on that theme and then in a wider conversation across at least one other theme. At Higher Level the starting point is an extract from one of the two literary works studied, which changes the preparation entirely.

SL candidates fail in a predictable way. They describe the photograph and stop. Four minutes of what is in the image, no interpretation, no link to the theme, no stance taken. The marks for message require the student to use the image as a route into an idea, not to inventory it. The drill is simple and effective: name three things in the image, then state one claim about the society or experience it shows, then support that claim. Students who learn that move gain message marks immediately, and the interactive marks often follow because the discussion has somewhere to go.

HL candidates fail differently. They treat the extract as a comprehension exercise or, worse, as literary criticism in the Group 1 style. Arabic B at Higher Level is not Arabic A. The examiner is assessing language, message and interaction through the extract, not the sophistication of literary analysis. An HL student who can summarise the extract's situation, connect it to a theme in the work as a whole, and sustain a conversation about it in fluent Modern Standard Arabic will outscore one who has memorised commentary and cannot answer an unexpected question.

The interactive skills criterion is worth 6 marks at both levels and is the one students assume cannot be revised. It can. It rewards responding to what was actually asked, asking for clarification when a question is unclear rather than guessing, and keeping a conversation going without waiting to be rescued. Each of those is a trainable behaviour, and all three are easier to fix in a recorded rehearsal than in a classroom where only one student can speak at a time.

sections.heading: Heritage speakers in Arabic B: the Abu Dhabi placement problem
paragraphs: In an emirate where a large share of households speak Arabic, Group 2 placement goes wrong in both directions more often than it does for French or Spanish. A student whose Arabic is a home language but whose schooling has been entirely in English may be too advanced for Arabic B and under-equipped for Arabic A. Arabic B then produces a comfortable 6 or 7 that teaches them nothing, while Arabic A would produce a 4 and two years of genuine difficulty. Neither is obviously the right answer and the family usually never has the conversation.

The diagnostic is reading and writing, not speaking. A heritage speaker who can read an unvocalised newspaper column at reasonable speed, follow an Arabic documentary without strain and write a page of formal Arabic with controlled syntax is an Arabic A candidate. One who speaks easily but reads slowly, guesses at unfamiliar words and writes the way they speak belongs in Arabic B and will benefit from it. The honest version of this conversation takes twenty minutes and a short reading sample, and schools with large cohorts cannot always find that time per student.

There is a university dimension worth understanding too, and it is frequently overstated by people selling tutoring. Taking Arabic A alongside an English A course is the usual route to the bilingual diploma, which requires grade 3 or above in two Language A courses; confirm the current conditions with your school's IB coordinator rather than with a website. Arabic B does not lead there. That is a reason to examine the placement properly in DP1, when a move is still possible, and not a reason to force a student into a Group 1 course they cannot sustain.

For families who conclude the placement is right and the grade still needs work, the heritage-speaker session plan is distinctive. Almost no time on comprehension, which is already strong. Most of the time on written register, script fluency and the discipline of producing Modern Standard forms under exam conditions. It is a narrow job and it moves quickly, which is the opposite of the broad language support such students are usually sold.

sections.heading: What a single Arabic B session fixes, and what needs a term
paragraphs: It is worth being specific about this, because the honest answer sells less tutoring and saves families money. Some Arabic B problems are technique and go away in one or two sessions. Some are knowledge and take a block. Some are habit and take a term. Confusing the three is how families end up paying for twenty sessions when four would have done, or expecting four sessions to undo a decade of reading avoidance.

One session fixes question-type technique on Paper 2: how to justify a true-or-false answer, when to lift from the text and when to paraphrase, what to do with the second hearing of an audio clip. One session fixes text-type conventions on Paper 1, which is where those six conceptual marks live. One session fixes the SL oral's description-only failure, because the three-step drill is immediately learnable. These are the highest-value hours available in the subject and they are rarely the ones a family books first.

A block of six to eight sessions is the right shape for a knowledge gap: the five prescribed themes unevenly covered, a vocabulary range too narrow for the writing task, two HL literary works read once and not understood. A block is also right for a timing problem, because pace improves by repetition under the clock and cannot be explained into existence. We would expect measurable movement in a timed component across six sessions, and if it is not there, something about the diagnosis was wrong and should be said out loud.

A term is what reading speed takes, and what written register takes for a dialect-dominant speaker. Both are built by volume. A tutor can set the material, measure the curve and keep the student honest, but no hour of teaching replaces the reading. Families told otherwise are being sold something. The useful promise is not speed, it is that the right thing is being worked on and that the evidence arrives weekly rather than at the end of term.

sections.heading: Permits, ADEK ethics rules and how Arabic B sessions are actually delivered
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE requires a permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through MoHRE, granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page lists it as 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing', applied for through the ministry's app, website and e-services, with a two-working-day completion time and no fee shown.

Anyone tutoring without the permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. The amounts are not published, so no honest page quotes one. In Abu Dhabi there is an additional restriction that matters for Arabic in particular, because Arabic teachers are often the staff a family knows best: press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules indicates that private and charter school staff may not provide paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct runs the same way. Check the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it. ADEK itself supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools across the emirate.

Our delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not provide in-person tutoring in Abu Dhabi and does not send anyone to a UAE address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. For Arabic B that model fits the subject unusually well, since audio clips, transcripts, reading passages and the student's own writing all sit in one shared window and the session leaves a saved record of what was heard, misheard and corrected.

A trial lesson comes first, one per subject, booked before any payment is taken, so you can judge the tutor on a real piece of work rather than on a profile. Where no UAE-based Arabic B specialist is free at the hour you need, we say so and offer the alternatives plainly: a different time with an available specialist, a wait for a named slot, or a specialist outside the UAE teaching on Gulf Standard Time. Nobody is substituted without being named.

process.title: Tell us which component is failing
process.description: Not the grade, the component. Send the last Paper 2 mark broken into listening and reading, a marked Paper 1 task with the three criterion numbers if the school gives them, and the oral mark. Arabic B has three moving parts and the right session plan is completely different depending on which one is dragging.

process.title: Sit the listening section to time
process.description: Before the first paid session we ask for one thing: the student sits a listening section under real conditions, audio twice, no pausing. That score is usually the surprise that reframes the whole plan, and it costs nothing to produce. Families who skip it tend to buy writing sessions they did not need.

process.title: Match to the level and the oral format
process.description: SL and HL orals are different exams, so we match a tutor who has prepared the format your child will sit, and who has taught the two HL literary works if HL applies. We name the level they have taught and how recently, and offer an alternative where one exists.

process.title: Take the trial lesson on a real task
process.description: One trial per subject, before payment, spent on an actual piece of the student's work rather than on introductions. You should finish it knowing which of the three components the block will target and what the first two sessions will do. If the tutor has not marked anything, the trial has not told you enough.

process.title: Book a block with a stated component target
process.description: Sessions are booked as a defined block aimed at one component, with the artefact each session produces agreed in advance: a marked task, a timed listening score, a recorded rehearsal. Marking between sessions is settled up front, not discovered later on an invoice.

process.title: Re-test the same component at the end
process.description: The block closes by re-sitting the component it targeted, under the same conditions as the baseline. The two scores sit side by side and the decision is explicit: continue on a different component, change tutor, or stop. A block with no end test cannot tell you whether it worked.

whyPoints.title: We start where half the grade is
whyPoints.description: Paper 2 carries 50% of Arabic B and receives the least practice of any component. Sessions begin with a timed listening score because that single number reframes most families' assumptions about what their child needs.

whyPoints.title: Dialect and Modern Standard are kept apart deliberately
whyPoints.description: Students in Abu Dhabi hear Gulf, Levantine and Egyptian Arabic daily and are examined in Modern Standard. We list the differences that cost marks on the student's own work rather than hoping exposure sorts it out.

whyPoints.title: The small criteria get the attention they are worth
whyPoints.description: Conceptual understanding on Paper 1 and interactive skills in the oral are 6 marks each and are routinely surrendered. They are the fastest gains in the subject and usually the last thing a student is taught.

whyPoints.title: Component-level evidence, not progress reports
whyPoints.description: Each session produces something measurable: a timed listening score, a task marked 12 / 12 / 6, a recorded rehearsal reviewed against criteria. Two of those a month tell you more than a term's worth of general feedback.

whyPoints.title: Honest timelines, including the slow ones
whyPoints.description: Question technique moves in one session. Theme coverage takes a block. Reading speed and written register take a term, and we say so before you book rather than at session fifteen.

whyPoints.title: Placement questioned when it looks wrong
whyPoints.description: A heritage speaker coasting to a 7 in Arabic B and a student drowning in Arabic A are both in the wrong room. We will say so in DP1 while a change is still possible, even when the honest answer means fewer sessions.

faqs.question: Which part of Arabic B carries the most marks?
faqs.answer: Paper 2, the receptive-skills paper, carries 50% of the grade. It combines listening and reading: at Standard Level a 45-minute listening section and an hour of reading, at Higher Level an hour of each. Paper 1, the single writing task, is 25%, and the individual oral is the remaining 25%. The imbalance matters because listening and reading are the two skills students revise least, since neither produces anything visible. A student at 4 who writes competently is very often a student whose listening section is scoring under half, and no amount of extra writing practice will change that.

faqs.question: Why does my child speak Arabic well but score badly in Arabic B?
faqs.answer: Because Arabic is two languages in one. The exam assesses Modern Standard Arabic. What your child speaks in Abu Dhabi is Gulf, Levantine or Egyptian dialect, which differs in negation, question forms, verb patterns, vocabulary and pronunciation. Fluency in the spoken variety does not transfer automatically to the written one, and colloquial forms leaking into a Paper 1 task cost language marks even when the meaning is perfectly clear. The work is not to remove the dialect. It is to make the switch between the two deliberate, which starts with someone listing the differences on the student's own writing.

faqs.question: How should my child practise Arabic B listening at home?
faqs.answer: Unfamiliar audio in Modern Standard Arabic, on a syllabus theme, at natural speed. Played twice and no more, as the exam does. Answers written under the clock. Only then the transcript, read against the answers, with every mis-heard word written down. That list is the revision product, and it is usually short: numbers, dates, connectives and the formal verbs carrying a sentence's meaning, appearing again and again. What does not work is pausing during practice, reading along with the transcript, or listening passively to Arabic radio in the car and calling it revision.

faqs.question: What are the six conceptual understanding marks on Arabic B Paper 1?
faqs.answer: Criterion C on Paper 1 is worth 6 of 30 marks and tests whether the student grasped the audience, context and purpose the task set, chose a suitable text type and used its conventions. They are the cheapest marks on the paper because they need no better Arabic. A task asking for a blog post, answered with four accurate paragraphs of general prose and no title, no reader addressed and no closing hook, loses most of them. Told once what a blog post needs, the same student produces it next time at no cost in accuracy.

faqs.question: How many words should an Arabic B writing task be?
faqs.answer: At Standard Level the task asks for 250 to 400 words; at Higher Level 450 to 600. Writing outside the range costs marks, and both directions matter. Short answers cannot develop a message enough for the 12 message marks, and very long ones lose control of language and run past the time. The practical fix is for the student to learn what their own handwriting looks like at the top and bottom of the range, measured once, so they can judge length in the exam without counting words and wasting minutes doing it.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the Arabic B oral at SL and at HL?
faqs.answer: They share a name, a weighting of 25% and an identical criterion sheet, and almost nothing else. Standard Level starts from a visual stimulus linked to one of the five prescribed themes: the student interprets the image, links it to the theme, then answers questions on that theme and at least one other. Higher Level starts from an extract from one of the two literary works studied. SL candidates fail by describing the photograph and stopping. HL candidates fail by delivering memorised literary commentary instead of sustaining a conversation about the extract.

faqs.question: Can interactive skills in the oral actually be improved?
faqs.answer: Yes, and students assume otherwise because it sounds like a personality trait. The criterion is worth 6 marks and credits specific behaviours: answering what was actually asked, asking for clarification when a question is unclear rather than guessing, and keeping a conversation moving without waiting to be rescued. Each is trainable. Recorded rehearsals are the fastest route, because the student hears themselves guess at a misunderstood question and the lesson lands in a way no amount of advice does. Three rehearsals usually produce a visible change in all three behaviours.

faqs.question: Do the two Higher Level literary works appear on the Arabic B exam papers?
faqs.answer: No. At Higher Level, Arabic B requires two literary works studied in Arabic, but they are not examined on Paper 1 or Paper 2. They feed the individual oral, where the starting extract is drawn from one of them. HL students who read the works carefully and then prepare only for the written papers are leaving a quarter of the grade to chance. Equally, students who treat the works as a Group 1 literature course are over-preparing: the oral assesses language, message and interaction through the extract, not the sophistication of literary analysis.

faqs.question: My child is a heritage Arabic speaker in Arabic B. Are they in the right course?
faqs.answer: Check reading and writing, not speaking. A heritage speaker who reads an unvocalised newspaper column at reasonable speed and writes a page of controlled formal Arabic is usually an Arabic A candidate. One who speaks easily but reads slowly, guesses at unfamiliar words and writes the way they speak is correctly placed in Arabic B and will gain from it. A student coasting to a 7 in Arabic B with no effort is learning nothing and worth reviewing in DP1, while the course is still changeable. The conversation needs a reading sample, not an opinion.

faqs.question: Does Arabic B count towards the IB bilingual diploma?
faqs.answer: No. The bilingual diploma route most Abu Dhabi families mean requires two Language A courses with a grade 3 or above in both, which means Arabic A rather than Arabic B. There is also a route involving a subject from the individuals and societies or sciences groups taken in a language other than the candidate's Language A. Conditions are set by the IB and reviewed periodically, so confirm the current rules with your school's IB coordinator rather than relying on any website, including this one. It is a reason to examine placement in DP1, not a reason to force a course.

faqs.question: Will a tutor come to our home in Abu Dhabi for Arabic B lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. Arabic B sessions for Abu Dhabi families are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For this subject the format is a genuine advantage: audio clips, transcripts, reading passages and the student's own marked writing sit in one shared window, and the session leaves a saved record of what was heard, misheard and corrected. In-home tuition is a real market here, priced around AED 180-500 an hour by published UAE surveys and listings, with travel inside the rate.

faqs.question: How many Arabic B sessions will my child need before the May papers?
faqs.answer: It depends on which of three categories the problem falls into, and the honest answer is often fewer than families expect. Technique gaps — Paper 2 question types, Paper 1 text-type conventions, the SL oral drill — move in one or two sessions each. Knowledge gaps such as uneven theme coverage or a narrow vocabulary range take a block of six to eight. Reading speed and written register take a term, because both are built by volume and no hour of teaching substitutes for the reading. We would rather say that before a block is booked than at session fifteen.

faqs.question: Is the school Arabic my child already studies the same as Arabic B?
faqs.answer: No, and conflating them wastes sessions. UAE private schools must teach Arabic alongside their licensed curriculum, and in Abu Dhabi those schools are supervised by ADEK, which handles licensing and accreditation and publishes inspection ratings. That mandatory stream follows a Ministry curriculum with set instructional time and separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students. Arabic B is a Diploma language acquisition course with three components and its own criteria. A student can do well in one and badly in the other, and the Diploma grade is the one a university sees.

faqs.question: Which Abu Dhabi schools do your Arabic B students come from?
faqs.answer: Enquiries spread across three clusters. The long-established island schools around the Corniche, Al Nahyan and Al Khalidiyah, where Arabic departments are large and groups are streamed. The newer island campuses on Saadiyat, Yas and Al Reem, where Group 2 cohorts are small and one teacher may cover a wide spread of prior Arabic. And the mainland belt through Al Reef, Al Shamkha, Al Falah and Khalifa City, where bus routes are long and sessions start after 18:00. Schools are named as context only; none has any relationship with IB Gram.

faqs.question: Can an Arabic B tutor help with the oral without breaking IB rules?
faqs.answer: Yes. The individual oral is conducted and marked by the school and moderated by the IB, and preparation for it is ordinary teaching. A tutor may run full rehearsals, review a recording against the criteria, practise the follow-up conversation across themes and drill the three-step move from image to claim to support. What a tutor may not do is script the assessment itself or supply memorised answers presented as the student's own thinking. Rehearsal builds a skill; a script builds a liability that falls on the student.

faqs.question: Do we need to check whether an Arabic tutor in Abu Dhabi is permitted to teach?
faqs.answer: It is worth asking. The private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued through MoHRE, is free of charge and valid for two years, and covers registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Tutoring without it carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published schedule of amounts. Abu Dhabi adds a second point: ADEK's reported ethics rules bar school staff from paid tutoring of students at their own school, so your child's own Arabic teacher is not the right answer.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.closingHeading: Send the component marks and we will tell you where the grade is going
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.closingBody: Arabic B is three components with uneven weights, and most families start with the one that is easiest to see. Send the last Paper 2 result split into listening and reading, a marked writing task, and the oral mark. If the school does not break Paper 2 down, have your child sit one listening section to time at home — audio twice, no pausing — and send that instead. We will say which component is costing the grade and what the first two sessions would do about it. A trial lesson follows, one per subject, booked before any payment, on a real piece of work. Sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

You see their teaching background before the trial lesson.

intro.heading: Four documents, produced early, that tell you where your child actually is
paragraphs: Arabic B is the Diploma subject where school reports are hardest for a parent to interpret, because a grade in it can describe several completely different situations. A student may understand spoken Arabic fluently and be unable to read a newspaper column. Another may read well and freeze in the oral. A third may do both competently and lose a quarter of the grade writing a formal report in a conversational register. All three can appear on a report as the same number, and none of them needs the same help.

The remedy is not a longer conversation with the school. It is four documents, produced in the first fortnight and kept. A timed listening section, marked. A timed reading section, marked. One piece of writing in a specified text type, marked with the errors counted by category rather than described. And a recorded oral run with its timings written down. Between them those four say which of the three situations above you are in, and they can be understood by a parent who reads no Arabic, because what they produce is numbers and categories.

This matters more in Abu Dhabi than it would elsewhere, because the Arabic B cohort here is unusually varied. A single Diploma class can hold a student who hears Arabic at home every day and has never studied it formally, a student who studied it for five years as an additional language in an English-medium school, and a student who has recently arrived from a system where Arabic instruction was minimal. The first of those often has strong listening and weak reading. The second frequently has the reverse. A report grade does not distinguish them; a marked listening section does, in forty minutes.

The split of the grade makes the diagnosis worth doing properly. The receptive-skills paper, covering listening and reading, carries half the marks. The productive writing task carries a quarter, and the individual oral assessment the remaining quarter. So half the grade sits in two skills that can be measured cheaply and improved largely through disciplined independent practice, and a quarter sits in writing, where a student genuinely cannot self-correct. Knowing which half is weak determines whether a family should buy contact hours or a practice schedule.

Everything below is built to be checkable. The four diagnostics and what each reveals. How an error log works and why counting beats describing. What a documented eight weeks looks like, and the specific signs that a block has stopped working. How the oral differs between Standard and Higher Level, and what a recording shows that a conversation does not. And the plain boundary on what a tutor may do with work a student submits, which in a language course is easier to blur than in any other subject.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-b-tutor.programmesIntro: Three Arabic routes sit next to each other in an Abu Dhabi Diploma school, and the evidence that distinguishes them is different in each case. Getting the route right is worth more than any amount of tutoring inside the wrong one.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Arabic B
programmes.description: A Group 2 language acquisition course at Standard or Higher Level, organised around five prescribed themes and conceptual understandings covering audience, context, purpose, meaning and variation. Assessment is one writing task, one receptive-skills paper covering listening and reading, and an individual oral assessment. Higher Level adds two literary works studied in Arabic.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi the Arabic B class is often the widest-ranging language class in the school, because household exposure to Arabic varies enormously between students who look similarly placed on paper. That is precisely why a cold listening and reading diagnosis is worth more here than a teacher's early impression.

programmes.name: Arabic ab initio, and when it is the honest choice
programmes.description: A beginner's Group 2 Arabic course for students with little or no prior experience of the language, available at Standard Level only. It is not a weaker version of Arabic B; it is a different syllabus with different expectations, and a genuine beginner placed in Arabic B will struggle regardless of effort or tutoring.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi families sometimes choose Arabic B over ab initio because it sounds more ambitious, and the evidence usually settles it faster than the debate does. A cold reading section attempted in a trial lesson shows within twenty minutes whether a student is working at B level or starting from the beginning.

programmes.name: Mandatory school Arabic, which is a separate stream
programmes.ageRange: All year groups in private schools
programmes.description: Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed international curriculum. That is a federal requirement rather than an IB course, it is covered by school fees, and its assessment is set by the school and the regulator rather than by the IB.
programmes.countryNote: A parent told that their child is weak in Arabic should always ask which stream is meant. A mark in the mandatory stream and a mark in Diploma Arabic B measure different things, and buying tutoring for one when the other is the problem is the commonest misdirected spend in Arabic provision here.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-b-tutor.subjectsIntro: What an Arabic B family buys hours against, with the evidence each component produces and the honest view on whether paid contact time is the right purchase.

subjects.name: Paper 2: listening
subjects.description: Recorded Arabic with comprehension questions, sat under time. The diagnostic that separates students who hear Arabic at home from those who have only read it. Produces a hard number in forty minutes and improves with volume of timed practice rather than with teaching.

subjects.name: Paper 2: reading
subjects.description: Authentic Arabic texts with comprehension questions. Marks are usually lost to script fluency and to time rather than to vocabulary. The evidence to look for is whether unanswered questions cluster at the end, which indicates pace rather than comprehension.

subjects.name: Paper 1: productive writing
subjects.description: One task from three in a specified text type and word range. The component where a student cannot self-correct and where an error log is worth building. Register and convention carry real marks independently of grammatical accuracy.

subjects.name: Text types in Arabic
subjects.description: Formal letter, report, blog, article, speech, brochure, set of instructions and others, each with expected conventions of address and layout. Five learned properly beats twelve recognised vaguely, because the paper offers a choice of tasks.

subjects.name: Register: fusha against dialect
subjects.description: Modern Standard Arabic is the language of assessment, and students with household exposure to a dialect import structures without noticing. Counting those imports by category in a log is the fastest route to removing them, and it is invisible to a student working alone.

subjects.name: Individual oral assessment at Standard Level
subjects.description: A visual stimulus linked to one of the prescribed themes, with a short presentation and then discussion. Recording a timed run is the evidence that matters, because students almost always misjudge their own length and their connection to the theme.

subjects.name: Individual oral assessment at Higher Level
subjects.description: An extract from one of the two literary works studied, followed by discussion of the themes. Candidates commonly explain what happens in the extract instead of using it to reach the themes, which is visible immediately in a recording.

subjects.name: The two literary works at Higher Level
subjects.description: Two works read in Arabic that feed the oral and the themes rather than being assessed as literature in their own right. A student who has read them attentively has a materially easier oral, and one who has skimmed them has a harder one.

subjects.name: The five prescribed themes
subjects.description: Identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. A student who can speak for two minutes in Arabic on each theme with concrete examples is prepared for most of what the course asks of them.

subjects.name: Script fluency and handwriting speed
subjects.description: Both papers are handwritten in Arabic under time. A student whose script is slow loses marks that have nothing to do with their Arabic, and the evidence is a timed piece that stops mid-answer rather than one that is wrong.

regions.note: Mixed villa communities where many Arabic B candidates are non-Arab students who have studied Arabic as an additional language since primary. Reading is usually stronger than listening here, and the timed listening section is the diagnostic that surprises families.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island

sections.heading: The four diagnostics, and what each one actually reveals
paragraphs: A first session that produces a document is worth several that produce a conversation. In Arabic B the four documents are a timed listening section, a timed reading section, one piece of writing in a specified text type, and a recorded oral run. Each can be produced inside a single session, and together they localise the problem precisely enough that a family knows what to buy and, often, what not to buy.

The listening section is the most informative and the one almost nobody sits voluntarily. Students with household exposure to spoken Arabic frequently score well on it and poorly on reading, which tells a family that script fluency rather than comprehension is the constraint. Students who learned Arabic in a classroom often score the reverse, which points at exposure to connected speech at examination pace. The same report grade covers both, and they need opposite plans.

The reading section carries a second signal that is easy to read and rarely looked for. If the unanswered questions cluster at the end of the paper, the problem is pace, not understanding, and pace is fixed with timed drills rather than with vocabulary work. If wrong answers are scattered throughout, comprehension is the issue. One marked script distinguishes these in a glance, and that distinction changes months of practice.

The writing piece and the oral recording complete the picture. Written errors counted by category show whether a student's problem is grammatical accuracy, register, or failure to meet the text type's conventions, and those three have different remedies and different costs. The oral recording, with its timings written down, shows whether a candidate can fill the time, whether they connect to a prescribed theme, and whether dialect structures surface under pressure. Four documents, two or three sessions, and a family that knows what it is dealing with.

sections.heading: Arabic B or Arabic ab initio: letting the evidence decide
paragraphs: Group 2 Arabic exists at two starting points. Arabic B is for students with some prior experience of the language; Arabic ab initio is a Standard Level course for genuine beginners, with its own syllabus and its own expectations. They are different courses rather than easier and harder versions of one, and a beginner placed in Arabic B will struggle however hard they work and however much tutoring is bought.

Families sometimes resist ab initio because it sounds like a step down, and the resistance is understandable and expensive. A student who cannot read a short authentic text at the pace the paper demands is not going to reach Arabic B standard by DP2 through effort alone, and the two years spent trying will cost both money and points. The reverse error happens too: a student with real household exposure parked in ab initio is under-placed and will find the course unchallenging without that showing up as a problem anyone reports.

The evidence settles it quickly. A cold reading section and a cold listening section, attempted honestly, show within forty minutes whether a student is operating at B level. Where a MYP Language Acquisition phase record exists, it adds a documented history and often removes the need for any paid assessment at all. The Diploma coordinator holds both the phase record and the professional judgement, and the conversation is free.

The timing point matters. This decision is made at DP1 subject choices and is difficult to reverse later, so the useful moment to gather evidence is before the choices close rather than in the second term when a first report arrives. Families who spend one session on a diagnostic in Year 11 routinely save considerably more than the session cost.

sections.heading: Counting errors instead of describing them
paragraphs: Feedback on written Arabic usually arrives as prose: more care needed with verb forms, register sometimes inconsistent, structure could be clearer. All of that may be accurate and none of it is measurable, which means neither the student nor the parent can tell whether the next piece is better. An error log replaces the prose with counts, and counts can fall.

The method is deliberately unsophisticated. Each marked piece is scored against a small fixed set of categories: verb form and agreement, definiteness and case endings where required, register slips from dialect into Modern Standard Arabic, text-type convention failures, and task completion gaps. Each category gets a number. The student rewrites the piece, and the rewrite is scored against the same categories. Three or four pieces later the pattern is unmistakable, and it is usually narrower than anyone expected: most students have two recurring categories, not six.

What this buys is the ability to stop. A student whose register slips have gone from eleven in the first piece to two in the fourth has finished with register, and continuing to work on it is comfortable and pointless. A parent holding four scored pieces can see that without reading Arabic, which is the whole purpose of counting. It also makes an honest case for ending a block, which prose feedback never does.

The categories also distinguish costs. Grammatical accuracy improves slowly and partly through reading volume, so it is a poor target for paid contact hours. Register and text-type conventions improve quickly with marked feedback, because the student simply does not know the convention and can be told. Task completion is usually a reading problem, not a writing one: the student missed part of the instruction. Each diagnosis points at a different and differently priced remedy.

sections.heading: The oral, recorded: evidence a parent can hear
paragraphs: The individual oral assessment carries a quarter of the grade, is examined inside the school, and is the one component a parent never witnesses. It is also the component where a recording made at home is almost as informative as the examination itself, which makes it the easiest place in Arabic B to generate evidence that a non-Arabic-speaking parent can evaluate directly.

At Standard Level the oral is built on a visual stimulus linked to one of the five prescribed themes: a short presentation, then discussion. The recurring failure is description. A photograph can be described accurately in Arabic for three minutes without the candidate ever connecting it to identities, social organisation or sharing the planet, and that candidate has answered a question nobody asked. The fix is a habit rather than a skill: name the theme within the first fifteen seconds, then return to it. Two recorded runs is usually enough to install it.

At Higher Level the oral is built on an extract from one of the two literary works studied, followed by discussion of the themes. Here the failure is treating the extract as a comprehension exercise and explaining what happens in it. The task is to use the extract as a way into the themes, which requires having actually read the work. A recording makes the difference obvious in the first minute, and it is the clearest signal available of whether the Higher Level reading has been done.

The timings are the part to write down. Log how long the presentation ran, how long each half of a two-source discussion took, and how long the candidate spent on their opening. Students consistently misjudge all three, and almost all of them cut their own opening after hearing one playback. Because the words spoken in the examination are the candidate's own, this is work a tutor can support with no authorship question arising at any point.

sections.heading: Eight documented weeks, and the signs a block has stopped working
paragraphs: A block of Arabic B tutoring should leave a paper trail that a parent can read without knowing the language. The pattern below is what we aim for, and it is written here so a family can hold us to it rather than as a description of good intentions.

Weeks one and two produce the four diagnostics and the one-page summary. Week three targets the single weakest component and nothing else, which in this course is most often register in writing or pace in reading. Week four produces a second comparable measurement of the same thing, so the numbers can be set side by side. Weeks five and six extend to a second component, usually the oral, with runs recorded and timings logged. Weeks seven and eight review against week one and give a stop-or-continue recommendation in writing, with the documents attached.

The signs of a block that has stopped working are specific and worth naming in advance. No new marked or recorded work for three weeks. Sessions spent on general conversation practice rather than on a measured component. Error categories that are discussed but never counted. A student who improves inside the session and not outside it. Any of those is a reason to ask which component is being worked on and what number is expected to move, and a tutor who cannot answer in one sentence has lost the plot of the engagement.

Grade movement lags all of it, and families should expect that. A student can halve their register errors and hold the same overall grade for a term, because the overall grade aggregates four things and only one has moved. That is why the record is component-level rather than grade-level, and why an honest answer about how quickly a grade shifts is that the school knows how close your child already was to a boundary and we do not.

sections.heading: What the school report is measuring, and what ADEK does and does not tell you
paragraphs: An Abu Dhabi family can be holding two Arabic marks at once without realising they measure different things. Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed international curriculum, which is a federal requirement rather than an IB one. Diploma Arabic B is a separate Group 2 course with its own assessment. A weak mark in the mandatory stream says nothing reliable about Arabic B performance, and a parent should always ask which is meant.

ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, licenses and inspects private schools in the emirate and publishes inspection outcomes. That gives a family a document about the school, which is genuinely useful for judging provision, and no information at all about why their own child's listening score is weak. The two are frequently confused, and a disappointing Arabic grade is not explained by an inspection report. It is explained by a marked section.

Predicted grades are the other document families misread. A predicted grade is the school's professional estimate for the IB, used in university applications. It is not a mark and not a promise. Where a predicted Arabic B grade sits below expectation, the productive question is which of the three components produced it, because that is answerable and actionable. Schools answer that question willingly; requests to revise a prediction rarely go anywhere.

One local rule closes off an obvious route. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition permit carries a code of conduct with the same restriction. So your child's own Arabic teacher cannot be their paid tutor here. What that teacher can do, at no cost, is say which component is weak, which is the most useful piece of information in the whole engagement.

sections.heading: Where a tutor's work ends in a language course
paragraphs: Language subjects blur the authorship line more easily than any others, because the obvious way to improve a piece of Arabic writing is to correct it, and a corrected piece can slide into a rewritten piece without anyone deciding to cross a line. The IB's academic honesty requirements apply to any work submitted as the candidate's own, and a breach is a matter for the student's Diploma rather than a disagreement between a parent and a tutor. So the boundary is worth stating in terms a family can enforce.

A tutor may mark the student's writing and count its errors, name the category of each error without supplying the correction, teach a text type and its conventions, explain register and demonstrate it on material the student is not submitting, run timed practice, record and review oral runs, and ask examiner-style questions. All of that is normal language teaching and is where the hours should go.

A tutor may not supply replacement sentences for a piece that will be submitted, rewrite a paragraph into its final form, correct a draft line by line so that the finished text is beyond what the student could produce alone, or hand over a model answer to adapt. The workable test in a language course is whether the student could reproduce the correction unprompted in a new piece. If they cannot, they have been given an answer rather than taught a rule, and the piece is no longer evidence of their Arabic.

This market makes the point less theoretical than it sounds. Operations selling completed assessed work advertise openly in the UAE search results, one of them with a published price. A family should expect any legitimate tutor to refuse that request plainly and in writing, and should treat a provider willing to take it as a risk to their child's Diploma rather than a convenience worth paying for.

sections.heading: Getting started, availability and the permit question
paragraphs: The first step is free and the second produces documents. Ask the school which component of Arabic B is weak and ask for any marked work they can release. Then take the free trial lesson, one per family with no card details taken, and use it to produce the first of the four diagnostics rather than to discuss the situation. A trial lesson that generates a marked listening section is worth more than one that generates a plan.

What follows is a named weakest component and an hours figure, which is sometimes zero. A student whose reading gaps cluster at the end of the paper needs timed drills they can run alone, not weekly sessions. A student with household Arabic and a register problem needs three or four marked writing pieces and then nothing. Both answers are cheaper than a package and more useful than an open-ended commitment, and both are checkable against the documents.

Availability in Arabic B is better than in Arabic A, because the course does not require a literary specialist, but Higher Level oral support built on a literary extract narrows the pool. Where nobody suitable is free for the level and component you need, you are told with a realistic date rather than matched to a general Arabic teacher. You see the matched tutor's actual teaching background before the trial rather than after it. Lessons are delivered one to one over live video; IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, and visiting tutors are a service we run only in India.

On legality the position is short and checkable. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18; MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and because no fine schedule is published, any amount quoted at you is unverified. IB Gram holds no regulator licence or accreditation of any kind and operates no office or centre in the UAE.

process.title: Ask the school which component is weak
process.description: Arabic B splits into listening, reading, writing and the oral, and the school's teacher usually knows which of them is costing the grade. That answer is free, it is the most valuable single piece of information in the engagement, and it should be obtained before any hours are bought.

process.title: Use the trial lesson to produce a document
process.description: One trial lesson per family, no card details taken, no obligation. Rather than discussing the situation, the session produces the first diagnostic: a marked timed listening or reading section, or a written piece with its errors counted. You leave with evidence rather than an impression.

process.title: Complete the four diagnostics in a fortnight
process.description: Marked listening, marked reading, one scored written piece and a recorded oral run with timings, summarised on one dated page. That page is what every later session is measured against, and it is deliberately legible to a parent who reads no Arabic.

process.title: Target one component and measure it twice
process.description: Sessions work on a single named component, and a second comparable measurement follows within a fortnight. If the number moved, the plan continues. If it did not, the plan changes, and we say which we think it should be rather than leaving the choice unspoken.

process.title: Review at eight weeks and stop where appropriate
process.description: A written comparison against the first measurements, with the documents attached. Error categories that have fallen to near zero are finished, and continuing to work on them is comfortable and wasteful. We would rather end a block early than keep a slot filled.

whyPoints.title: Evidence a non-Arabic-speaking parent can read
whyPoints.description: Marked sections produce numbers, error logs produce counts, and oral runs produce recordings with timings. None of those require a parent to read Arabic to evaluate, which is the whole point of generating them rather than describing progress in prose.

whyPoints.title: Counting rather than describing
whyPoints.description: Written errors are scored against a small fixed set of categories on every piece, and the same categories are scored on the rewrite. Most students turn out to have two recurring categories rather than six, and a count that falls is the only honest way to show that.

whyPoints.title: A plan that can end
whyPoints.description: Oral improvement saturates after a few recorded runs and register errors fall away quickly once counted. When the numbers say a component is finished, we say so rather than extending the block, including when the honest answer after a trial lesson is that nothing needs buying.

whyPoints.title: The ab initio question answered with evidence
whyPoints.description: A cold reading and listening section shows within forty minutes whether a student is working at Arabic B level or starting from the beginning. That is a far better basis for a two-year subject decision than an impression, and it is worth gathering before DP1 choices close.

whyPoints.title: The authorship line stated in enforceable terms
whyPoints.description: A tutor names the category of an error without supplying the correction, and demonstrates register on material the student is not submitting. The test a family can apply is whether their child could reproduce the correction unprompted in a new piece.

faqs.question: How will I know whether Arabic B tutoring is working if I do not read Arabic?
faqs.answer: By insisting on documents that produce numbers rather than descriptions. A marked listening section gives a score. A marked reading section shows whether unanswered questions cluster at the end, which indicates pace. A written piece with errors counted by category gives counts that can fall across pieces. A recorded oral run with its timings written down lets you hear the opening getting shorter. None of those requires you to read Arabic to evaluate. Ask for the four, dated, in the first fortnight, and compare them against the same four eight weeks later.

faqs.question: Why should my daughter sit a timed listening section before anything else?
faqs.answer: Because it is the fastest way to separate two very different students who look identical on a report. A candidate with household exposure to spoken Arabic often scores well on listening and poorly on reading, which means script fluency is the constraint. A candidate who learned Arabic in a classroom frequently scores the reverse, which points at exposure to connected speech at examination pace. Those two need opposite plans, and the listening section distinguishes them in forty minutes. It is also half of a paper that carries half the grade.

faqs.question: Should my son be on Arabic B or Arabic ab initio?
faqs.answer: Let the evidence decide rather than the label. Arabic ab initio is a Standard Level course for genuine beginners with its own syllabus; Arabic B assumes prior experience. A beginner placed in Arabic B will struggle however hard they work. A cold reading section and a cold listening section, attempted honestly, show within forty minutes which course fits, and where a MYP Language Acquisition phase record exists it adds a documented history. The decision is made at DP1 subject choices and is hard to reverse, so gather the evidence before they close.

faqs.question: What is an error log and why would it be better than written feedback?
faqs.answer: An error log scores each marked piece against a small fixed set of categories: verb form and agreement, register slips from dialect into Modern Standard Arabic, text-type convention failures, task completion gaps and word range control. Each gets a number, the student rewrites, and the rewrite is scored on the same categories. Feedback written as prose may be accurate and cannot be measured, so nobody can tell whether the next piece is better. A count can fall, and a count that has fallen to near zero tells you a block is finished.

faqs.question: My daughter speaks Arabic at home. Why is she losing marks in writing?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly register. Modern Standard Arabic is the language of assessment, and a student who speaks a dialect at home imports vocabulary and structures without noticing, more so under time pressure. That is not a knowledge gap and it responds quickly once it is counted rather than described: most students cut their register slips sharply across three or four marked pieces. The second common cause is text-type convention, where accurate Arabic is written in the wrong voice for the task, which is also quick to fix once the convention is taught.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether a weak reading score is comprehension or speed?
faqs.answer: Look at where the gaps are on the marked script. If unanswered questions cluster at the end of the section, the student ran out of time and the problem is pace, which responds to timed drills they can run independently. If wrong answers are scattered through the whole section, comprehension is the issue and the remedy is different and slower. This distinction takes one marked script and a glance, and getting it wrong means months of practice aimed at the wrong thing, which is the most common quiet waste in this course.

faqs.question: Does the Higher Level oral really require reading both literary works?
faqs.answer: Yes, and a recording exposes whether it has happened within the first minute. At Higher Level the individual oral assessment is built on an extract from one of the two works studied, and the task is to use the extract as a route into the prescribed themes rather than to explain what happens in it. A candidate who has skimmed the work can describe the extract and cannot move outward from it. That is audible to anyone listening to a practice run, including a parent who does not read Arabic.

faqs.question: How many recorded oral practice runs does a candidate actually need?
faqs.answer: Usually two or three, and then improvement saturates. What candidates get wrong is structural rather than linguistic: describing a visual stimulus without naming a prescribed theme at Standard Level, or treating a literary extract as a comprehension passage at Higher Level, plus misjudging length. All of those surface on the first recording and are mostly corrected by the second or third. A tutor proposing ten oral sessions has misread the component. The recordings themselves are the evidence, and the timings should be written down each time.

faqs.question: Can my son practise listening and reading without paying for sessions?
faqs.answer: Largely yes, once the format has been explained, and it would not be honest to pretend otherwise. Listening and reading improve with the volume of timed practice and with identifying which question types he consistently misses, both of which he can do alone. What paid time adds is the initial explanation, the marking of the first few sections, and a monthly review that checks whether the practice is happening and what the error pattern is. One taught session plus a schedule plus a monthly review is the usual proposal.

faqs.question: Is the Arabic on my child's school report the same as her Arabic B grade?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, and this is worth clarifying before buying anything. Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum, which is a federal requirement separate from the IB. A report may carry a mark from that mandatory stream, a mark from Diploma Arabic B, or both. They measure different things against different expectations. Ask the school which stream a comment refers to, because the answer determines whether you need a Group 2 Diploma tutor or general Arabic support.

faqs.question: How long is the Arabic B writing task, and does length affect the mark?
faqs.answer: The task specifies a word range that differs between Standard and Higher Level, and it binds at both ends. A piece that falls substantially short has not met the task; one that overshoots loses structural control and time for checking. Students should know their range as a number and should have written to it under timed conditions at least three times, which is practice they can do alone once it has been set up. Confirm the current range and paper timing with your child's Diploma coordinator, as published figures are revised between guide editions.

faqs.question: Can a tutor correct my daughter's Arabic draft before she submits it?
faqs.answer: A tutor can mark it and name the category of each error without supplying the correction, which is teaching. A tutor cannot work through it line by line so that the finished text is beyond what she could produce alone, because at that point the piece stops being evidence of her Arabic and the submission is no longer authentically hers. The test a family can apply is simple: could she reproduce the correction unprompted in a new piece? If not, she was given an answer rather than taught a rule, and the line has been crossed.

faqs.question: Do shortened Ramadan school days change the Arabic B plan?
faqs.answer: They change what the sessions contain rather than how often they run. School days shorten across the UAE and household evenings reorganise around Iftar, so the usable window moves later and compresses. Long timed papers fit poorly into a post-Iftar slot; short listening practice, register work on a piece already written, and recorded oral runs all work well at 60 to 75 minutes. The sensible plan moves timed practice before or after those weeks and identifies in advance any internal oral assessment date falling in or just after them.

faqs.question: What should the session notes for an Arabic B lesson contain?
faqs.answer: Four things, and they should be specific enough to argue with: which component the session targeted, what the student produced during it, what they are doing before the next session, and which measurement will show whether it worked. A note reporting good engagement tells a parent nothing. A note saying register slips were counted at seven in this piece against eleven in the last, and a new text type is due on Sunday, can be checked when Sunday's piece arrives. Notes go out the same day.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-b-tutor.closingHeading: Ask for four documents, then judge
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-arabic-b-tutor.closingBody: Arabic B is easy to buy badly and straightforward to measure. Ask the school which component is weak, then take a free trial lesson, one per family with no card details taken, and use it to produce a marked section rather than a conversation. Within a fortnight you should hold four dated documents and a one-page summary, and eight weeks later you should hold the same four again for comparison. If the numbers moved, the hours worked. If they did not, the plan changes or stops. Lessons run one to one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.
