sections.heading: What CAS actually requires, stated plainly
paragraphs: CAS asks for experiences across three strands, creativity, activity and service, undertaken over at least eighteen months from the start of DP1, together with a project lasting a minimum of one month. The student keeps a portfolio of evidence and reflections and has three documented interviews with the school's CAS coordinator: one near the beginning, one part-way through and one at the end. The coordinator confirms completion.

There is no grade. CAS contributes nothing to the forty-five points and cannot lift a diploma score by a single mark. What it can do is prevent the award of the diploma if it is not completed, which is why it carries real weight despite carrying no marks. A student with excellent examination results and an unfinished portfolio has a problem that no amount of academic strength resolves.

The requirement families most often ask about is hours, and the answer has changed. Older guidance attached a total number of hours to CAS, and that figure still circulates widely in the Gulf. The IB's current guidance works instead on duration and balance across the strands rather than on an hours total, while many schools keep an internal hours expectation of their own for practical tracking. Ask your child's coordinator what their school requires, because that is the number that actually applies to your child.

The seven learning outcomes are the real specification, and they are the part students read last. Each experience in the portfolio should connect to one or more of them, and across the whole programme all seven need evidence. A portfolio with forty entries all evidencing the same two outcomes is incomplete; one with twelve entries spread across all seven is finished.
bullets: Three strands: creativity, activity, service, with a reasonable balance across them
At least eighteen months, beginning at the start of DP1
A CAS project of at least one month, involving one or more strands
A portfolio of evidence and reflections, kept by the student
Three documented interviews with the school's CAS coordinator
No grade, no points, but completion is required for the diploma

sections.heading: The seven learning outcomes and the evidence each one needs
paragraphs: The outcomes are where portfolios are won and lost, and most students never audit against them until the final interview. They cover identifying strengths and areas for growth, taking on a new challenge, planning and initiating, showing commitment and perseverance, working collaboratively, engaging with issues of global significance, and recognising the ethical implications of actions.

Read that list against a typical portfolio and the gaps are usually the same three. Taking on a new challenge is missing, because every activity listed is something the student already did before DP1. Ethical implications is missing, because nobody asked the student to think about them. Engaging with issues of global significance is thin, because the service work was local and nobody connected it to anything wider.

None of those gaps requires new activities. A student already coaching a younger team can evidence ethical implications by thinking seriously about safeguarding, fairness in selection or the pressure placed on children. A student doing coastal clean-ups can connect it to waste and water policy, which is global and locally visible at once. The portfolio changes without the schedule changing, which is why an audit is worth more than a package of new experiences.

The table sets out what each outcome looks for and what counts as evidence. Use it as a checklist against the portfolio before the final interview, not after it, because the coordinator can only sign off what the portfolio shows. An hour spent with that checklist in early DP2 is worth more than any paid intervention later, and it is work a student can do alone.

sections.heading: Where families in Abu Dhabi waste money on CAS
paragraphs: Four purchases recur, and all four are poor value. The first and largest is the paid volunteering placement. Providers across the Gulf sell structured volunteering with a certificate at the end, sometimes for several hundred dirhams and sometimes for a great deal more. The certificate is the product. A certificate evidences attendance, and attendance is not one of the seven learning outcomes.

The second is the event package: a weekend of festival or sporting volunteering sold as a CAS block. The evidence it generates is a one-off with photographs, which is exactly what the commitment and perseverance outcome does not accept. A student who needs commitment evidence needs something recurring over months, and the cheapest version of that is usually free and five minutes from home.

The third is reflection and portfolio writing, which is sold more quietly and is the one item on this list that cannot be bought legitimately at all. The portfolio is the student's record of what they did and thought. Reflections written by anyone else are not the student's, and a coordinator who signs off a portfolio they suspect is not authentic is being asked to do something they should not do.

The fourth is the open mentoring arrangement: a weekly CAS session running through DP1 and DP2. CAS does not contain enough content to fill eighty sessions. After the first few, the agenda becomes a progress conversation that the coordinator holds three times for nothing. The tell is a session that opens with how is CAS going and ends with keep going.
bullets: Paid placements sell certificates, and no outcome asks for a certificate

sections.heading: The three cases where paying for CAS mentoring is justified
paragraphs: The first is executive function. A student who genuinely cannot hold an eighteen-month commitment, remember to capture evidence, or write a reflection within a week of an experience is not lazy and will not be fixed by being told to try harder. Three or four front-loaded sessions that build a realistic weekly pattern, an evidence habit and a reflection routine can change the whole programme for that student, and the gains extend beyond CAS to internal assessment deadlines.

The second is a late entry. A student arriving in Abu Dhabi mid-DP1, or transferring into the diploma from another system, faces the same eighteen-month expectation with less time. That compression needs planning rather than tutoring: which strands can run concurrently, which single commitment can serve two strands, what the project will be and when it can realistically occupy a month. Two sessions and an agreement with the coordinator usually settles it.

The third is a collapsed project. CAS projects fail for predictable reasons: a group formed on friendship rather than reliability, no single owner of the schedule, scope chosen before the calendar was checked. When a project dies in DP2 and the month-minimum requirement still has to be met, scoping a smaller achievable replacement and getting it approved before starting is worth a couple of hours of someone's attention.

Outside those three, the honest recommendation is to spend nothing. We say that in the consultation, and families who hear it once tend to trust our scoping on the subjects where we do recommend hours. A CAS block sold to a student whose coordinator would have handled it costs money and teaches the student that this part of the diploma is somebody else's problem.

sections.heading: The CAS project, and the four reasons it fails
paragraphs: The project is the only part of CAS with a hard structural requirement beyond the outcomes: at least one month, involving one or more strands, collaborative, with planning, action and reflection documented. It is also the part that most often goes wrong, and the reasons are boringly consistent.

The first is group composition. Students form project groups with friends, and friendship does not predict reliability. A group of five where two people do everything produces a resentful month and weak collaboration evidence for three of them. The second is ownership: when the schedule belongs to everybody it belongs to nobody, and the project drifts past the month it was supposed to occupy without the planning stage ever ending.

The third is scope chosen before the calendar was read. An ambitious project announced in October runs into mock examinations in January and internal assessment deadlines in February. A month-long project needs a month in which the students involved are actually available, and in a diploma calendar those months are specific and few.

The fourth is documentation. A project that happened and was not recorded is, for CAS purposes, a project that is hard to sign off. Planning notes, messages, photographs, a short reflection at the start and the end: all of it takes minutes at the time and is painful to reconstruct afterwards. The students who find the final interview easy are the ones who wrote things down while they were happening.
bullets: Choose a group for reliability, not for friendship
Name one person who owns the schedule
Check the diploma calendar before fixing the scope
Document planning and reflection as it happens, not at the end
Agree the project with the coordinator before starting it

sections.heading: Eighteen months counted backwards
paragraphs: CAS fails on timing far more often than on effort, because nothing in it has a weekly deadline. It is the easiest thing in the diploma to postpone and the hardest to compress, since commitment and perseverance cannot be demonstrated retrospectively. Planning backwards from the school's final interview is the only approach that works.

Three fixed points structure the eighteen months: the first documented interview near the start of DP1, the mid-point interview, and the final interview at which completion is confirmed. Everything else is the student's own schedule, which is precisely why it slips. The portfolio should be audited against the seven outcomes well before the final interview rather than during it.

Ramadan is a specific planning factor in this emirate and is usually treated as an obstacle when it is an opportunity. Community and charitable activity increases, school hours shorten, and service work with a real purpose is abundant and genuinely valued. Families who plan service commitments around that period rather than pausing them tend to come out of it with the strongest ethical-implications reflections in the portfolio.

We publish no IB dates on this page. Internal interview dates and portfolio deadlines are set by your child's school, and the IB's own site is the authority for anything beyond that; it does not permit automated checking, so any date printed here would be second-hand. Ask the CAS coordinator for their schedule and build the plan from it, and note the dates somewhere the student will see them rather than somewhere a parent will.

sections.heading: Reflections, interviews and what the coordinator is looking for
paragraphs: CAS reflections are not essays and should not read like them. A good reflection is short, specific and honest about something that did not go to plan. What did I expect, what happened, what did I notice about myself, what will I do differently. Four sentences written the evening after an experience beats four hundred words written in DP2 about an experience in DP1.

Coordinators are not looking for polish. They are looking for authenticity and for coverage of the outcomes. A portfolio of beautifully written entries that all describe success is weaker than a plain one that records a failed fundraising attempt, a disagreement inside a project group, and what the student did about both. The outcomes explicitly ask for growth, challenge and ethical awareness, and none of those appear in a portfolio of triumphs.

The three documented interviews are conversations, not examinations. The student should arrive able to say what they are committed to, how long they have been doing it, which outcomes the portfolio currently evidences and which it does not. A student who can name their own gaps is in a strong position, because the coordinator's job becomes helping rather than chasing.

The single habit that makes all of this easy costs nothing: write the reflection immediately. Students who maintain that habit finish CAS without noticing. Students who do not spend DP2 reconstructing eighteen months from memory and photographs, which is both unpleasant and, in the parts that matter, not really possible.

sections.heading: Authenticity, and what simply cannot be bought
paragraphs: CAS is unmarked, which sometimes leads families to treat it as a paperwork exercise where authenticity matters less. The opposite is closer to true. There is no mark scheme to hide behind, so the only thing the coordinator can assess is whether the record is genuine, and they know the student.

What cannot be bought: reflections, because they must be the student's own thinking about their own experience. Evidence of commitment, because it is a function of time and nothing compresses it. A learning outcome, because an outcome is something that happened to a person rather than a document that can be supplied. A certificate is not an outcome, a receipt is not evidence, and a package of experiences arranged entirely by adults undermines the planning and initiating outcome it was bought to satisfy.

IB Gram does not supply reflections or portfolio entries, does not sell or broker volunteering placements, and does not issue certificates of any kind. Where we work on CAS the student writes every word, and the sessions are about structure, scheduling and reading the outcomes properly. We will also decline work when the consultation shows the coordinator can cover it, which is most of the time.

The wider point for a parent weighing any offer in this space: ask what the product actually is. If the answer is a document, a certificate or a set of pre-arranged activities, it is not addressing the seven outcomes. If the answer is a habit, a schedule or an honest audit against the outcomes, it might be, and it should take hours rather than terms.

process.title: Email your coordinator first
process.description: Ask which of the seven learning outcomes the portfolio currently evidences and which it does not. That list costs nothing, comes from the person who signs off completion, and in most cases is the only thing a family actually needed.

process.title: Bring the gap list to the consultation
process.description: With the coordinator's list in hand, one free consultation is enough to say whether anything is worth buying. We will often conclude that the school can finish it and recommend spending nothing, which is the most common outcome of a CAS enquiry here.

process.title: Name which of the three cases applies
process.description: Executive-function difficulty, a late entry into the programme, or a collapsed project. If none of the three fits, paid mentoring is unlikely to earn its cost, and we would rather say that than scope a block for the sake of it.

process.title: Audit the portfolio against the outcomes
process.description: Where we do work, the first session reads the portfolio against all seven outcomes and names what is missing and what would evidence it, using activities the student is already doing wherever possible rather than adding new commitments.

process.title: Build the habit, then withdraw
process.description: Three or four sessions establish a sustainable weekly commitment, an evidence-capture routine and the practice of writing reflections immediately. Once the habit holds, the block ends. CAS does not contain enough material for an ongoing arrangement.

process.title: Hand the student back to the coordinator
process.description: Every plan is agreed with the school, including a rebuilt project, because the coordinator approves completion. We write up what was done and what remains, and the student takes that into their next documented interview.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you to buy nothing
whyPoints.description: Most CAS enquiries end with a recommendation to email the coordinator and spend no money, because the coordinator's time is already inside your fees and only they can confirm completion. That is the most useful answer in this part of the diploma core.

whyPoints.title: Outcome-led, not activity-led
whyPoints.description: The seven learning outcomes are the specification, and most gaps can be closed with activities the student is already doing rather than with new ones. An audit against the outcomes changes the portfolio without changing the schedule.

whyPoints.title: No placements, no certificates, no reflections
whyPoints.description: We do not sell or broker volunteering, do not issue certificates and do not write reflections or portfolio entries. Those are the four things most readily sold in this market and none of them evidences a learning outcome.

whyPoints.title: Three named cases, published
whyPoints.description: Executive-function difficulty, late entry, collapsed project. Publishing the cases where paid support is justified also publishes the cases where it is not, which is a check a family can hold us to.

whyPoints.title: AED market bands with sources
whyPoints.description: The hourly figures on this page carry their survey date and origin, including Bestimate's 2026 rate table, so a family can judge any CAS quote against the market rather than against a feeling.

whyPoints.title: Local to the emirate, not generic
whyPoints.description: What CAS looks like depends on where a family lives, so the suggestions are specific to Abu Dhabi communities, including coastal and mangrove service, the Saadiyat cultural district and the coaching opportunities in the larger residential areas.

faqs.question: Should we be paying anyone for CAS at all?
faqs.answer: Usually not. CAS carries no grade and no marks, and the person who confirms completion is your child's CAS coordinator, whose time is already inside your fees. The cheapest first step is an email asking which of the seven learning outcomes the portfolio currently evidences. Most of the time the answer is two or three gaps the student can close in a fortnight using activities they are already doing. Paid mentoring is justified in three specific cases, and outside those it is money spent on a part of the diploma that cannot be improved by spending.

faqs.question: Is CAS graded, and can it stop my child getting the diploma?
faqs.answer: CAS is not graded and contributes no points to the total, so it cannot raise a diploma score by a single mark. It can, however, prevent the diploma being awarded if it is not completed, which is why it carries real weight despite carrying no marks. A candidate with strong examination results and an unfinished portfolio has a problem that academic strength does not solve. Completion is confirmed by the school's CAS coordinator after three documented interviews and a portfolio that evidences all seven outcomes.

faqs.question: Does CAS still require 150 hours?
faqs.answer: Older guidance attached an hours total to CAS and that figure still circulates widely in the Gulf. Current IB guidance works on duration and a reasonable balance across the three strands rather than on an hours count, while many schools keep an internal hours expectation of their own for tracking purposes. Ask your child's coordinator what their school requires, because the school's expectation is the one that applies to your child. Chasing a legacy number from an old document is a common way to spend a term on the wrong target.

faqs.question: What are the seven CAS learning outcomes actually asking for?
faqs.answer: They cover identifying strengths and areas for growth, undertaking a new challenge, planning and initiating, showing commitment and perseverance, working collaboratively, engaging with issues of global significance, and recognising ethical implications. The three most commonly missing are the new challenge, because every listed activity predates DP1; ethical implications, because nobody asked the student to think about them; and global significance, because the service work was local and never connected to anything wider. All three can usually be evidenced from existing activities.

faqs.question: What makes a CAS project different from a CAS experience?
faqs.answer: The project has structural requirements beyond the outcomes: it must last at least one month, involve one or more strands, be collaborative, and have documented planning, action and reflection. An experience can be a single activity or an ongoing commitment. The project is the part that most often fails, usually because the group was chosen for friendship rather than reliability, nobody owned the schedule, or the scope was fixed before anyone checked the diploma calendar for a month in which the students were actually free.

faqs.question: Are paid volunteering placements in Abu Dhabi worth the money?
faqs.answer: Rarely, because what they sell is a certificate and no learning outcome asks for one. A certificate evidences attendance; the outcomes ask for challenge, initiative, sustained commitment, collaboration, global awareness and ethical recognition. School-brokered placements usually cost nothing and often provide better evidence, because the student has to arrange their own participation, which is the planning and initiating outcome. If a package arranges everything on the student's behalf, it quietly undermines the outcome it was bought to satisfy.

faqs.question: Can someone else write my child's CAS reflections?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the one item in the CAS market that cannot be bought legitimately. The portfolio is the student's record of what they did and what they thought about it, and reflections written by anyone else are not the student's work. A coordinator asked to sign off a portfolio they suspect is not authentic is being put in an impossible position. We do not write reflections or portfolio entries, and any provider offering to is selling something a school should refuse.

faqs.question: How long does CAS run and when does the clock start?
faqs.answer: At least eighteen months, beginning at the start of DP1 rather than when the student gets round to it. That duration is why CAS cannot be compressed: commitment and perseverance are functions of elapsed time and cannot be demonstrated retrospectively. Activities from before the Diploma Programme do not count, and a portfolio assembled from a curriculum vitae of earlier achievements will not satisfy the outcomes. Students who start a recurring commitment in the first term of DP1 generally finish without noticing the requirement at all.

faqs.question: What do the three CAS interviews with the coordinator involve?
faqs.answer: They are conversations rather than examinations: one near the start of DP1, one around the mid-point, and one at the end at which completion is confirmed. The student should arrive able to say what they are committed to, how long it has been running, which outcomes the portfolio currently evidences and which it does not. A student who can name their own gaps turns the coordinator's role from chasing into helping, which is a far more productive meeting for everyone in the room.

faqs.question: Can a paid activity like private football coaching count towards CAS?
faqs.answer: Receiving coaching that the family pays for can sit in the activity strand, but it is weak evidence on its own because the planning and initiating outcome asks what the student organised rather than what was arranged for them. It also struggles with the new-challenge outcome if the student has been playing for years. Coaching others, by contrast, is strong: it often spans activity and service, generates collaboration evidence, and raises genuine ethical questions about fairness and pressure on younger children.

faqs.question: What CAS options actually exist across Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: More than most families use. Coastal and mangrove environmental work is accessible along the Corniche and the eastern side of the island. The Saadiyat cultural district supports arts-related creativity and visitor-facing service through schools. The larger residential communities, Khalifa City and Mohammed Bin Zayed City among them, have dense sports networks and plenty of younger children to coach or tutor. The constraint is rarely availability; it is choosing something recurring rather than a one-off event with photographs attached.

faqs.question: My child has left CAS until DP2. What now?
faqs.answer: Plan rather than panic, and involve the coordinator immediately. The questions are which commitments can run concurrently, which single activity can serve two strands, and when a month exists in the calendar for the project. Commitment and perseverance is the outcome that cannot be compressed, so start a recurring activity this week whatever else happens. Two sessions of planning plus an agreement with the coordinator usually produces a workable route, but it will involve a real weekly commitment rather than a purchase.

faqs.question: Can family business work or a part-time job count as CAS service?
faqs.answer: Paid employment and routine family obligations generally do not count, because service means benefit to a community rather than to the student or the household. There can be nuance where a student initiates something genuinely additional, such as building a community resource that happens to use skills learned at a family business. That is a judgement for the coordinator, not for a tutor, and it should be asked before the hours accumulate rather than after the portfolio is written.

faqs.question: Do universities ever look at the CAS portfolio?
faqs.answer: Universities do not receive the portfolio, and admissions decisions rest on grades, predicted grades, the personal statement or application essays and any subject requirements. What CAS can do is give a student something real to write about in an application, because a sustained commitment with honest reflection behind it produces better material than a list of one-off events. That is an argument for doing CAS properly, not for buying an impressive-looking portfolio that no admissions officer will ever read.

faqs.question: What does a legitimate CAS mentoring arrangement cost per hour?
faqs.answer: If it is justified at all, it is bought in one to four hours, not in terms. Market rates in the UAE surveyed in October 2026 put the subject-specialist band at AED 200 to 450 and above per hour, with the wider range running from about AED 45 at the university-student end to AED 650 and above at the premium end. Those are market figures with sources, not our prices. A weekly CAS arrangement running across DP1 and DP2 is the clearest sign that a provider has nothing specific to deliver.

faqs.question: Does a certificate from a volunteering provider prove a learning outcome?
faqs.answer: No. A certificate records that a student attended something, and attendance is not among the seven outcomes. What evidences an outcome is the student's own account of what they planned, what they attempted, what went wrong and what they noticed about themselves, supported by dated entries over time. A coordinator confirming completion is checking the portfolio against the outcomes, not counting certificates, which is why a folder of them can sit alongside a portfolio that is still incomplete.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-cas-tutor.closingHeading: Send one email before you spend anything
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-cas-tutor.closingBody: Ask your child's CAS coordinator which of the seven learning outcomes the portfolio currently evidences and which it does not. That list is free, it comes from the person who signs off completion, and for most families it is the whole answer. If what comes back shows a student who cannot hold an eighteen-month commitment, a late entry into the programme with time to make up, or a project that has collapsed, those are the three cases where a few hours of mentoring earn their cost. Tell us which one applies and we will scope it in hours, with one free consultation and an honest recommendation to spend nothing if that is what the gap list shows.

intro.heading: What should be in your hands after six weeks of Chemistry Higher Level sessions
paragraphs: Most Abu Dhabi families start paying for Chemistry Higher Level support in the term after a disappointing mock. Six weeks later the honest question is not whether the tutor is pleasant or punctual. It is whether anything measurable has changed. A Chemistry Higher Level tutor in Abu Dhabi who cannot put a marked script, a dated draft and a short written record on the table is asking you to judge the work on impressions, and impressions are exactly what the mock already contradicted.

So this page is built around evidence rather than promises. It sets out what a session produces, what arrives in your inbox afterwards, how a marked Paper 2 is read, how the scientific investigation draft trail is kept, and what the record looks like in month two when the grade has not yet moved. It also sets out what the record cannot tell you, because a tutor who claims the paperwork proves more than it does is doing the same thing as one who keeps no paperwork at all.

Chemistry Higher Level is a 240-hour course assessed through two written papers and one internal investigation. Paper 1 carries 36 per cent and splits into multiple-choice items and a data-based section. Paper 2 carries 44 per cent and is where extended reasoning, mechanisms and multi-step calculations are tested. The investigation carries the remaining 20 per cent and is marked by the school against published criteria before external moderation. Those three numbers decide where paid hours are worth spending, and a record that does not reference them is not a record of anything.

The delivery model matters to the evidence. Because lessons run over live video with a shared whiteboard, the written work a student produces in the session is already a file: the annotated question, the corrected mechanism, the recalculated energetics problem. An in-home tutor in the Abu Dhabi market may do identical teaching, but the artefacts usually leave with the tutor or stay in the student's notebook, and the parent sees a verbal summary at the door. The format is not better because it is online. It is easier to audit.

Read the sections below in order if your child is in DP1 and you are deciding whether to start. Skip to the twelve-week log and the stalled-grade section if you are already paying someone and want to work out whether to continue. Every AED figure on this page is a market band taken from published rate cards and rate surveys, attributed where it appears, and is not a price list for this service. If your child is in DP2 with a mock already behind them, the pre-session intensive format described further down is usually the right starting point rather than a standard weekly slot, because the remaining weeks are finite and the diagnosis has to come quickly.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-chemistry-hl-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Chemistry Higher Level is the end of a long runway. Most Abu Dhabi students arrive at it from MYP sciences or from an IGCSE double or triple award, and the gap between those starting points and DP1 chemistry explains a large share of the marks lost in the first year.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The two-year Diploma, in which Chemistry Higher Level is one of three subjects taken at the deeper level. The course is organised around structure and reactivity, with Higher Level extensions layered onto the same themes rather than taught as separate units. Assessment is two written papers plus one scientific investigation, and the investigation is marked internally against published criteria before the IB moderates a sample. Students also carry the core: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi Diploma cohorts are small, so a chemistry class of twelve is common and a class of six is not unusual. That has two consequences for paid support. A student who falls behind is visible quickly, which is useful. A student whose difficulty is unusual within a small class may wait a long time for teaching that addresses it, which is where one-to-one hours earn their place.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The five-year programme that feeds most IB continuum schools in the emirate. MYP sciences are assessed against four criteria: knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The criteria reward investigation design and evaluation heavily, which prepares a student well for the Diploma investigation and less well for the recall density and calculation speed that Chemistry Higher Level papers demand.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP-to-Diploma step is the single most common reason an Abu Dhabi family first contacts a chemistry tutor. A student who scored 7s against MYP criteria can still open DP1 with no fluency in moles, limiting reagents or significant figures, because those were never the thing being marked. Six to eight focused hours in the first term usually closes that gap before it becomes a grade.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Edexcel upper secondary
programmes.description: Many Abu Dhabi students take Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 or Edexcel 4CH1 before moving into the Diploma, sometimes at a different school. Both cover bonding, stoichiometry, rates, equilibrium and organic families, but at a depth that stops well short of Higher Level. Entropy, Gibbs energy, electrode potentials and mechanism curly-arrow notation are Diploma material, and the transition year is when a student discovers that memorising reactions no longer suffices.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi has a large British-curriculum sector feeding IB Diploma cohorts, so chemistry classes in DP1 often mix students from 0620, 4CH1 and MYP backgrounds. Tutors working with these students spend the first sessions establishing which of the three a student came from, because the missing foundations are different in each case and guessing wastes paid hours.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-chemistry-hl-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Chemistry Higher Level rarely arrives alone. The subjects below are the ones Abu Dhabi families most often pair with it, and the notes say what each one assesses rather than how enjoyable it is.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Two written papers plus the scientific investigation. Paper 1 mixes multiple-choice with a data-based section; Paper 2 carries the extended reasoning. Higher Level adds entropy and Gibbs energy, electrode potentials, pH curves and buffer calculations, and a substantially longer organic mechanism list. Mark loss concentrates in mechanism notation and multi-step quantitative work.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The same themes to a shallower depth, with the same 20 per cent investigation weighting and shorter papers. Students who move down from Higher Level mid-course often carry notation habits that cost them nothing at Standard Level, so the tutoring focus shifts to coverage and calculation accuracy rather than reasoning depth.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Four themes and a heavier recall load than chemistry, assessed through the same paper architecture and the same 20 per cent investigation. Students taking both sciences at Higher Level usually need their revision sequenced rather than doubled, because the two investigations tend to fall in the same weeks.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Shares the chemistry paper structure but tests mathematical modelling far harder. Abu Dhabi students pairing Chemistry and Physics at Higher Level for engineering applications frequently need the same algebra taught twice, in two notations, which is a reason to use one tutor across both where possible.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The route most UAE and overseas engineering and medicine applicants are advised towards. Logarithms, exponentials and rates of change surface directly in chemistry kinetics and pH work, so weakness here shows up as a chemistry problem long before it shows up as a mathematics one.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics-heavy and, at Standard Level, a common pairing with Chemistry Higher Level for students heading to business or health-science routes. Its statistical content is directly useful for processing investigation data, which the chemistry course assumes but does not teach.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: A transdisciplinary subject that can satisfy both the sciences and the individuals-and-societies requirement. Students who drop Chemistry Higher Level mid-DP1 sometimes land here, and the transfer requires catching up on systems thinking rather than more chemistry.

subjects.name: Sports, Exercise and Health Science
subjects.description: Draws on the same biochemistry and energetics that Chemistry Higher Level treats formally. Abu Dhabi schools with strong sports programmes offer it widely, and students taking it alongside chemistry can reuse the energetics work across both syllabuses.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The core course whose exhibition and essay sit in the same DP1 and DP2 weeks as the chemistry investigation. Families who plan paid hours around the chemistry calendar alone are often surprised by how much of a student's writing capacity Theory of Knowledge absorbs in those weeks.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: A 4,000-word independent piece that a Chemistry Higher Level student may choose to write in chemistry. Supervision belongs to the school; a tutor's role is teaching the research skills and giving feedback on the student's own drafts, never supplying content for the submission.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-chemistry-hl-home-tutor.regionsTitle: Where in Abu Dhabi our Chemistry Higher Level students live
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-chemistry-hl-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Delivery is online, so none of these areas is easier or harder to serve than another. What differs is the school-run timetable, which decides when a Chemistry Higher Level session can realistically start on a weekday.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Home to several of the emirate's IB and British Diploma cohorts. School days end late and the bridge back to the island absorbs the rest of the afternoon, so Saadiyat Island chemistry sessions usually sit at 18:00 or later.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Dense apartment living with families spread across several Diploma schools on the mainland. Commutes are short but staggered, so siblings in the same household often need separate slots rather than one shared evening.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: A villa community feeding a cluster of Diploma and British schools nearby. Khalifa City Chemistry Higher Level tuition is most often booked at 17:00, which is early enough to finish before late study and prep.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Mixed apartment and villa communities on the airport corridor. Families here are used to long school-bus runs, and a 90-minute online block on a Saturday morning frequently works better than two weekday evenings.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: A newer residential base with growing Diploma numbers. Weekday traffic off the island at pick-up time is the practical constraint, which is why an online slot at 17:30 is easier to hold than any arrangement requiring travel.

regions.name: Al Bateen

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one with a marked question each time
modes.description: The default for a DP1 or DP2 student whose grade needs to move rather than hold. One 60 or 90-minute session a week, built on a question the student attempts first and the tutor marks live, with the annotated script and a correction note sent afterwards. The weekly rhythm matters more than the length: a student who writes chemistry once a week under correction improves faster than one who is explained to for three hours a month.

This format suits a student whose content coverage is adequate and whose marks are not.

sections.heading: The first session produces a diagnosis, not a lesson plan
paragraphs: A first Chemistry Higher Level session that opens with teaching has skipped the only step that saves money. Before anything is explained, the student attempts a short set of past-paper items under time, and the tutor marks them in front of them. What comes out of that is not a score. It is a split of the marks lost into categories, because the fix for each category is different and the hours needed for each are different.

The categories recur with enough consistency across Abu Dhabi Diploma students to be worth naming. A recall gap is cheap to close and shows improvement within a fortnight. A command-term mismatch, where a student explains what the question asked them to deduce, takes longer because it requires rewriting their own answers against markscheme wording until the habit changes. Mechanism notation errors look severe and are among the fastest to fix. Quantitative slips, by contrast, often turn out to be a mathematics problem wearing a chemistry costume.

This matters for the evidence trail because a diagnosis is a prediction, and a prediction can be checked. If the first session says the dominant loss is command-term mismatch and estimates three to four weeks, then four weeks later you have something specific to test: do the same question types now score, and does the marked script show the correct verb being answered? A tutor who never commits to a diagnosis can never be shown to have been wrong, which is comfortable for the tutor and useless for you.

sections.heading: Reading a marked Chemistry Higher Level script the way a moderator reads it
paragraphs: A school report says a grade. A marked script says why. The difference matters because Chemistry Higher Level marks are awarded against specific wording, and a student can produce chemically correct work that earns nothing because it answered a different command term. When a tutor marks a Paper 2 question on screen, the useful part is not the tick or the cross. It is reading the markscheme line that was available and asking the student to say, in their own words, what they would have had to write to claim it.

Three habits show up repeatedly in Abu Dhabi scripts. The first is answering the chemistry rather than the question: a correct explanation of why a reaction is exothermic, where the question asked the student to deduce a sign from given data. The second is stopping one step short on multi-stage calculations, usually because the final conversion was assumed to be obvious. The third is writing a mechanism that works chemically but notates badly, with arrows starting from an atom rather than a bond or a lone pair.

None of these is a knowledge problem, and that is why the fix is rapid once the student can see it. What makes it visible is the annotated script, kept and compared. A parent who has three marked Paper 2 questions from three consecutive weeks can see for themselves whether the same annotation keeps reappearing. That is a far more reliable signal than a tutor's verbal report, and it is the single artefact worth insisting on from anyone you pay.

sections.heading: Twelve weeks of Chemistry Higher Level, logged
paragraphs: A term of weekly sessions produces twelve records if someone is keeping them. The table below is the shape of that log for a DP2 student who started in the term after a mock, which is the most common entry point for Abu Dhabi families. It is not a syllabus plan. It is a record of what was taught, what the parent received and how the claim was checked, which are three different things that often get collapsed into one cheerful message.

The order is driven by the diagnosis, not by the syllabus sequence. A student whose dominant loss is quantitative starts with energetics and equilibrium calculations even if the class is on organic chemistry, because the point of paid hours is to work on what is costing marks. Content coverage gaps are addressed where they appear, in the weeks where the school has moved on and the student has not.

Two features of the log are deliberate. First, every week names a check, so the following session opens by testing the previous one rather than by asking how things have been going. Second, the log records what was not covered as well as what was, which is how a family avoids paying twice for the same topic when they change tutors or add a second subject later in the year. Twelve weeks is also roughly the length of one Abu Dhabi school term, so the review at the end of the log lands at a point where the school has its own assessment data to compare against, and the two records can be read side by side.

sections.heading: The Higher Level extensions, and which of them do the most damage to a script
paragraphs: Higher Level chemistry is not a separate course from Standard Level. It is the same themes with additional depth folded in, which is why a student who moved up or down a level mid-course can be hard to diagnose. The extensions that generate the most marked-script damage in Abu Dhabi cohorts are consistent enough to plan around: entropy and Gibbs energy, electrode potentials and electrochemical cells, pH curves and buffer calculations, and the extended organic mechanism list with its stereochemistry.

Entropy and Gibbs energy cause trouble because they are the first point in the course where a student must hold a sign convention, a unit conversion and a conceptual argument at once. Marks are lost to arithmetic rather than to chemistry: kilojoules against joules, a temperature left in Celsius, a spontaneity conclusion stated without reference to the calculated value. Electrode potentials fail differently, usually through the direction of the reaction being read backwards from the table.

Buffers and pH curves are where a weak mathematical foundation becomes unavoidable, because logarithms arrive with no warning and the student who has been coping without them stops coping. The organic extension is the opposite case: the content is learnable and the notation is where the marks go, which is why mechanism drills by hand, corrected one arrow at a time, produce visible movement in a fortnight. A tutor who knows which of these four is dominant for your child is worth more than one who covers all four evenly.

sections.heading: The scientific investigation: dated drafts and the line that does not move
paragraphs: The investigation is 20 per cent of the Chemistry Higher Level grade, marked by the school against published criteria and moderated externally on a sample. It is also the part of the course where a paid tutor can most easily cross a line that gets a student into serious difficulty. The safe position is simple and worth stating plainly: a tutor teaches methodology, uncertainty treatment and evaluation structure, reads what the student has written, and responds with questions. The words in the report stay the student's own from the first version to the submitted one.

In practice that means feedback phrased as a question rather than a replacement sentence. Not a rewritten paragraph, but: what does this graph show that your conclusion does not mention? Where did that uncertainty figure come from? If a reader repeated this method from your description alone, what would they get wrong? Each question sends the student back to their own draft, and each returned draft is dated, so the trail of versions shows whose thinking moved.

That trail is also the parent's protection. Finished investigations are sold in this market, and some families are approached with them. The risk is not theoretical: submitting work that is not the student's own is a malpractice matter handled by the IB, and the consequences fall on the candidate rather than on the person who sold it. A dated draft history, visibly getting better in the student's own voice, is the record that makes the question moot. Your school's supervisor remains the authority on scope, approval and submission.

sections.heading: Month two, when the grade stops moving
paragraphs: Grades do not improve in a straight line, and the second month is where most families lose confidence. The pattern is recognisable. Weeks one to four produce visible gains, because the cheapest errors go first: notation tidied, a recall gap closed, arithmetic habits corrected. Weeks five to eight often look flat, because what remains is reasoning depth, and reasoning depth changes slowly and then all at once when a student stops translating questions and starts reading them.

A log makes that period survivable, because it distinguishes a plateau from a failure. In a genuine plateau the category split is still changing even while the total holds: fewer notation marks lost, more marks lost on the long extended-response items that were previously left blank. That is progress inside a static score, and it is visible only if someone recorded the categories in week one. Without the record there is nothing to compare, and the conversation becomes a matter of faith.

A failure looks different. The same annotation keeps appearing on the same question type, the named action from the previous session was not attempted, or the student cannot say what last week's session was about. Those are the signals worth acting on, and acting usually means changing the approach rather than adding hours. More sessions on top of an approach that is not landing is the most common way an Abu Dhabi family spends four thousand dirhams and ends the term where it started.

sections.heading: An in-home Chemistry tutor in Abu Dhabi against online, judged on what each produces
paragraphs: Families searching for a home tutor are asking a reasonable question, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a sales pitch. In-home chemistry tuition in Abu Dhabi is a real market, charging roughly AED 180-350 an hour according to the Bestimate 2026 Dubai and UAE rate survey, with specialist in-home rates reported up to AED 500 where travel is long or the subject is scarce. Part of that price is the travel, and the travel is also what limits who you can hire: your pool is whoever will cross the emirate to reach you at 17:30.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home visits are a service run only in India. Tuition for Abu Dhabi families is delivered one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. That is a genuine trade: you give up a person in the room, and you get a Chemistry Higher Level specialist chosen for the papers your child is losing marks on rather than for their postcode, at a rate that carries no travel.

For this subject the trade tilts further than it would for most, because chemistry at Higher Level is written work. Mechanisms, calculations and extended responses are produced on a shared screen, annotated as they are written, and saved. The evidence trail that this whole page is built on is a by-product of the format. The table below sets out the comparison on the things that actually differ, rather than on atmosphere.

sections.heading: ADEK, your school's reporting cycle, and the meeting to ask for
paragraphs: Private schools in Abu Dhabi are overseen by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes inspection outcomes on its own site. For a parent weighing chemistry support, the inspection report is useful background and a poor diagnostic: it describes a school, not your child's Paper 2. The more useful documents are the ones your school already produces and rarely explains.

Ask the chemistry teacher three questions at the next meeting. Which assessment objectives is my child losing marks against, rather than which grade did they get? Where is the class against the scheme of work, and which topics will be taught after the next mock? And when are the internal investigation deadlines, as opposed to the IB submission date? The answers let a tutor plan around the school rather than across it, which is the difference between support and duplication.

Abu Dhabi has one further rule worth knowing. ADEK's professional-ethics expectations for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and a teacher tutoring outside school hours is required to hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct points the same way. Verify the current wording with the school or on ADEK's own policy pages before acting on it, but the practical implication is clear: paying your child's own chemistry teacher for private sessions is not the shortcut it appears to be.

sections.heading: What we will not claim, and what to ask for instead
paragraphs: This page publishes no success rate, no average grade movement and no satisfaction score. That is deliberate. A figure of that kind is meaningful only with the number of students behind it, the dates it covers and the method used to collect it, and a provider that quotes one without those three things is quoting a marketing number. Several providers in this market publish ratings and improvement percentages that contradict other figures on their own pages, which is worth checking before you treat any of them as evidence.

What can honestly be offered instead is a specific, checkable thing: a diagnosis after the first session, a written record after every session, dated drafts for the investigation, and a comparison of the week-one category split with the week-twelve one. None of that predicts a grade. All of it can be audited by you, which is more than a percentage can.

The same caution applies to credentials. A tutor described as an examiner should be able to evidence current status, and examiner status gives no access to unreleased papers, boundaries or marking decisions. Nobody can promise a 7, and nobody honest will. What a good Chemistry Higher Level tutor can promise is that your child will write chemistry every week under correction, and that you will be able to see what changed. Ask one more question before you pay anyone in this market: what will I receive after each session, and in what form? A provider who cannot answer that in a sentence is unlikely to produce a record worth auditing at week twelve.

process.title: Tell us the script, not the story
process.description: The useful opening message is not that chemistry is going badly. It is the grade on the last mock, the paper it came from and what the teacher said was weak. If you have a marked script, send a photograph of one question. Matching improves sharply when the first conversation starts from evidence rather than from a general worry.

process.title: A free 45-minute diagnostic trial
process.description: The trial is a working session, not a sales call, and no card details are required to book it. The student attempts timed items, the tutor marks them live, and you receive the category split with an estimate in weeks for each category. If the diagnosis does not match what you are seeing at home, say so before any block is booked.

process.title: Fix the slot in Gulf Standard Time
process.description: Sessions are booked at a fixed weekly time in Gulf Standard Time, chosen around the school run rather than around the tutor. Saadiyat and Al Reef families usually land after 18:00; Al Bateen and Khalifa City families often take 16:30 or 17:00. The slot holds through the term so the weekly rhythm is not renegotiated every Sunday.

process.title: Work, marked and recorded
process.description: Each session ends with an annotated script, a short correction note and one named action, sent the same evening. The next session opens by checking that action. Investigation drafts are kept dated. Nothing in the record is a score on its own; the point is that it can be compared with last week and with week one.

process.title: Review at week six and week twelve
process.description: At six weeks the question is whether the dominant error category has shifted, not whether the grade has. At twelve weeks the week-one split is compared with the current one and the plan is either continued, changed or stopped. Stopping is a legitimate outcome, and a tutor who never raises it is not reading the record.

whyPoints.title: A diagnosis you can test
whyPoints.description: The first session commits to a ranked split of where marks are being lost and an estimate in weeks for each category. That is a prediction, which means it can be checked at week six and found wrong. A tutor who avoids committing to one cannot be held to anything.

whyPoints.title: Written work every week, marked live
whyPoints.description: Chemistry Higher Level is assessed on what a student writes under time, so sessions are built around the student writing under correction rather than listening. Explanation is cheap and plentiful; marked practice with the markscheme wording read aloud is the part that moves a Paper 2 score.

whyPoints.title: Specialists chosen by paper, not by postcode
whyPoints.description: Because delivery is online, the pool is Chemistry Higher Level specialists rather than whoever will drive to your area at 17:30. A student losing marks on mechanisms and a student losing them on energetics are matched to different tutors, which is not possible when geography sets the shortlist.

whyPoints.title: An honesty line stated in advance
whyPoints.description: On the investigation and the Extended Essay, feedback arrives as questions about the student's own draft. Dated versions are kept so the progression is visible. This is a real difference in a market where finished coursework is openly sold, and the risk of that falls on the candidate.

whyPoints.title: No invented numbers
whyPoints.description: No success rate, no average improvement, no star rating. AED figures on this page are market bands with their source named, not a fee list. What is offered instead is an auditable record, which is a smaller claim and a checkable one.

whyPoints.title: Continuity that survives a change of tutor
whyPoints.description: The log travels with the student. If a tutor moves on or the subject mix changes, the next person starts from the category split and the coverage record rather than re-diagnosing from scratch, which is where families most often pay twice for the same topic.

faqs.question: What should we have received after a month of Chemistry Higher Level sessions in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Four annotated scripts, four short correction notes naming one action each, and the category split from the first session to compare against. If an investigation is running, you should also have the dated drafts. What you should not have is only a verbal account of how things are going. The point of the paperwork is that it lets you check a claim rather than trust one: if the first session said command terms were the dominant loss and estimated three to four weeks, the fourth script should show the correct command term being answered.

faqs.question: How does a tutor mark a Chemistry Higher Level Paper 2 differently from our school?
faqs.answer: A school marks to produce a grade for a report. A tutor marks to produce a diagnosis, so the output is different. The useful part is not the score but the annotation: which markscheme line was available, what wording would have claimed it, and which of the five error categories this loss belongs to. Marking also happens with the student present and reading the markscheme aloud, which is where the habit changes. Schools have thirty scripts and a deadline; one-to-one marking can afford to spend fifteen minutes on a four-mark question.

faqs.question: Which Chemistry Higher Level topics show up first in a marked script as a problem?
faqs.answer: Energetics and entropy usually surface earliest, because they are the first place a student must manage a sign convention, a unit conversion and a written argument at the same time. Mark loss there is typically arithmetic rather than chemical: kilojoules against joules, a temperature left in Celsius, a spontaneity conclusion stated without reference to the calculated value. Organic mechanism notation appears next, and buffers and pH curves tend to arrive later because they expose a weak logarithm foundation that the student had been managing without.

faqs.question: Our daughter's mechanism answers lose marks even when the product is right. Why?
faqs.answer: Because mechanism marks are awarded for notation, not for the outcome. The common losses are arrows starting from an atom rather than from a bond or a lone pair, missing lone pairs on a nucleophile, absent formal charges on an intermediate, and partial charges omitted where the question asked for them. None of this is a knowledge gap, which is why it is among the fastest categories to fix. Hand-drawn mechanism sets with the arrow origin corrected every time usually produce visible movement inside a fortnight.

faqs.question: How many past papers should a DP2 Chemistry Higher Level student have marked before mocks?
faqs.answer: Fewer than most families imagine, properly marked, beats a stack done unmarked. A reasonable pattern through a term is one timed part-paper a fortnight with full annotation, rising to one full paper a week in the final six weeks. The variable that matters is whether each paper was marked by error category and whether the categories are shrinking. Twenty unmarked papers teach a student their own mistakes more thoroughly; six marked ones with the markscheme wording read aloud change what they write.

faqs.question: Can you show us what changed between two drafts of the chemistry investigation?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the reason the drafts are kept dated. Each version sits alongside the feedback that prompted it, and the feedback is written as questions rather than as replacement text: what does this graph show that your conclusion does not mention, where did that uncertainty figure come from, what would a reader get wrong if they repeated this method from your description. Reading two consecutive versions side by side shows whose thinking moved. The words stay the student's own throughout, and the school supervisor remains the authority on scope and approval.

faqs.question: The school report says satisfactory and the mock says 4. Which record do we believe?
faqs.answer: Neither on its own. A report describes engagement and classwork across a term; a mock measures performance on specific question types under time. They can both be accurate and still disagree. The way to settle it is a marked script, because that shows which assessment objectives are costing marks. In practice a satisfactory report with a mid-band mock usually means a student who understands the chemistry in class and cannot yet produce it to markscheme wording under pressure, which is a technique problem rather than a content one.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a Chemistry tutor to our home in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home visits are a service we run only in India. Chemistry Higher Level tuition for Abu Dhabi families is delivered one-to-one over live video, in Gulf Standard Time slots. The in-home market here is real and charges roughly AED 180-350 an hour according to the Bestimate 2026 rate survey, with more for scarce subjects. What online delivery buys you instead is a specialist chosen for the papers your child is losing marks on, and a written record of each session.

faqs.question: What does a Chemistry Higher Level specialist charge per hour in the Abu Dhabi market?
faqs.answer: Published market bands put qualified online subject tutors at roughly AED 150-300 an hour, IB and A-Level specialists at AED 200-450 and above, and in-home one-to-one at AED 180-350 with scarce subjects reported higher. TutorChase publishes AED 270 for its specialist tier and Unitors quotes IB tuition from AED 200. Those are other providers' figures, cited as market context rather than as our price. Ask for the current quote alongside the free trial, and check what the hour includes: marking, written notes and draft feedback are often billed separately elsewhere.

faqs.question: How long before a logged Chemistry Higher Level grade actually moves?
faqs.answer: Notation and recall categories usually show movement in two to three weeks. Command-term habits take three to four. Reasoning depth on the long extended-response items is the slow one, and it often stays flat through weeks five to eight before changing quickly. That middle period is where families lose confidence, which is why the category split matters more than the total: fewer notation marks lost and more marks attempted on long items is progress inside a static score. Without a week-one record there is nothing to compare, and the conversation becomes guesswork.

faqs.question: Is the chemistry data booklet something our son should be memorising?
faqs.answer: No, but he should be able to navigate it under time. The booklet is provided in the examination, and students lose marks less from not knowing a constant than from hunting for it, or from taking a value from the wrong table. The drill is mechanical and quick: timed searches for specific values before any chemistry is attempted, until the location of each section is automatic. Knowing which quantities are given also changes revision priorities, because effort spent memorising provided data is effort not spent on the reasoning the papers actually reward.

faqs.question: Can lessons shift to post-Iftar slots during Ramadan without losing the weekly record?
faqs.answer: Yes. Abu Dhabi school timetables compress during Ramadan and most families move sessions later in the evening, after Iftar, or to weekend mornings. Because delivery is online there is no travel to reschedule around, so a slot change is a calendar edit rather than a renegotiation. The written record continues unchanged: each session still returns an annotated script, a note and one named action. Families often use the shortened school days for a longer weekend block, which suits investigation work better than a weekday evening does.

faqs.question: Does ADEK publish anything that tells us whether our school's chemistry teaching is sound?
faqs.answer: ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in Abu Dhabi and publishes inspection outcomes, which are useful background about a school as a whole. They will not tell you about one department's Paper 2 results, and no inspection band answers the question you are actually asking. For that, request the assessment-objective breakdown behind your child's grade and ask where the class sits against the scheme of work. Those two answers tell you more about chemistry teaching than any published rating.

faqs.question: What is the tutor allowed to do with the investigation draft, and what is off limits?
faqs.answer: Allowed: teaching methodology, uncertainty treatment and evaluation structure; explaining the published criteria; reading the student's draft and responding with questions; showing worked examples on different data. Off limits: supplying text for the submission, rewriting paragraphs, choosing and processing the data, or anything that makes the report less than the student's own work. Submitting work that is not the candidate's own is a malpractice matter handled by the IB, and the consequence falls on the student. Dated drafts in the student's own voice are what makes the question unanswerable in the first place.

faqs.question: Do you publish an average grade improvement for Chemistry Higher Level students?
faqs.answer: No, and you should be careful with anyone who does. A figure like that means nothing without the number of students it covers, the dates it spans and the method used to collect it, and in this market such numbers frequently contradict other claims on the same page. No tutor can promise a grade, and nobody honest will. What is offered instead is auditable: a ranked diagnosis after the first session, an annotated script every week, dated investigation drafts, and a direct comparison of the week-one error categories with the week-twelve ones.

faqs.question: What happens if no Chemistry Higher Level specialist is free in our slot?
faqs.answer: You are told, rather than matched with the nearest available science graduate. If the slot is the constraint, the usual options are a different weekday evening, a weekend morning block, or a fortnightly 90-minute session with marked work in between. If the subject depth is the constraint, matching may take several days, and for Higher Level organic or electrochemistry work it occasionally takes longer. Where no UAE-based specialist covers the need, a tutor working from India at a Gulf Standard Time slot may be offered, and that is stated plainly before you book.

intro.heading: Chemistry HL is a reasoning subject that students revise as a memory subject
paragraphs: Chemistry at Higher Level is where a large number of Abu Dhabi Diploma students discover that their study method has stopped working. Up to IGCSE, chemistry rewards memory: learn the tests, learn the trends, learn the equations, reproduce them. From the first term of DP1 the subject starts asking why instead of what, and a student whose technique is recall arrives at a question about why one acid is stronger than another with nothing to deploy. The grade drops, the effort goes up, and the two stop being connected.

The current guide makes the reasoning structure explicit, which helps once a student notices it. The course is built from three Structure themes and three Reactivity themes. Structure covers models of the particulate nature of matter, models of bonding and structure, and the classification of matter. Reactivity covers what drives chemical reactions, how much and how fast and how far a reaction goes, and the mechanisms of chemical change. Higher Level content is folded inside those themes rather than sitting in a separate section, and the old core-plus-options arrangement is gone entirely.

That reorganisation has a consequence for anyone revising from older material. Topics have moved, option units are no longer examined, and the two internal assessments of the previous courses have become one scientific investigation worth 20% of the grade. A student working through a second-hand guide is revising a course that no longer exists, and will reach the examination having over-prepared on deleted content and under-prepared on the Higher Level parts of Reactivity, which is where a disproportionate share of the hardest marks live.

The other structural fact worth understanding early is the data booklet. It is supplied in the examinations, with the periodic table, and it contains the constants, the relationships and much of the data a student might expect to have memorised. That changes what the papers test. Recall marks are scarce; selection and reasoning marks are everywhere. A student who has memorised a hundred facts and never practised choosing between two plausible relationships under time pressure is prepared for the wrong examination.

Abu Dhabi supplies the usual constraint. Chemistry HL sets in the emirate's Diploma cohorts are small, and a tutor who teaches the current guide at Higher Level, can handle organic mechanisms properly, and is free at 5pm Gulf Standard Time is a narrow intersection. Searching inside a twenty-minute drive of Khalifa City returns very little. Searching every time zone that teaches the Diploma returns a genuine choice, and the only thing surrendered is physical presence in the room.

So the delivery model, stated plainly as it is on every UAE page here: IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the Emirates. A tutor travelling to a family's address is an India-only service. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video, with a shared whiteboard that suits mechanism arrows well and screen sharing of the student's own calculations. What follows is the content: the six themes and what sits inside the Higher Level parts, the organic mechanism problem, spectroscopy, the energetics and equilibrium cluster, calculation discipline, the investigation, and what the Abu Dhabi market charges.

sections.heading: The six themes, and what sits inside the Higher Level content
paragraphs: The current Chemistry guide is organised into two groups of three. The Structure themes cover models of the particulate nature of matter, which includes the nuclear atom, electron configurations, the mole and ideal gases; models of bonding and structure, which covers the ionic, covalent and metallic models and the step from models to materials; and the classification of matter, which covers the periodic table and the classification of organic compounds by functional group.

The Reactivity themes cover what drives chemical reactions, which includes measuring enthalpy changes, energy cycles, energy from fuels and entropy and spontaneity; how much, how fast and how far, which covers amount of chemical change, rate of reaction and extent of reaction; and the mechanisms of chemical change, which covers proton transfer, electron transfer, electron sharing and electron-pair sharing reactions. Those four mechanism headings are the acid-base, redox, radical and organic chemistry a student will recognise under new names.

Higher Level content sits inside these themes rather than in an appendix, and it concentrates in identifiable places. Energy cycles and entropy and spontaneity are Higher Level work in Reactivity 1. Quantitative treatment of the extent of reaction, including equilibrium constants, is Higher Level in Reactivity 2. The quantitative sides of proton transfer and electron transfer — weak acid and base calculations, buffers, electrode potentials and electrolysis arithmetic — and the mechanisms of the organic reactions are Higher Level in Reactivity 3. Spectroscopic identification and stereoisomerism are Higher Level additions in the Structure themes.

The exact sub-topic list and its Higher Level markings should be confirmed in the current subject guide through the school, because the guide is the authoritative document and this is a summary of it. What does not change is where the difficulty clusters: the Higher Level additions are overwhelmingly quantitative or mechanistic, which means they reward a student who can reason from a model and punish one who has learned a list.

sections.heading: Organic mechanisms: the wall, and how to get over it
paragraphs: Organic chemistry is the topic Abu Dhabi families name most often when they ask for Higher Level chemistry help, and the reason is almost always the same. The student has learned mechanisms as pictures. They can reproduce the nucleophilic substitution they were shown, with the arrows in the places they memorised, and then a question changes the substrate from a primary to a tertiary halogenoalkane and the memorised picture gives the wrong answer. Memory has no way to adapt; reasoning does.

Teaching mechanisms as reasoning means starting from two questions and asking them in order every time. Where is there electron density, and where is there electron deficiency? An arrow starts at a lone pair or a pi bond and ends where a positive or partially positive centre can accept it. Once a student genuinely applies that pair of questions rather than recalling a diagram, nucleophilic substitution, electrophilic addition and the behaviour of carbonyl compounds stop being three memorised items and become three applications of one habit.

The second thing that opens up this content is structure recognition. A great many mechanism errors are not mechanism errors at all; they are failures to notice that a carbon is tertiary, that a leaving group is poor, that a molecule has a chiral centre, or that an aromatic ring changes what is possible. Ten minutes a session spent labelling structures before any arrow is drawn removes a surprising share of the losses, and it is the sort of drill that works well on a shared whiteboard with two people looking at the same molecule.

The third is the examination's own vocabulary. Higher Level questions ask candidates to state the type of reaction, identify the reagent and conditions, draw the mechanism with curly arrows showing the movement of electron pairs, and explain the relative rate of two substrates. Each of those is a separate mark, and students commonly answer two of the four because they read the question as one task. Marking a student's own mechanism answers against the published wording usually finds two recoverable marks per question.
